Aṅguttara Nikāya
## Aṅguttara Nikāya Pāḷi
Burmese Translation
Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.
## The Book of the Tens
## 1. First Fifty
1. The First Fifty
## 1. Chapter on Benefits, 1. Kimatthiya Sutta
1. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of skillful virtues?"

"Ānanda, the purpose of skillful virtues is freedom from remorse (avippaṭisāra), and their benefit is freedom from remorse."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of freedom from remorse?" "Ānanda, the purpose of freedom from remorse is joy (pāmojja), and its benefit is joy."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of joy?" "Ānanda, the purpose of joy is rapture (pīti), and its benefit is rapture."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of rapture?" "Ānanda, the purpose of rapture is tranquillity (passaddhi), and its benefit is tranquillity."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of tranquillity?" "Ānanda, the purpose of tranquillity is happiness (sukha), and its benefit is happiness."
258:
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of happiness?" "Ānanda, the purpose of happiness is concentration (samādhi), and its benefit is concentration."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of concentration?" "Ānanda, the purpose of concentration is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (yathābhūtañāṇadassana), and its benefit is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are?" "Ānanda, the purpose of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is disenchantment (nibbidā) and dispassion (virāga), and its benefit is disenchantment and dispassion."

"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of disenchantment and dispassion?" "Ānanda, the purpose of disenchantment and dispassion is the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana), and its benefit is the knowledge and vision of liberation."

"Thus, Ānanda, skillful virtues lead to freedom from remorse, freedom from remorse leads to joy, joy leads to rapture, rapture leads to tranquillity, tranquillity leads to happiness, happiness leads to concentration, concentration leads to the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are leads to disenchantment and dispassion, and disenchantment and dispassion lead to the knowledge and vision of liberation. In this way, Ānanda, skillful virtues lead step by step to the fruit of arahantship."

The First Sutta.

## 2. Cetanākaraṇีya Sutta
2. "Bhikkhus, for one who is virtuous, for one who has fulfilled virtue, there is no need for an act of will: 'May freedom from remorse arise in me.' It is the nature of things, bhikkhus, that freedom from remorse arises for one who is virtuous, for one who has fulfilled virtue.

Bhikkhus, for one who is free from remorse, there is no need for an act of will: 'May joy arise in me.' It is the nature of things, bhikkhus, that joy arises for one who is free from remorse.

Bhikkhus, for one who is joyful, there is no need for an act of will: 'May rapture arise in me.' It is the nature of things, bhikkhus, that rapture arises for one who is joyful.

Bhikkhus, for one who is rapturous in mind, there is no need for an act of will: 'May my body be tranquil.' It is the nature of things, bhikkhus, that the body becomes tranquil for one who is rapturous in mind.

Bhikkhus, for one whose body is tranquil, there is no need for an act of will: 'I shall feel happiness.'"
259:
Monks, for one whose body is tranquil, it is the nature of things that they feel happiness.

Monks, for one who is happy, there is no need for an act of will: 'May my mind be concentrated.' It is the nature of things, monks, that the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.

Monks, for one who is concentrated, there is no need for an act of will: 'May I know and see things as they really are.' It is the nature of things, monks, that one who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are. Monks, for one who knows and sees things as they really are, there is no need for an act of will: 'May I be disenchanted and dispassionate.' It is the nature of things, monks, that one who knows and sees things as they really are becomes disenchanted and dispassionate. Monks, for one who is disenchanted and dispassionate, there is no need for an act of will: 'May I realize the knowledge and vision of liberation.' It is the nature of things, monks, that one who is disenchanted and dispassionate realizes the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Thus, monks, disenchantment and dispassion have the knowledge and vision of liberation as their purpose and benefit. Knowledge and vision of things as they really are has disenchantment and dispassion as its purpose and benefit. Concentration has knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its purpose and benefit. Happiness has concentration as its purpose and benefit. Tranquility has happiness as its purpose and benefit. Joy has tranquility as its purpose and benefit. Rapture has joy as its purpose and benefit. Non-remorse has rapture as its purpose and benefit. Wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose and benefit. Thus, monks, states flow into states, states fulfill states, for the sake of going from this shore (the suffering of Saṃsāra) to the further shore (Nibbāna).

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Paṭhama Upanisa Sutta

3. Monks, for one who is immoral, whose virtue is deficient, non-remorse lacks its supporting cause. When there is no non-remorse, for one whose non-remorse is deficient, rapture lacks its supporting cause. When there is no rapture, for one whose rapture is deficient, joy lacks its supporting cause. When there is no joy, for one whose joy is deficient, tranquility lacks its supporting cause. When there is no tranquility, for one whose tranquility is deficient, happiness lacks its supporting cause. When there is no happiness, for one whose happiness is deficient, right concentration lacks its supporting cause. When there is no right concentration, for one whose concentration is deficient, knowledge and vision of things as they really are lacks its supporting cause. When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one whose knowledge and vision of things as they really are is deficient, disenchantment and dispassion lack their supporting cause.
260:
When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one whose disenchantment and dispassion are deficient, the knowledge and vision of liberation from defilements lacks its supporting cause.

Monks, just as when a tree is deficient in branches and foliage, its outer bark does not come to fulfillment, its bark... its softwood... its heartwood does not come to fulfillment. In the same way, monks, for one who is immoral, whose virtue is deficient, non-remorse lacks its supporting cause. When there is no non-remorse, for one whose non-remorse is deficient... p... the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its supporting cause. Monks, for one who is virtuous, whose virtue is complete, non-remorse possesses its supporting cause. When there is non-remorse, for one who is complete in non-remorse, rapture possesses its supporting cause. When there is rapture, for one who is complete in rapture, joy possesses its supporting cause. When there is joy, for one who is complete in joy, tranquility possesses its supporting cause. When there is tranquility, for one who is complete in tranquility, happiness possesses its supporting cause. When there is happiness, for one who is complete in happiness, right concentration possesses its supporting cause. When there is right concentration, for one who is complete in right concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they really are possesses its supporting cause. When there is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one who knows and sees things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion possess their supporting cause. When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one who is complete in disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation possesses its supporting cause. Monks, just as when a tree is complete in branches and foliage, its outer bark comes to fulfillment, its bark... its softwood... its heartwood comes to fulfillment. In the same way, monks, for one who is virtuous, whose virtue is complete, non-remorse possesses its supporting cause. When there is non-remorse, for one who is complete in non-remorse, rapture possesses its supporting cause... p... the knowledge and vision of liberation possesses its supporting cause.

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Dutiya Upanisa Sutta

4. Then the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: "Friends, for one who is immoral, whose virtue is deficient, non-remorse lacks its supporting cause. When there is no non-remorse, for one whose non-remorse is deficient, rapture lacks its supporting cause... p... the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its supporting cause. Friends, just as when a tree is deficient in branches and foliage, its outer bark does not come to fulfillment, its bark... its softwood... its heartwood does not come to fulfillment. In the same way, friends, for one who is immoral, whose virtue is deficient, non-remorse lacks its supporting cause. When there is no non-remorse, for one whose non-remorse is deficient, rapture lacks its supporting cause... p... the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its supporting cause."
261:
Friends, for one who is virtuous, for one who is accomplished in virtue, freedom from remorse has its supporting condition. When there is freedom from remorse, for one accomplished in freedom from remorse, gladness has its supporting condition... [p]... liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation have their supporting condition. Friends, just as for a tree that is accomplished in branches and leaves, the outer bark also reaches fulfillment, the inner bark... the sapwood... the heartwood also reaches fulfillment; even so, friends, for one who is virtuous, for one who is accomplished in virtue, freedom from remorse has its supporting condition. When there is freedom from remorse, for one accomplished in freedom from remorse, gladness has its supporting condition... [p]... liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation have their supporting condition. (said he).

Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Third Upanisa Sutta

5. There, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, for one who is immoral, for one whose virtue has failed, freedom from remorse lacks its supporting condition. When there is no freedom from remorse, for one whose freedom from remorse has failed, gladness lacks its supporting condition. When there is no gladness, for one whose gladness has failed, rapture lacks its supporting condition. When there is no rapture, for one whose rapture has failed, tranquility lacks its supporting condition. When there is no tranquility, for one whose tranquility has failed, happiness lacks its supporting condition. When there is no happiness, for one whose happiness has failed, right concentration lacks its supporting condition. When there is no right concentration, for one whose right concentration has failed, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are lacks its supporting condition. When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one whose knowledge and vision of things as they really are has failed, revulsion and dispassion lack their supporting condition. When there is no revulsion and dispassion, for one whose revulsion and dispassion have failed, liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation lack their supporting condition. Friends, just as for a tree whose branches and leaves have failed, the outer bark does not reach fulfillment, the inner bark... the sapwood... the heartwood does not reach fulfillment; even so, friends, for one who is immoral, for one whose virtue has failed, freedom from remorse lacks its supporting condition. When there is no freedom from remorse, for one whose freedom from remorse has failed, gladness lacks its supporting condition... [p]... liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation lack their supporting condition. Friends, for one who is virtuous, for one who is accomplished in virtue, freedom from remorse has its supporting condition. When there is freedom from remorse, for one accomplished in freedom from remorse, gladness has its supporting condition. When there is gladness, for one accomplished in gladness, rapture has its supporting condition. When there is rapture, for one accomplished in rapture, tranquility has its supporting condition. When there is tranquility, for one accomplished in tranquility, happiness has its supporting condition. When there is happiness, for one accomplished in happiness, right concentration has its supporting condition. When there is right concentration, for one accomplished in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are has its supporting condition."
262:
When there is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one accomplished in the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, revulsion and dispassion have their supporting condition. When there is revulsion and dispassion, for one accomplished in revulsion and dispassion, liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation have their supporting condition. Friends, just as for a tree that is accomplished in branches and leaves, the outer bark also reaches fulfillment, the inner bark... the sapwood... the heartwood also reaches fulfillment; even so, friends, for one who is virtuous, for one who is accomplished in virtue, freedom from remorse has its supporting condition. When there is freedom from remorse, for one accomplished in freedom from remorse, gladness has its supporting condition... [p]... liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation have their supporting condition. (said he).

Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Samādhi Sutta

6. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One... [p]... Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, could a bhikkhu obtain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, not be percipient of water in water, not be percipient of fire in fire, not be percipient of air in air, not be percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, not be percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, not be percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, not be percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not be percipient of this world in this world, and not be percipient of the other world in the other world; and yet he would still be percipient?"

"Ānanda, a bhikkhu could obtain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, not be percipient of water in water, not be percipient of fire in fire, not be percipient of air in air, not be percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, not be percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, not be percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, not be percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not be percipient of this world in this world, and not be percipient of the other world in the other world; and yet he would still be percipient." (said the Blessed One).

"But in what way, Venerable Sir, could a bhikkhu obtain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, not be percipient of water in water, not be percipient of fire in fire, not be percipient of air in air, not be percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, not be percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, not be percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness..."
263:
“...nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor would he be perceptive of this world in this world, nor would he be perceptive of the other world in the other world; and yet he would be perceptive. How could such a gain of concentration for a bhikkhu come to be?”

“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is perceptive thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ In this way, Ānanda, there could be such a gain of concentration for a bhikkhu where he would not be perceptive of earth in earth, nor would he be perceptive of water in water, nor would he be perceptive of fire in fire, nor would he be perceptive of air in air, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of infinite space in the sphere of infinite space, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of infinite consciousness in the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of nothingness in the sphere of nothingness, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor would he be perceptive of this world in this world, nor would he be perceptive of the other world in the other world; and yet he would be perceptive.”

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Sāriputta Sutta

7. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. Having concluded the greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Ānanda said to the venerable Sāriputta:

“Friend Sāriputta, could there be such a gain of concentration for a bhikkhu where he would not be perceptive of earth in earth, nor would he be perceptive of water in water, nor would he be perceptive of fire in fire, nor would he be perceptive of air in air, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of infinite space in the sphere of infinite space, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of infinite consciousness in the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of nothingness in the sphere of nothingness, nor would he be perceptive of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor would he be perceptive of this world in this world, nor would he be perceptive of the other world in the other world; and yet he would be perceptive?”
264:
“There could be, friend Ānanda, such a gain of concentration for a bhikkhu where he would not be perceptive of earth in earth... (as before) ...nor would he be perceptive of the other world in the other world; and yet he would be perceptive.”

“But how, friend Sāriputta, could there be such a gain of concentration for a bhikkhu where he would not be perceptive of earth in earth... (as before) ...and yet he would be perceptive?”

“Once, friend Ānanda, I was staying right here in Sāvatthī in the Blind Men’s Grove (Andhavana). There I attained such a concentration that I was not perceptive of earth in earth, nor was I perceptive of water in water, nor was I perceptive of fire in fire, nor was I perceptive of air in air, nor was I perceptive of the sphere of infinite space in the sphere of infinite space, nor was I perceptive of the sphere of infinite consciousness in the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor was I perceptive of the sphere of nothingness in the sphere of nothingness, nor was I perceptive of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor was I perceptive of this world in this world, nor was I perceptive of the other world in the other world; and yet I was perceptive.”

“What kind of perception did the venerable Sāriputta have at that time?”

“Friend, ‘The cessation of existence is Nibbāna, the cessation of existence is Nibbāna’—one perception arose in me and another perception ceased. Just as, friend, when a fire of wood-splinters is burning, one flame arises and another ceases, so too, ‘The cessation of existence is Nibbāna, the cessation of existence is Nibbāna’—one perception arose and another ceased. At that time, friend, I was perceptive that ‘The cessation of existence is Nibbāna.’”

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Jhāna Sutta

8. “Monks, a bhikkhu has faith but is not virtuous. Thus he is incomplete in that factor. He should fulfill that factor, thinking: ‘How can I be both faithful and virtuous?’ Monks, when a bhikkhu has faith and is also virtuous, then he is complete in that factor. Monks, a bhikkhu has faith and is virtuous, but he is not learned... (as before) ...he is learned, but he is not a speaker of the Dhamma.”
265:
He is a Dhamma speaker, but he does not frequent assemblies. He frequents assemblies, but he does not teach the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence. He teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence, but he is not a master of the discipline. He is a master of the discipline, but he is not a forest-dweller in remote lodgings. He is a forest-dweller in remote lodgings, but he is not one who obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, but he does not, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life, realize for himself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and abide in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In such a case, he is incomplete in that factor. He should fulfill that factor, thinking: 'How may I be one who has faith, is virtuous, is learned, is a Dhamma speaker, frequents assemblies, teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence, is a master of the discipline, is a forest-dweller in remote lodgings, obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, and by the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and abide in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom?'

Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has faith, is virtuous, is learned, is a Dhamma speaker, frequents assemblies, teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence, is a master of the discipline, is a forest-dweller in remote lodgings, obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, and by the destruction of the taints, in this very life, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and abide in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; in such a case, he is complete in those factors. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities is inspiring in all aspects and is complete in every way.

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Santavimokkha Sutta

9. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has faith, but is not virtuous. ...pe... He is virtuous, but is not learned. He is learned, but is not a Dhamma speaker. He is a Dhamma speaker, but he does not frequent assemblies.
266:
He frequents assemblies, but he cannot teach the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence. He teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence, but he is not a master of the discipline. He is a master of the discipline, but he is not a forest-dweller in remote lodgings. He is a forest-dweller in remote lodgings, but he does not dwell having touched with his body those peaceful deliverances that are formless, having transcended forms. He dwells having touched with his body those peaceful deliverances, but he does not, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life, realize for himself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and abide in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In such a case, he is incomplete in that factor. He should fulfill that factor, thinking: 'How may I be one who has faith, is virtuous, is learned, is a Dhamma speaker, frequents assemblies, teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence, is a master of the discipline, is a forest-dweller in remote lodgings, dwells having touched with his body those peaceful deliverances that are formless, having transcended forms, and by the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and abide in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom?'

Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has faith, is virtuous, is learned, is a Dhamma speaker, frequents assemblies, teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence, is a master of the discipline, is a forest-dweller in remote lodgings, dwells having touched with his body those peaceful deliverances that are formless, having transcended forms, and by the destruction of the taints, in this very life, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and abide in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; in such a case, he is complete in those factors. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities is inspiring in all aspects and is complete in every way.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Vijjā Sutta

10. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has faith, but is not virtuous. In such a case, he is incomplete in that factor. He should fulfill that factor, thinking: 'How may I be one who has faith and is virtuous?' Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has faith and is virtuous, then he is complete in that factor.

Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has faith and is virtuous, but is not learned. He is learned, but is not a Dhamma speaker. ...pe... He is a Dhamma speaker, but he does not frequent assemblies. He frequents assemblies, but he cannot teach the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence.
267:
He can teach the Dhamma confidently in the assembly, but he is not an expert in the Vinaya. He is an expert in the Vinaya, but he does not recollect his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... and so on; thus he does not recollect his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. He can recollect his manifold past lives... but he does not, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, understand beings passing away and rearising according to their kamma. He understands beings passing away and rearising according to their kamma with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... but he does not, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, dwell therein. In such a case, that monk is incomplete in that factor.

Therefore, he should fulfill that factor, thinking: 'How may I become one who has faith, who is virtuous, who is learned, who is a speaker of Dhamma, who frequents assemblies, who teaches the Dhamma confidently in the assembly, who is an expert in the Vinaya, who recollects manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... and so on; thus recollecting manifold past lives with their aspects and details, who understands beings passing away and rearising according to their kamma with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... and who, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, dwells therein?'

Monks, when a monk has faith, is virtuous, is learned, is a speaker of Dhamma, frequents assemblies, teaches the Dhamma confidently in the assembly, is an expert in the Vinaya, recollects manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... and so on; thus recollecting manifold past lives with their aspects and details, understands beings passing away and rearising according to their kamma with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... and through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, dwells therein; then he is complete in that factor. Monks, a monk endowed with these ten qualities is one who is inspiring in all respects and is complete in every way."

The tenth sutta is finished.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Benefits (Ānisaṃsavagga), is finished.

The summary of the chapter:
Purpose, Volition, and the three on Proximate Causes,
Concentration, Sāriputta, Jhāna, Peace, and Knowledge.
268:
The tenth sutta.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Benefits, is finished.

## 2. Nāthavagga
## 1. Senāsanasutta

11. "Monks, a monk endowed with five factors, while using and frequenting a lodging endowed with five factors, would before long, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, dwell therein.

And how, monks, is a monk endowed with five factors? Here, monks, a monk (1) has faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'The Blessed One is an Arahant... the Blessed One.' (2) He is free from illness and affliction, possessing a digestive fire that is even, neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and suitable for striving. (3) He is not deceitful or hypocritical; he reveals himself as he really is to the Teacher or to the wise companions in the holy life. (4) He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, not casting off the duty of cultivating wholesome states. (5) He is wise; he possesses wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. In this way, monks, a monk is endowed with five factors.

And how, monks, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, monks, (1) the lodging is neither too far nor too near, and has a good path for coming and going. (2) By day it is not crowded, and by night it is quiet and free from noise. (3) There is little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. (4) For one dwelling in that lodging, robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick are obtained without difficulty. (5) In that lodging, there dwell elder monks who are learned, masters of the scriptures, experts in the Dhamma, experts in the Vinaya, and experts in the Matika (summaries); from time to time, he approaches them and asks: 'How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerable ones then reveal to him what is hidden, clarify what is obscure, and dispel his doubts on various points of doubt. In this way, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors.

Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors, while using and frequenting a lodging endowed with these five factors, would before long, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, dwell therein."
269:
First Sutta.

## 2. Pañcaṅgasutta

12. "Monks, a bhikkhu who has abandoned five factors and is possessed of five factors is called in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'one who is consummate, who has lived the life, a superior man.' And how, monks, has a bhikkhu abandoned five factors? Here, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire (kāmacchanda), has abandoned ill will (byāpāda), has abandoned sloth and torpor (thinamiddha), has abandoned restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), and has abandoned doubt (vicikicchā). In this way, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors.

"And how, monks, is a bhikkhu possessed of five factors? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is possessed of the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha), the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, the aggregate of liberation (arahantship) of one beyond training, and the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation (reviewing knowledge) of one beyond training. In this way, monks, a bhikkhu is possessed of five factors.

"Monks, a bhikkhu who has abandoned five factors and is possessed of five factors is called in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'one who is consummate, who has lived the life, a superior man.'

"Sensual desire and ill will, sloth and torpor in a bhikkhu,
Restlessness and doubt are completely absent.

"Possessed of the virtue of one beyond training, and the concentration of one beyond training,
Endowed with liberation and likewise with knowledge.

"He is indeed possessed of the five factors, having abandoned the five factors,
In this Dhamma-Vinaya, he is called one who is consummate."

Second Sutta.

## 3. Saṃyojanasutta

13. "Monks, there are these ten fetters. Which ten? The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. And what are the five lower fetters?"
270:
"Identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), which is the wrong view regarding the five aggregates that truly exist in the ultimate sense; doubt (vicikicchā); misapprehension of precepts and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa), which is the wrong grasp of practices such as the bovine or canine duty as the path to purification from defilements; sensual desire (kāmacchanda); and ill will (byāpāda). These are the five lower fetters.

"And what are the five higher fetters? Lust for the realm of form (rūparāga), lust for the formless realm (arūparāga), conceit (māna), restlessness (uddhacca), and ignorance (avijjā). These are the five higher fetters. Monks, these are the ten fetters."

Third Sutta.

## 4. Cetokhilasutta

14. "Monks, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who has not abandoned the five mental barrennesses and has not cut through the five mental shackles, whatever night or day comes, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.

"And what are the five mental barrennesses that he has not abandoned? Here, monks, a bhikkhu doubts the Teacher, is perplexed, is not convinced, and is not satisfied. Monks, when a bhikkhu doubts the Teacher, is perplexed, is not convinced, and is not satisfied, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and exertion. When his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and exertion, this is the first mental barrenness that he has not abandoned. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu doubts the Dhamma... [as above] ...doubts the Saṅgha... [as above] ...doubts the training (sikkhā)... When his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and exertion, this is the fifth mental barrenness that he has not abandoned. These are the five mental barrennesses he has not abandoned.

"And what are the five mental shackles that he has not cut through? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is not free from lust (rāga) for sensual pleasures, not free from desire (chanda), not free from affection (pema), not free from thirst (pipāsa), not free from fever (pariḷāha), and not free from craving (taṇhā). Having eaten as much as his stomach can hold, he lives indulging in the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of sleep. For a monk whose mind does not incline toward ardor, exertion, perseverance, and striving, this fifth mental shackle has not been cut. These five mental shackles have not been cut for him. Bhikkhus, for any monk or nun for whom these five mental spikes have not been abandoned and these five mental shackles have not been cut, whether by night or by day, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.

Just as, bhikkhus, in the dark fortnight, whether by night or by day, the moon wanes in appearance, wanes in its orb, wanes in brightness, and wanes in its diameter and circumference; even so, bhikkhus, for any monk or nun for whom these five mental spikes have not been abandoned and these five mental shackles have not been cut, whether by night or by day, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.

Which five mental shackles have been well cut for that person? The Fourth Sutta.

## 5 - Appamāda Sutta

15. Monks, as far as there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared the foremost among them. Even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness (appamāda), and converge in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among those wholesome states.

Monks, just as the footprints of all animals that walk on the earth are encompassed in the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant's footprint is declared the foremost among them because of its great size; even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness, and converge in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among those states.

Monks, just as all the rafters of a gabled house lead to the roof peak, slope toward the roof peak, and converge at the roof peak, and the roof peak is declared the foremost among them; even so, monks...
274:
...even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness, and converge in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among those states.

Monks, just as among all root fragrances, black sandalwood is declared the foremost; even so, monks... [as above].

Monks, just as among all heartwood fragrances, red sandalwood is declared the foremost; even so, monks... [as above].

Monks, just as among all flower fragrances, jasmine is declared the foremost; even so, monks... [as above].

Monks, just as all petty kings are followers of a Wheel-turning Monarch, and the Wheel-turning Monarch is declared the foremost among them; even so, monks... [as above].

Monks, just as the radiance of all the stars does not equal a sixteenth part of the radiance of the moon, and the moonlight is declared the foremost among them; even so, monks... [as above].

Monks, just as in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and the clouds have vanished, the sun, ascending into the sky, dispels all darkness from space and shines, blazes, and radiates; even so, monks... [as above].

Monks, just as all the great rivers—namely, the Ganges, the Yamuna, the Aciravati, the Sarabhu, and the Mahi—flow, slope, incline, and lead toward the ocean, and the great ocean is declared the foremost among them; even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness, and converge in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among those states.

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6 - Āhuneyya Sutta

16. Monks, these ten persons are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Which ten?

The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; a Paccekabuddha; one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta); one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta); a body-witness (kāyasakkhī); one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta); one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta); a faith-follower (saddhānusārī); a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī); and a gotrabhū.

Monks, these ten persons are worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7 - Pathama Nātha Sutta
17. Monks, live with a protector, not without a protector. Monks, one who lives without a protector lives in suffering. Monks, there are these ten qualities that make for a protector. What are the ten? Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk is virtuous; he lives restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, is possessed of proper conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), sees danger in even slight faults, and trains himself by undertaking the rules of training. Monks, that a monk is virtuous... ...and trains himself by undertaking the rules of training; this quality also makes for a protector. (1)

Furthermore, monks, a monk is one of great learning, a retainer of what he has heard, a storehouse of learning. Those teachings which are beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end, which with meaning and phrasing proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings have been much learned by him, retained, recited, pondered in the mind, and well-penetrated by wisdom. Monks, that a monk is of great learning... ...and well-penetrated by wisdom; this quality also makes for a protector. (2)

Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and inclines toward good friends. Monks, that a monk has good friends, good companions, and inclines toward good friends; this quality also makes for a protector. (3)

Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to speak to, possessed of qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, and respectful in receiving instruction. Monks, that a monk is easy to speak to... ...and respectful in receiving instruction; this quality also makes for a protector. (4)

Furthermore, monks, a monk is skillful and diligent in the various duties, whether large or small, to be done for his fellow monks, saying 'what should be done?'; he is possessed of investigative wisdom regarding the means for those various tasks, capable of doing them and capable of organizing them. Monks, that a monk is... ...capable of doing them and capable of organizing them; this quality also makes for a protector. (5)

Furthermore, monks, a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, pleasant in speech, and feels great delight in the sublime Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya. Monks, that a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, pleasant in speech...
276:
...and feels great delight in the sublime Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya; this quality also makes for a protector. (6)

Furthermore, monks, a monk lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states; he is possessed of strength and firm effort, and does not shirk his responsibility regarding wholesome states. Monks, that a monk lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states, is possessed of strength and firm effort, and does not shirk his responsibility regarding wholesome states; this quality also makes for a protector. (7)

Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick he receives. Monks, that a monk is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick he receives; this quality also makes for a protector. (8)

Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, possessed of supreme and mature mindfulness, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago. Monks, that a monk is mindful, possessed of supreme and mature mindfulness, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago; this quality also makes for a protector. (9)

Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise, possessed of noble and penetrative wisdom that sees the arising and passing away and leads well to Nibbāna, the end of suffering. Monks, that a monk is wise, possessed of noble and penetrative wisdom that sees the arising and passing away and leads well to Nibbāna, the end of suffering; this quality also makes for a protector. (10)

Monks, live with a protector, not without a protector. Monks, one who lives without a protector lives in suffering. Monks, these are the ten qualities that make for a protector. (Thus He spoke.)

Seventh Sutta.
## 8 - Dutiya Nātha Sutta
18. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks." "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
277:
"Monks, live with a protector, not without a protector. Monks, one who lives without a protector lives in suffering. Monks, there are these ten qualities that make for a protector. What are the ten?

Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [etc.] ...he undertakes and trains in the training rules. 'This bhikkhu is indeed virtuous; he lives restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; he undertakes and trains in the training rules.' Senior bhikkhus think that such a bhikkhu should be spoken to and exhorted; middle-ranking bhikkhus... and newly ordained bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and exhorted. For one who is thus pitied by the senior, middle-ranking, and newly ordained bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a protector. (1)

Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is one of great learning... [etc.] ...well-penetrated by wisdom. For one who is thus pitied by the senior, middle-ranking, and newly ordained bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a protector. (2)

Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates. 'This bhikkhu indeed has good friends, good companions, and good associates.' Senior bhikkhus think that such a bhikkhu should be spoken to and exhorted; middle-ranking bhikkhus... and newly ordained bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and exhorted. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is easy to admonish, possessed of qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, and he accepts instruction respectfully. 'This bhikkhu is indeed easy to admonish, possessed of qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, and he accepts instruction respectfully.' For one who is thus pitied by the senior, middle-ranking, and newly ordained bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected,"

For one who is thus pitied by the senior, middle-ranking, and newly ordained bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a protector. (5)

Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is a lover of the Dhamma, pleasant in speech, and feels great joy in the excellent Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya. Senior bhikkhus think that such a bhikkhu should be spoken to and exhorted; middle-ranking bhikkhus... and newly ordained bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and exhorted. For one who is thus pitied by the senior, middle-ranking,"
279:
For that bhikkhu who is pitied by the junior monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a refuge. (8)

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and discretion, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago. "This bhikkhu is indeed mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and discretion, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago"—thinking thus, the elder bhikkhus consider that he should be spoken to and exhorted; the middle-standing bhikkhus... the junior bhikkhus also consider that he should be spoken to and exhorted. For that bhikkhu who is pitied by the elders, pitied by the middle-standing, and pitied by the juniors, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. "This bhikkhu is indeed wise, possessing wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering"—thinking thus, the elder bhikkhus consider that he should be spoken to and exhorted; the middle-standing bhikkhus... the junior bhikkhus also consider that he should be spoken to and exhorted. For that bhikkhu who is pitied by the elders, pitied by the middle-standing, and pitied by the juniors, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. Bhikkhus, live with a refuge, not without a refuge. Bhikkhus, one who lives without a refuge lives in suffering. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities that make for a refuge. This is what the Blessed One said. Those bhikkhus were delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9 - Paṭhama Ariyāvāsa Sutta

19. Bhikkhus, there are these ten abodes of the Noble Ones, which the Noble Ones have dwelt in, are dwelling in, or will dwell in. What ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, possesses six factors, has one guard, has four supports, has dispelled individual truths, has completely abandoned all searches, has unclouded intentions, has calmed bodily formations, is well-liberated in mind, and is well-liberated in wisdom. Bhikkhus, these are the ten
280:
abodes of the Noble Ones, which the Noble Ones have dwelt in, are dwelling in, or will dwell in.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10 - Dutiya Ariyāvāsa Sutta

20. On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus... [as before]... Bhikkhus, there are these ten abodes of the Noble Ones, which the Noble Ones have dwelt in, are dwelling in, or will dwell in.

What ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, possesses six factors, has one guard, has four supports, has dispelled individual truths, has completely abandoned all searches, has unclouded intentions, has calmed bodily formations, is well-liberated in mind, and is well-liberated in wisdom.

And how, bhikkhus, has a bhikkhu abandoned five factors? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, has abandoned ill will, has abandoned sloth and torpor, has abandoned restlessness and remorse, and has abandoned doubt. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors. (1)

And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu possess six factors? Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither elated nor depressed, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear... Having smelled an odor with the nose... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having felt a tactile object with the body... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither elated nor depressed, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses six factors. (2)

And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu have one guard? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of a mind guarded by mindfulness. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has one guard. (3)

And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu have four supports? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having reflected, uses some things; having reflected, endures some things;
281:
Having reflected, he avoids some; having reflected, he dispels others. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has four supports. (4)

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has abandoned individual truths? Here, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, those many individual truths of many recluses and brahmins—such as: 'The world is eternal,' or 'The world is not eternal,' or 'The world is finite,' or 'The world is infinite,' or 'The soul and the body are the same,' or 'The soul is one thing and the body is another,' or 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' or 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' or 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'—all these have been removed, abandoned, relinquished, vomited up, released, given up, and renounced. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has abandoned individual truths. (5)

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has completely relinquished all searches? Here, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, the search for sensual pleasures has been abandoned, the search for existence has been abandoned, and the search for a holy life has been stilled. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has completely relinquished all searches. (6)

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one of unclouded thoughts? Here, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, the thought of sensual pleasure has been abandoned, the thought of ill will has been abandoned, and the thought of harming has been abandoned. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one of unclouded thoughts. (7)

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has calmed bodily formations? Here, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has calmed bodily formations. (8)

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one of well-liberated mind? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from lust, his mind is liberated from hatred, and his mind is liberated from delusion. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one of well-liberated mind. (9)

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one of well-liberated wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands: 'Lust has been abandoned by me,
282:
cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no longer subject to future arising.' He understands: 'Hatred has been abandoned by me... [etc.] ...Delusion has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no longer subject to future arising.' In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one of well-liberated wisdom. (10)

Bhikkhus, whatever noble ones in the past dwelt in the noble abodes, they all dwelt in these same ten noble abodes. Bhikkhus, whatever noble ones in the future will dwell in the noble abodes, they all will dwell in these same ten noble abodes. Bhikkhus, whatever noble ones at present dwell in the noble abodes, they all dwell in these same ten noble abodes. These, bhikkhus, are the ten noble abodes in which the noble ones have dwelt, are dwelling, or will dwell.

Tenth Discourse.
The second chapter, the Nātha Vagga, is finished.

## 3 - Mahā Vagga
## 1 - Sīhanāda Sutta

21. Bhikkhus, the lion, the king of beasts, comes out from his lair in the evening. Having come out from his lair, he stretches himself. Having stretched himself, he looks around in the four directions. Having looked around in the four directions, he roars the lion’s roar three times. Having roared the lion’s roar three times, he sets out in search of food. Why is that? So that, (he thinks,) 'May I not cause the death of small creatures that have gone astray in unsuitable places.'

Bhikkhus, 'lion' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Bhikkhus, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma in an assembly, this is his lion’s roar. Bhikkhus, these are the ten powers of the Tathāgata:
283: The Blessed One, being endowed with these powers, claims the supreme place (Buddhahood), roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. What are the ten? Here, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. That the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible is also a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the supreme place, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (1) Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the result of kamma undertaken, past, future, and present, by way of its possibilities and causes. That the Tathāgata understands as it really is the result of kamma undertaken, past, future, and present, by way of its possibilities and causes is also a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the supreme place, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (2) Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the practice leading to all destinations (the five destinations and Nibbāna). That the Tathāgata understands as it really is the practice leading to all destinations is also a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the supreme place, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (3) Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the world with its many and various elements. That the Tathāgata understands as it really is the world with its many and various elements is also a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the supreme place, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (4) Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the various dispositions of beings. That the Tathāgata understands as it really is the various dispositions of beings is also a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which... [Pe]... sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (5) Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the state of the faculties, whether dull or sharp, of other beings and individuals. That the Tathāgata understands as it really is the state of the faculties, whether dull or sharp, of other beings and individuals is also a power of the Tathāgata.
284: ...[Pe]... sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (6) Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence regarding the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. That the Tathāgata understands... [Pe]... is also a power of the Tathāgata... [Pe]... sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (7) Furthermore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘In that birth, I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the limit of my life; passing away from there, I reappeared in such a birth; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the limit of my life; passing away from there, I reappeared here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. That the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives... [Pe]... is also a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the supreme place, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma. (8) Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and reappearing—base and precious, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘Friends, these beings were endowed with bad conduct of body (kāya-duccarita), bad conduct of speech (vacī-duccarita), and bad conduct of mind (mano-duccarita), who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views; with the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell. But these beings were endowed with good conduct of body (kāya-sucarita), good conduct of speech (vacī-sucarita), and good conduct of mind (mano-sucarita)...’
285:
...they do not revile the Noble Ones, they hold right views, and they undertake actions based on right views. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. Monks, that the Tathāgata, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans... understands how beings fare according to their kamma, this is a power of the Tathāgata, by which he claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion. (9)

Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. Monks, that the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, can dwell therein, this is also a power of the Tathāgata, by which he claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion. (10)

Monks, these are the ten powers of the Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion.

The First Sutta.

## 2 - Adhivuttipada Sutta

22. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him: "Ānanda, regarding those qualities (the knowledge of the ten powers and omniscience) that lead to the direct knowledge and realization of those various expressions (adhivuttipada) of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements—Ānanda, I claim to be confident therein. I can teach the Dhamma to those beings in such a way that one who practices accordingly will know what is present as 'present,' what is absent as 'absent,' and what is inferior as 'inferior'...
286:
...will know the noble as 'noble,' the surpassed as 'surpassed,' and the unsurpassed as 'unsurpassed.' That one will know, see, and realize those things that ought to be known, seen, and realized—this is possible. Ānanda, among knowledges, this knowledge of things as they really are (omniscience) in each instance is supreme. Ānanda, I say there is no other knowledge higher or more excellent than this omniscience.

Ānanda, there are these ten powers of the Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion. What are the ten? Here, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. Ānanda, that the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible, this is a power of the Tathāgata, by which he claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion. (1)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the results of kamma undertaken—past, future, and present—by way of their possibilities and causes. Ānanda... [as above]... (2)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the way leading to all destinations (the five realms and Nibbāna). ... Ānanda... [as above]... (3)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the world with its many and various elements. ... Ānanda... [as above]... (4)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the various dispositions of beings. ... Ānanda... [as above]... (5)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the state of the faculties (superior or inferior) of other beings and individuals. ... Ānanda... [as above]... (6)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the defilement, cleansing, and emergence regarding the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. ... Ānanda... [as above]... (7)
287:
“Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [and so on]... Thus, he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. Ānanda... [and so on]... This also... [and so on]. (8)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), purified and surpassing that of humans... understands beings according to their kamma. Ānanda... [and so on]... This also... [and so on]. (9)

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints (āsavas), realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind (cetovimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti), and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. Ānanda, that the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself... and dwells therein, this is a power of the Tathāgata. By virtue of this power, the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma (brahmacakka). (10)

Ānanda, these are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma.”

The Second Sutta.

## 3 - Kāyasutta

23. “Monks, there are things to be abandoned by the body, not by speech. Monks, there are things to be abandoned by speech, not by body. Monks, there are things to be abandoned neither by the body nor by speech, but having seen with wisdom, they are to be abandoned.

And what, monks, are the things to be abandoned by the body, not by speech? Here, monks, a monk has committed some kind of unwholesome act (offense) by the body. Wise fellow practitioners, having investigated, say to him: ‘Venerable, you have committed some kind of unwholesome act by the body. It would be good if the venerable would abandon bodily misconduct and develop bodily good conduct.’

Being spoken to by wise fellow practitioners after their investigation, he abandons bodily misconduct and develops bodily good conduct. These, monks, are called things to be abandoned by the body, not by speech.”
288: "And what, monks, are the things to be abandoned by speech, not by the body? Here, monks, a monk has fallen into some unwholesome state (offense) by speech. Wise companions in the holy life, having investigated, say to him: 'Venerable sir, you have fallen into some unwholesome state by speech. It would be good if the venerable one would abandon verbal misconduct and develop verbal good conduct.' Being spoken to by wise companions in the holy life who have investigated, he abandons verbal misconduct and develops verbal good conduct. These, monks, are called things to be abandoned by speech, not by the body. And what, monks, are the things to be abandoned neither by the body nor by speech, but having seen them with wisdom, they are to be abandoned? Monks, greed (lobha) is to be abandoned neither by the body nor by speech, but having seen it with wisdom, it is to be abandoned. Monks, hatred (dosa)... [pe]... delusion (moha), anger (kodha), resentment (upanāha), contempt (makkha), insolence (paḷāsa), and stinginess (macchariya) are to be abandoned neither by the body nor by speech, but having seen them with wisdom, they are to be abandoned. Monks, evil envy (pāpikā issā) is to be abandoned neither by the body nor by speech, but having seen it with wisdom, it is to be abandoned. And what, monks, is evil envy? Here, monks, a householder or a householder's son prospers in wealth, grain, silver, or gold. Then some slave or dependent thinks: 'Oh, would that this householder or householder's son not prosper in wealth, grain, silver, or gold.' Or a recluse or a brahmin receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. Then some other recluse or brahmin thinks: 'Oh, would that this venerable one not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites.' This, monks, is called evil envy. Monks, evil desire (pāpikā icchā) is to be abandoned neither by the body nor by speech, but having seen it with wisdom, it is to be abandoned. And what, monks, is evil desire? Here, monks, someone who is faithless desires, 'May they know me as one who has faith.' Someone who is immoral desires, 'May they know me as one who is virtuous.' Someone who has little learning desires, 'May they know me as one who is learned.' Someone who delights in company desires, 'May they know me as one who is secluded.' Someone who is lazy desires, 'May they know me as one who is energetic.' Someone who is muddle-minded desires, 'May they know me as one who is mindful'..."
289:
Being unmindful, he wishes, 'May they know me as one who is mindful.' Being unconcentrated, he wishes, 'May they know me as one who is concentrated.' Being unwise, he wishes, 'May they know me as one who is wise.' Being one whose taints are not destroyed, he wishes, 'May they know me as one whose taints are destroyed.' Monks, this is called an evil wish. Monks, these things are said to be not abandoned by the body, nor abandoned by speech, but abandoned by seeing with wisdom.

Monks, if greed overcomes and persists in that monk, if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... if evil wish overcomes and persists, he should be known thus: 'This venerable one does not understand in such a way that greed does not occur to one who understands; for greed overcomes and persists in this venerable one. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, stinginess, evil envy, and evil wish do not occur; for evil wish overcomes and persists in this venerable one.'

Monks, if greed does not overcome and persist in that monk, if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... if evil wish does not overcome and persist, he should be known thus: 'This venerable one understands in such a way that greed does not occur to one who understands; for greed does not overcome and persist in this venerable one. This venerable one understands in such a way that hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, stinginess, evil envy, and evil wish do not occur; for evil wish does not overcome and persist in this venerable one.'

The Third Discourse.

## 4. Mahācunda Sutta

24. At one time, the venerable Mahācunda was staying among the Cetis at Sahajāti. There, the venerable Mahācunda addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Friend,' those monks replied to the venerable Mahācunda. The venerable Mahācunda said this:

'Friends, a monk speaking a claim to knowledge (ñāṇavāda) says: "I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma." Friends, if greed overcomes and persists in that monk, if hatred... delusion...'
290:
...anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, stinginess, evil envy, if evil wish overcomes and persists, he should be known thus: 'This venerable one does not understand in such a way that greed does not occur to one who understands; for greed overcomes and persists in this venerable one. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, stinginess, evil envy, and evil wish do not occur; for evil wish overcomes and persists in this venerable one.'

Friends, a monk speaking a claim to development (bhāvanāvāda) says: 'I am one who has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind (concentration), developed wisdom.' Friends, if greed overcomes and persists in that monk, if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... if evil wish overcomes and persists, he should be known thus: 'This venerable one does not understand in such a way that greed does not occur to one who understands; for greed overcomes and persists in this venerable one. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, stinginess, evil envy, and evil wish do not occur; for evil wish overcomes and persists in this venerable one.'

Friends, a monk speaking both a claim to knowledge and a claim to development says: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma, I am one who has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind (concentration), developed wisdom.' Friends, if greed overcomes and persists in that monk, if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... if evil wish overcomes and persists, he should be known thus: 'This venerable one does not understand in such a way that greed does not occur to one who understands; for greed overcomes and persists in this venerable one. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, stinginess, evil envy, and evil wish do not occur; for evil wish overcomes and persists in this venerable one.'
291:
Friends, suppose a man, being poor, were to claim to be wealthy; being without property, were to claim to have property; being without possessions, were to claim to have possessions. When some business requiring wealth arises, he would not be able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold. People would know of him: 'This venerable one, being poor, claims to be wealthy; being without property, claims to have property; being without possessions, claims to have possessions. Why is that? Because when some business requiring wealth arises, this venerable one is unable to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold.'

In the same way, friends, a monk making a claim to knowledge (ñāṇavāda) and a claim to development (bhāvanāvāda) says: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; I have developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind (concentration), and developed wisdom.' Friends, if greed remains overcoming that monk; if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire remains overcoming him, then it should be understood of him: 'This venerable one does not know in such a way that greed does not occur to one who knows; for greed remains overcoming this venerable one. This venerable one does not know in such a way that hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not occur; for evil desire remains overcoming this venerable one.'

Friends, a monk making a claim to knowledge says: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma.' Friends, if greed does not remain overcoming that monk; if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not remain overcoming him, then it should be understood of him: 'This venerable one knows in such a way that greed does not occur to one who knows; for greed does not remain overcoming this venerable one. This venerable one knows in such a way that hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not occur; for evil desire does not remain overcoming this venerable one.'

Friends, a monk making a claim to development says: 'I have developed the body...
292:
...developed virtue, developed the mind (concentration), and developed wisdom.' Friends, if greed does not remain overcoming that monk; if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not remain overcoming him, then it should be understood of him: 'This venerable one knows in such a way that greed does not occur to one who knows; for greed does not remain overcoming this venerable one. This venerable one knows in such a way that hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not occur; for evil desire does not remain overcoming this venerable one.'

Friends, a monk making a claim to knowledge and a claim to development says: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; I have developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind (concentration), and developed wisdom.' Friends, if greed does not remain overcoming that monk; if hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not remain overcoming him, then it should be understood of him: 'This venerable one knows in such a way that greed does not occur to one who knows; for greed does not remain overcoming this venerable one. This venerable one knows in such a way that hatred... delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not occur; for evil desire does not remain overcoming this venerable one.'

Friends, suppose a man, being truly wealthy, were to claim to be wealthy; being one with property, were to claim to have property; being one with possessions, were to claim to have possessions. When some business requiring wealth arises, he would be able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold. People would know of him: 'This venerable one, being wealthy, claims to be wealthy; being one with property, claims to have property; being one with possessions, claims to have possessions. Why is that? Because when some business requiring wealth arises, this venerable one is able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold.'
293:
In the same way, friends, a bhikkhu who speaks of the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of development says: 'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; I have developed the body, I have developed virtue, I have developed the mind (concentration), I have developed wisdom.' Friends, if greed does not overwhelm and remain in that bhikkhu, nor hatred, nor delusion, nor anger, nor hostility, nor disparaging, nor domineering, nor stinginess, nor evil envy, nor evil desire; then he should be known thus: 'This venerable one understands in such a way that while he understands, greed does not arise; for greed does not overwhelm and remain in this venerable one. This venerable one understands in such a way that while he understands, hatred... delusion... anger... hostility... disparaging... domineering... stinginess... evil envy... evil desire does not arise; for evil desire does not overwhelm and remain in this venerable one.'

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5 - Kasiṇa Sutta

25. Monks, there are these ten kasiṇa bases. Which ten? One perceives the earth kasiṇa—above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. One perceives the water kasiṇa... (pe)... One perceives the fire kasiṇa... One perceives the air kasiṇa... One perceives the blue kasiṇa... One perceives the yellow kasiṇa... One perceives the red kasiṇa... One perceives the white kasiṇa... One perceives the space kasiṇa... One perceives the consciousness kasiṇa (the first formless state)—above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. Monks, these are the ten kasiṇa bases.

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6 - Kāḷī Sutta

26. On one occasion, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the Avanti country on Pavatta Mountain at Kuraraghara.
