Then Kāḷī the lay follower of Kuraraghara approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: "Venerable sir, this was said by the Blessed One in the Questions of the Maidens: 'Having attained the goal and the peace of heart, having conquered the army of pleasant and agreeable forms, alone, meditating, I have realized bliss;
294:
Therefore, I do not make friends with people; I do not become a friend with anyone.' Venerable sir, how should the meaning of this brief statement by the Blessed One be understood in detail?"

"Sister, some ascetics and brahmins, considering the attainment of the earth kasiṇa to be the supreme goal (attainment of Arahantship), produce that attainment. Sister, the Blessed One directly knew the extent of the supremacy of the earth kasiṇa attainment. Having directly known the extent of the supremacy of the earth kasiṇa attainment, the Blessed One saw its gratification (the truth of origin), its danger (the truth of suffering), the escape from it (the truth of cessation), and the knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (the truth of the path). Because of seeing its gratification, its danger, the escape from it, and the knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, he understood the attainment of the goal and the peace of heart.

Sister, some ascetics and brahmins, considering the attainment of the water kasiṇa... the fire kasiṇa... the air kasiṇa... the blue kasiṇa... the yellow kasiṇa... the red kasiṇa... the white kasiṇa... the space kasiṇa... the consciousness kasiṇa (the first formless state) to be the supreme goal, produce that attainment. Sister, the Blessed One directly knew the extent of the supremacy of the consciousness kasiṇa attainment. Having directly known the extent of the supremacy of the consciousness kasiṇa attainment, the Blessed One saw its gratification (the truth of origin), its danger (the truth of suffering), the escape from it (the truth of cessation), and the knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (the truth of the path). Because of seeing its gratification, its danger, the escape from it, and the knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, he understood the attainment of the goal and the peace of heart. Thus, sister, regarding what was said by the Blessed One in the Questions of the Maidens..."
295:
Sister, thus the Blessed One, regarding the problems of women, spoke these words: 'Having conquered the army of the pleasant and the agreeable, meditating alone, I have realized the attainment of the goal (Arahantship) and the peace of the heart; therefore, I do not form friendships with the people, I am not a friend to anyone.'

Sister, the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One should be understood in detail in this way.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7 - Paṭhama Mahāpañhā Sutta

27. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, many bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning and taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: 'It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. What if we were to approach the park of the wanderers of other sects?'

Then those bhikkhus approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, they exchanged friendly and polite greetings with those wanderers of other sects and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said this to the bhikkhus:

'Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: "Come, bhikkhus, fully understand all things; dwell having fully understood all things." We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples thus: "Come, friends, fully understand all things; dwell having fully understood all things." Here, friends, what is the distinction, what is the divergence, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, between his teaching of the Dhamma and our teaching of the Dhamma, or between his instruction and our instruction?'

Then those bhikkhus neither rejoiced in nor rejected the words of those wanderers of other sects. Without rejoicing and without rejecting, they rose from their seats and departed, thinking, 'We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'
296:
Then those bhikkhus, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after their meal, upon returning from their alms round, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:

'Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking our bowls and robes, we entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then, Bhante, it occurred to us: "It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. What if we were to approach the park of the wanderers of other sects?" Then, Bhante, we approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, we exchanged friendly and polite greetings with those wanderers of other sects and sat down to one side. As we were sitting there, Bhante, those wanderers of other sects said this to us:

"Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: 'Come, bhikkhus, fully understand all things; dwell having fully understood all things.' We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples thus: 'Come, friends, fully understand all things; dwell having fully understood all things.' Here, friends, what is the distinction, what is the divergence, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, between his teaching of the Dhamma and our teaching of the Dhamma, or between his instruction and our instruction?"

Then, Bhante, we neither rejoiced in nor rejected the words of those wanderers of other sects. Without rejoicing and without rejecting, we rose from our seats and departed, thinking, "We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One."' 

Bhikkhus, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be spoken to and questioned in this way: 'Friends, one question, one summary, one answer; two questions, two summaries, two answers; three questions, three summaries, three answers; four questions, four summaries, four answers; five questions, five summaries, five answers; six questions, six summaries, six answers; seven questions, seven summaries, seven answers; eight questions, eight summaries, eight answers; nine questions, nine summaries, nine answers;'
297:
“Ten questions, ten summaries, ten answers”—thus they should speak and ask.

Monks, when wanderers of other sects are asked in this way, they will not be able to answer properly and fully; they will also meet with extreme frustration. Why is that? Monks, because it is not their domain.

Monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, I do not see anyone who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.

“One question, one summary, one answer”—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, when a bhikkhu, regarding one thing, becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. What is that one thing? “All beings are sustained by nutriment.” Monks, in this one thing (nutriment), when a bhikkhu becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. “One question, one summary, one answer”—thus it was said, and it was said in reference to this.

“Two questions, two summaries, two answers”—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, when a bhikkhu, regarding two things, becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the two? Name and form. Monks, in these two things (name and form), when a bhikkhu becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. “Two questions, two summaries, two answers”—thus it was said, and it was said in reference to this.

“Three questions, three summaries, three answers”—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, when a bhikkhu, regarding three things, becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the three? The three feelings.
298:
Monks, in these three things (feelings), when a bhikkhu becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. “Three questions, three summaries, three answers”—thus it was said, and it was said in reference to this.

“Four questions, four summaries, four answers”—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, when a bhikkhu, regarding four things, becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the four things? The four nutriments. Monks, in these four things (nutriments), when a bhikkhu becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. “Four questions, four summaries, four answers”—thus it was said, and it was said in reference to this.

“Five questions, five summaries, five answers”—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, when a bhikkhu, regarding five things, becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.

What are the five? The five aggregates of clinging. Monks, in these five things (aggregates of clinging), when a bhikkhu becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. “Five questions, five summaries, five answers”—thus it was said, and it was said in reference to this.

“Six questions, six summaries, six answers”—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, when a bhikkhu, regarding six things, becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the six? The six internal (ajjhattika) sense bases (āyatana). Monks, in these six things (internal sense bases), when a bhikkhu becomes fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. “Six questions, six summaries, six answers”—thus it was said, and it was said in reference to this.

“Seven questions, seven summaries, seven answers”—thus it was said. In reference to what was this said?
299:
Monks, in seven things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the seven? The seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). Monks, in these seven things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What was said: 'Seven questions, seven summaries, seven expositions' was said in reference to this.

What was said: 'Eight questions, eight summaries, eight expositions'—in reference to what was this said? Monks, in eight things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the eight? The eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). Monks, in these eight things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What was said: 'Eight questions, eight summaries, eight expositions' was said in reference to this.

What was said: 'Nine questions, nine summaries, nine expositions'—in reference to what was this said? Monks, in nine things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the nine? The nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). Monks, in these nine things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What was said: 'Nine questions, nine summaries, nine expositions' was said in reference to this.

What was said: 'Ten questions, ten summaries, ten expositions'—in reference to what was this said?

Monks, in ten things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the ten? The ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala kammapatha). Monks, in these ten things, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life.
300:
What was said: 'Ten questions, ten summaries, ten expositions' was said in reference to this.

The seventh discourse.

## 8 - Dutiya Mahāpañha Sutta

28. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Kajangalā in the Bamboo Grove. Then many lay followers of Kajangalā approached the nun of Kajangalā, paid homage to her, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the lay followers of Kajangalā said to the nun of Kajangalā:

'Venerable lady, the Blessed One has spoken these words in the Great Questions: "One question, one summary, one exposition; two questions, two summaries, two expositions; three questions, three summaries, three expositions; four questions, four summaries, four expositions; five questions, five summaries, five expositions; six questions, six summaries, six expositions; seven questions, seven summaries, seven expositions; eight questions, eight summaries, eight expositions; nine questions, nine summaries, nine expositions; ten questions, ten summaries, ten expositions." Venerable lady, how should the meaning of this brief teaching by the Blessed One be understood in detail?'

'Friends, I have not heard this directly from the Blessed One, nor have I received it directly from him; nor have I heard it or received it from esteemed monks. Nevertheless, I will tell you how it appears to me in this matter. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable lady,' the lay followers of Kajangalā replied to the nun of Kajangalā. The nun of Kajangalā said this:

'What was said by the Blessed One: "One question, one summary, one exposition"—in reference to what was this said? Friends, in one thing, a monk, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, fully seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life.

What is the one thing? All beings subsist on nutriment (āhāraṭṭhitikā).'
301:
Lay followers, regarding this one thing (nutriment), a bhikkhu, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. That which was said by the Blessed One: 'One question, one summary, one exposition,' was said in reference to this.

'Two questions, two summaries, two expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, in reference to what was it said? Lay followers, regarding two things, a bhikkhu, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the two? Name and form. ... What are the three? The three kinds of feeling. Lay followers, regarding these three things, a bhikkhu, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. 'Three questions, three summaries, three expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, was said in reference to this.

'Four questions, four summaries, four expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, in reference to what was it said? Lay followers, regarding four things, a bhikkhu, with a well-developed mind, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the four? The four foundations of mindfulness. Lay followers, regarding these four things, a bhikkhu, with a well-developed mind, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. 'Four questions, four summaries, four expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, was said in reference to this.

'Five questions, five summaries, five expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, in reference to what was it said? Lay followers, regarding five things, a bhikkhu, with a well-developed mind, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the five? The five faculties. ... What are the six? The six elements of deliverance (nissaraṇīya dhātu). ... What are the seven? The seven factors of enlightenment. ... What are the eight? The Noble Eightfold Path.
302:
Lay followers, regarding these eight things (the Noble Path), a bhikkhu, with a well-developed mind, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. 'Eight questions, eight summaries, eight expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, was said in reference to this.

'Nine questions, nine summaries, nine expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, in reference to what was it said? Lay followers, regarding nine things, a bhikkhu, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the nine? The nine abodes of beings. Lay followers, regarding these nine things, a bhikkhu, being fully disenchanted, fully dispassionate, fully liberated, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life.

'Nine questions, nine summaries, nine expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, was said in reference to this. 'Ten questions, ten summaries, ten expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, in reference to what was it said? Lay followers, regarding ten things, a bhikkhu, with a well-developed mind, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. What are the ten? The ten wholesome courses of action. Lay followers, regarding these ten things, a bhikkhu, with a well-developed mind, seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the meaning, makes an end of suffering in this very life. 'Ten questions, ten summaries, ten expositions'—that which was said by the Blessed One, was said in reference to this.

Thus, lay followers, regarding the Great Questions spoken in brief by the Blessed One—'One question, one summary, one exposition... up to... ten questions, ten summaries, ten expositions'—I understand the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One in detail in this way. If you wish, lay followers, you may approach the Blessed One himself and ask about this meaning. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it.

"Very well, venerable lady," the lay followers of Kajangalā, having rejoiced and appreciated the words of the bhikkhunī of Kajangalā, rose from their seats, paid homage to her, and keeping her on their right, went to the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat to one side. Sitting there, the lay followers of Kajangalā reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation they had with the bhikkhunī of Kajangalā.
303:
"Excellent, householders, excellent! The bhikkhunī of Kajangalā is wise, householders. The bhikkhunī of Kajangalā is of great wisdom. If you had approached me and asked about this matter, I would have explained it in the same way as the bhikkhunī of Kajangalā has explained it. This is indeed the meaning of that statement, and so you should remember it."

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9 - Pathama Kosala Sutta

29. "Monks, as far as the Kāsī and Kosala countries extend, as far as the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala reaches, King Pasenadi of Kosala is considered the foremost. Yet, monks, even for King Pasenadi of Kosala, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, monks, the educated noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted, he loses passion for the foremost, let alone for what is inferior. (1)

Monks, as far as the sun and moon revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance, so far does the thousandfold world system extend. In that thousandfold world system, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru kings of mountains, a thousand Jambudīpa continents, a thousand Aparagoyāna continents, a thousand Uttarakuru continents, a thousand Pubbavideha continents, four thousand great oceans, four thousand Great Kings, a thousand Cātumahārājika heavens, a thousand Tāvatiṃsa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tusita heavens, a thousand Nimmānarati heavens, a thousand Paranimmitavasavatti heavens, and a thousand Brahma worlds. Monks, as far as the thousandfold world system extends, Mahābrahmā is considered the foremost there. Yet, monks, even for Mahābrahmā, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, monks, the educated noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted, he loses passion for the foremost, let alone for what is inferior. (2)

Monks, there is a time when this world system dissolves. When the world system is dissolving, monks, beings for the most part arise in the Ābhassara realm. There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, dwelling in glory, and they remain for a very long time. Monks, when the world system is dissolving, the Ābhassara Brahmas are considered the foremost. Yet, monks, even for the Ābhassara Brahmas, there is change and transformation."
304:
"Seeing this, monks, the educated noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted, he loses passion for the foremost, let alone for what is inferior. (3)

Monks, there are these ten spheres of totality (kasiṇāyatana). What ten? One person perceives the earth totality—above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. One person perceives the water totality... [as before]... One person perceives the fire totality... One person perceives the air totality... One person perceives the blue totality... One person perceives the yellow totality... One person perceives the red totality... One person perceives the white totality... One person perceives the space totality... One person perceives the consciousness totality—above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. These, monks, are the ten spheres of totality. Monks, among these ten spheres of totality, the foremost is when one perceives the consciousness totality—above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. Monks, there are beings who have such a perception. Yet, monks, even for those beings who have such a perception, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, monks, the educated noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted, he loses passion for the foremost consciousness totality, let alone for what is inferior. (4)

Monks, there are these eight spheres of mastery (abhibhāyatana). What eight? One person, perceiving forms internally, sees small forms externally, beautiful or ugly; mastering them, he has the perception: 'I know, I see.' This is the first sphere of mastery.

One person, perceiving forms internally, sees immeasurable forms externally, beautiful or ugly; mastering them, he has the perception: 'I know, I see.' This is the second sphere of mastery.

One person, not perceiving forms internally, sees small forms externally, beautiful or ugly; mastering them, he has the perception: 'I know, I see.' This is the third sphere of mastery.

One person, not perceiving forms internally, sees immeasurable forms externally, beautiful or ugly..."
305:
Mastering those forms, one has the perception: "I know, I see." This is the fourth base of mastery.

Someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luster. Just as the flax flower is blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luster; or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luster; in the same way, someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are blue, of blue color, blue in appearance, blue in luster. Mastering those forms, one has the perception: "I know, I see." This is the fifth base of mastery.

Someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster. Just as the kaṇikāra flower is yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster; or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster; in the same way, someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are yellow, of yellow color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster. Mastering those forms, one has the perception: "I know, I see." This is the sixth base of mastery.

Someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are red, of red color, red in appearance, red in luster. Just as the bandhujīvaka flower is red, of red color, red in appearance, red in luster; or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is red, of red color, red in appearance, red in luster; in the same way, someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are red, of red color, red in appearance, red in luster. Mastering those forms, one has the perception: "I know, I see." This is the seventh base of mastery.

Someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white in appearance, white in luster. Just as the morning star is white, of white color, white in appearance, white in luster; or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is white, of white color, white in appearance, white in luster; in the same way, someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white in appearance, white in luster,
306:
Mastering those forms, one has the perception: "I know, I see." This is the eighth base of mastery. These, bhikkhus, are the eight bases of mastery.

Bhikkhus, among these eight bases of mastery, the foremost is this: when someone, not perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white in appearance, white in luster, and mastering those forms, has the perception: "I know, I see." Bhikkhus, there are beings who have such a perception. Yet even for those beings who have such a perception, there is change, there is alteration. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that base of mastery. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes detached from the foremost, let alone from the inferior. (5)

Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of practice. Which four? Painful practice with slow intuition (dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā), painful practice with swift intuition (dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā), pleasant practice with slow intuition (sukhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā), and pleasant practice with swift intuition (sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā). These, bhikkhus, are the four ways of practice. Bhikkhus, among these four ways of practice, the foremost is this: pleasant practice with swift intuition. Bhikkhus, there are beings who practice in this way. Yet even for those beings who practice in this way, there is change, there is alteration. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that pleasant practice with swift intuition. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes detached from the foremost practice, let alone from the inferior practice. (6)

Bhikkhus, there are these four perceptions. Which four? One perceives the limited; one perceives the exalted; one perceives the immeasurable; one perceives the base of nothingness, thinking "there is nothing." These, bhikkhus, are the four perceptions. Bhikkhus, among these four perceptions, the foremost is this: when one perceives the base of nothingness, thinking "there is nothing." Bhikkhus, there are beings who have such a perception. Yet even for those beings who have such a perception, there is change, there is alteration. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that perception of the base of nothingness. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes detached from the foremost perception, let alone from the inferior perception. (7)
307:
Monks, among the views held by those outside [this teaching], this is the foremost: 'I might not have been, and it might not be for me; I shall not be, and it shall not be for me.' Monks, for one with such a view, this is to be expected: 'That lack of revulsion for existence will not be, and that revulsion for the cessation of existence will not be.' Monks, there are beings who hold such a view. Monks, even for beings with such a view, there is change, there is transformation. Seeing this, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that [annihilationist view]. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes detached from the foremost, let alone the inferior. (8)

Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim supreme purity. Monks, among those who proclaim supreme purity, this is the foremost: when one, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. They teach the Dhamma for the direct knowledge and realization of that state. Monks, there are beings who speak thus. Monks, even for beings who speak thus, there is change, there is transformation. Seeing this, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that [attainment]. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes detached from the foremost, let alone the inferior. (9)

Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim supreme Nibbāna in the present life. Monks, among those who proclaim supreme Nibbāna in the present life, this is the foremost: liberation without clinging, having known as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact. Monks, although I speak thus and declare thus, some ascetics and brahmins misrepresent me with what is false, empty, lying, and untrue, saying: 'The ascetic Gotama does not proclaim the full understanding of sensual pleasures, he does not proclaim the full understanding of forms, he does not proclaim the full understanding of feelings.' Monks, I do proclaim the full understanding of sensual pleasures, I do proclaim the full understanding of forms, and I do proclaim the full understanding of feelings. Even in this very life, being without hunger, extinguished, cooled, and without clinging, I proclaim Parinibbāna.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Dutiya Kosala Sutta

30. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala had returned from the battlefield, having been victorious and achieved his purpose. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala drove towards the monastery. Having gone as far as the ground for vehicles allowed, he dismounted from his vehicle and entered the monastery on foot. At that time, many monks were walking back and forth in the open air.
308:
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached those monks and said to them: "Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, staying now? Venerable sirs, we wish to see the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
"Great King, this is the dwelling with the door closed. Approach it quietly, enter the porch slowly, cough, and knock on the bolt. The Blessed One will open the door for you."

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the dwelling with the door closed quietly, entered the porch slowly, coughed, and knocked on the bolt. The Blessed One opened the door. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala entered the dwelling, fell with his head at the Blessed One's feet, kissed the Blessed One's feet with his mouth, and stroked them with his hands, and announced his name: "Venerable sir, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala; venerable sir, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala."
"Great King, what benefit do you see that you show such extreme humility towards this body and offer such a tribute of affection?"
"Venerable sir, it is because I see gratitude (kataññutā) and gratefulness (katavedita) that I show such extreme humility towards the Blessed One and offer this tribute of affection.

Venerable sir, the Blessed One has practiced for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many; he has established many people in the noble way, namely, in the nature of goodness and the nature of wholesomeness. Venerable sir, since the Blessed One has practiced for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, and has established many people in the noble way, namely, in the nature of goodness and the nature of wholesomeness—seeing this benefit, I show such extreme humility towards the Blessed One and offer this tribute of affection. (1)

Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is virtuous, possessed of mature virtue, noble virtue, wholesome virtue, and is endowed with wholesome virtue. Venerable sir, since the Blessed One is virtuous, possessed of mature virtue, noble virtue, wholesome virtue, and is endowed with wholesome virtue—seeing this benefit, I show such extreme humility towards the Blessed One and offer this tribute of affection. (2)

Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One has for a long time been a forest-dweller, frequenting remote forest lodgings."
309: Venerable sir, furthermore, seeing this reason—that the Blessed One has for a long time been a forest-dweller, frequenting remote forest lodgings—I show such supreme humility and offer such a tribute of love to the Blessed One. (3) Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is content with whatever robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick he receives. Seeing this reason—that the Blessed One is content with whatever robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick he receives—I show such supreme humility and offer such a tribute of love to the Blessed One. (4) Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Seeing this reason—that the Blessed One is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and an unsurpassed field of merit for the world—I show such supreme humility and offer such a tribute of love to the Blessed One. (5) Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is one who obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, such talk as is effacing and conducive to opening up the mind—that is, talk on wanting little, on contentment, on seclusion, on aloofness from society, on arousing energy, on virtue, on concentration, on wisdom, on liberation, and on the knowledge and vision of liberation. Seeing this reason—that the Blessed One obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, such talk as is effacing and conducive to opening up the mind, namely, talk on wanting little... up to the knowledge and vision of liberation—I show such supreme humility and offer such a tribute of love to the Blessed One. (6) Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is one who obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life. Seeing this reason—that the Blessed One obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life—I show such supreme humility,
310: and offer such a tribute of love to the Blessed One. (7) Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.' Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. Seeing this reason—that the Blessed One recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details—I show such supreme humility and offer such a tribute of love to the Blessed One. (8) Furthermore, venerable sir, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, the Blessed One sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: 'These worthy beings, who were endowed with bad conduct of body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views and undertook actions based on wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell. But these worthy beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right views and undertook actions based on right views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world.' Thus he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. Venerable sir, with the Blessed One's divine eye, which is especially purified and surpasses the human sight...
311:
Furthermore, Bhante, seeing also this special reason, that the Blessed One knows beings according to their deeds (kamma), I show such supreme humility towards the Blessed One and offer my tribute of love. (9)

Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, he dwells therein. Bhante, seeing also this special reason, that the Blessed One, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, he dwells therein, I show such supreme humility towards the Blessed One and offer my tribute of love. (10)

'Bhante, now we depart. We have much business, many things to be done.'

'Great King, you may go at your own convenience.'

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed.

The tenth sutta.
The third Great Chapter (Mahāvagga) is finished.
The summary (uddāna) of it:
Sīha, Adhivutti, Kāya, Cunda, Kasiṇa,
Kāḷī, two Great Questions, and two more with the Kosalans.

## 4. Upālivagga
## 1. Upālisutta

31. Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said to the Blessed One: 'Bhante, for how many special reasons has the Tathāgata prescribed training rules for his disciples and set forth the Pātimokkha?'

'Upāli, for ten special reasons the Tathāgata has prescribed training rules for his disciples and set forth the Pātimokkha. What ten? For the excellence of the Saṅgha; for the comfort of the Saṅgha; for the restraint of ill-behaved persons; for the ease of well-behaved monks; for the restraint of taints belonging to this life; for the warding off of taints belonging to future lives; for the inspiring of those who are not yet inspired; for the increase of those who are inspired; for the longevity of the True Dhamma; and for the support of the Vinaya. Upāli, for these ten special reasons the Tathāgata has prescribed training rules for his disciples and set forth the Pātimokkha.'
312:
...and set forth the Pātimokkha.'

The first sutta.

## 2. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanāsutta

32. 'Bhante, how many are the grounds for suspending the Pātimokkha?'

'Upāli, there are ten grounds for suspending the Pātimokkha. What ten? A pārājika offender is sitting in that assembly; the discussion concerning a pārājika is unfinished; an unordained person is sitting in that assembly; the discussion concerning an unordained person is unfinished; one who has renounced the training is sitting in that assembly; the discussion concerning one who has renounced the training is unfinished; a eunuch (paṇḍaka) is sitting in that assembly; the discussion concerning a eunuch is unfinished; a violator of a nun is sitting in that assembly; the discussion concerning a violator of a nun is unfinished. Upāli, these are the ten grounds for suspending the Pātimokkha.'

The second sutta.

## 3. Ubbāhikāsutta

33. 'Bhante, with how many qualities should a monk be endowed to be appointed to a committee (ubbāhikā)?'

'Upāli, a monk endowed with ten qualities should be appointed to a committee. What ten? Here, Upāli, a monk (1) is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. (2) He is learned, a bearer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has heard much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, pondered in the mind, and well-penetrated by view. (3) Both Pātimokkhas have been well transmitted to him in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, and well-decided, sutta by sutta and phrase by phrase.

(4) He is firm in the Vinaya, not to be led away. (5) He is capable of convincing, informing, making see, making look, and inspiring both parties (involved in a dispute). (6) He is skilled in the origin and settling of legal issues. (7) He knows the legal issue. (8) He knows the origin of the legal issue. (9) He knows the cessation of the legal issue. (10) He knows the way leading to the cessation of the legal issue. Upāli, a monk endowed with these ten qualities should be appointed to a committee.'
313:
The Third Sutta.

## 4. Upasampadā Sutta

34. "Venerable Sir, possessed of how many qualities should a bhikkhu confer ordination (upasampadā)?"
"Upāli, possessed of ten qualities, a bhikkhu should confer ordination. What are the ten?

Upāli, here in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu (1) is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults; he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. (2) He is very learned, a bearer of what he has heard, a hoarder of what he has heard; those teachings which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which with the right meaning and phrasing proclaim the entirely complete and pure holy life—such teachings have been much heard by him, retained, practiced verbally, pondered in the mind, and well-penetrated by view. (3) The Pātimokkha has been well-handed down to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-determined according to the Suttas and their details (Ubhatovibhaṅga). (4) He is capable of attending to the sick or having them attended to. (5) He is capable of dispelling dissatisfaction or having it dispelled. (6) He is capable of dispelling arisen remorse (kukkucca) according to the Dhamma. (7) He is capable of dispelling arisen wrong views according to the Dhamma. (8) He is capable of encouraging one in higher virtue (adhisīla). (9) He is capable of encouraging one in higher mind (adhicitta). (10) He is capable of encouraging one in higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Upāli, possessed of these ten qualities, a bhikkhu should confer ordination."

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Nissaya Sutta

35. "Venerable Sir, possessed of how many qualities should a bhikkhu give dependence (nissaya)?"

Upāli, possessed of ten qualities, a bhikkhu should give dependence. What are the ten? Upāli, here in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...trains himself by undertaking the training rules. He is very learned... [as above] ...well-penetrated by view. The Pātimokkha has been well-handed down to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-determined according to the Suttas and their details. He is capable of attending to the sick or having them attended to. He is capable of dispelling dissatisfaction or having it dispelled. He is capable of dispelling arisen remorse according to the Dhamma. He is capable of dispelling arisen wrong views according to the Dhamma. He is capable of encouraging one in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Upāli, possessed of these ten qualities, a bhikkhu should give dependence.
314:
The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Sāmaṇera Sutta

36. "Venerable Sir, possessed of how many qualities should a bhikkhu have a novice (sāmaṇera) attend to him?"

Upāli, possessed of ten qualities, a bhikkhu should have a novice attend to him. What are the ten? Upāli, here in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...trains himself by undertaking the training rules. He is very learned... [as above] ...well-penetrated by view. The Pātimokkha has been well-handed down to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-determined according to the Suttas and their details. He is capable of attending to the sick or having them attended to. He is capable of dispelling dissatisfaction or having it dispelled. He is capable of dispelling arisen remorse according to the Dhamma. He is capable of dispelling arisen wrong views according to the Dhamma. He is capable of encouraging one in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Upāli, possessed of these ten qualities, a bhikkhu should have a novice attend to him."

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Saṅghabheda Sutta

37. "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Schism in the Saṅgha, schism in the Saṅgha.' To what extent, Venerable Sir, is the Saṅgha divided?"

Upāli, here in this Dispensation, monks explain non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and Dhamma as non-Dhamma; they explain non-Vinaya as Vinaya, and Vinaya as non-Vinaya; they explain what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata, and what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata; they explain what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata, and what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata; they explain what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as prescribed by the Tathāgata, and what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as not prescribed by the Tathāgata. By means of these ten grounds, they draw away and separate [the assembly], perform separate formal acts, and recite a separate Pātimokkha. Upāli, to this extent, the Saṅgha is divided.
315:
The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Saṅghasāmaggī Sutta

38. "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'communal harmony, communal harmony.' To what extent, Venerable Sir, is there communal harmony in the Saṅgha?"

"Here, Upāli, the bhikkhus explain what is not-Dhamma as not-Dhamma, and they explain what is Dhamma as Dhamma. They explain what is not-Vinaya as not-Vinaya, and they explain what is Vinaya as Vinaya. They explain what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as not prescribed by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as prescribed by the Tathāgata. These bhikkhus, by means of these ten grounds, do not draw away [the assembly], do not set [them] apart, do not perform separate formal acts, and do not recite a separate Pātimokkha. To this extent, Upāli, there is communal harmony in the Saṅgha."

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Paṭhama Ānanda Sutta

39. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'schism in the Saṅgha, schism in the Saṅgha.' To what extent, Venerable Sir, is the Saṅgha divided?"

"Here, Ānanda, the bhikkhus explain what is not-Dhamma as Dhamma, and they explain what is Dhamma as not-Dhamma. They explain what is not-Vinaya as Vinaya... [as above] ... they explain what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as not prescribed by the Tathāgata. These bhikkhus, by means of these ten grounds, draw away [the assembly], set [them] apart, perform separate formal acts, and recite a separate Pātimokkha. To this extent, Ānanda, the Saṅgha is divided."

"But, Venerable Sir, having divided a harmonious Saṅgha, what does that person produce?"

"He produces, Ānanda, a grievous demerit that lasts for an aeon."

"But what, Venerable Sir, is a grievous demerit that lasts for an aeon?"

"He is boiled in hell, Ānanda, for an aeon.

'Destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, staying for an aeon is the schismatic;
Delighting in factions, not standing in Dhamma, he falls away from security from the yokes;
Having divided a harmonious Saṅgha, he is boiled in hell for an aeon.'"
316:
The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Dutiya Ānanda Sutta

40. "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'communal harmony, communal harmony.' To what extent, Venerable Sir, is there communal harmony in the Saṅgha?"

"Here, Ānanda, the bhikkhus explain what is not-Dhamma as not-Dhamma, and they explain what is Dhamma as Dhamma. They explain what is not-Vinaya as not-Vinaya, and they explain what is Vinaya as Vinaya. They explain what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as not prescribed by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as prescribed by the Tathāgata. These bhikkhus, by means of these ten grounds, do not draw away [the assembly], do not set [them] apart, do not perform separate formal acts, and do not recite a separate Pātimokkha. To this extent, Ānanda, there is communal harmony in the Saṅgha."

"But, Venerable Sir, having reconciled a divided Saṅgha, what does that person produce?"

"He produces, Ānanda, sublime merit."

"But what, Venerable Sir, is sublime merit?"

"He rejoices in heaven, Ānanda, for an aeon.

'Happy is the harmony of the Saṅgha, and the support of those in harmony;
Delighting in harmony, standing in Dhamma, he does not fall away from security from the yokes;
Having made the Saṅgha harmonious, he rejoices in heaven for an aeon.'"

The Tenth Sutta.

The fourth chapter, the Upālivagga, is finished.

## 5. Akkosavagga

## 1. Vivāda Sutta

41. Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, [the Venerable Upāli said to the Blessed One]: "Venerable Sir, in the Saṅgha, there are disputes, quarrels, contentions, and arguments..."
317:
The monks do not live in comfort. "What, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason, for the arising of quarrels, strife, contention, and disputes in the Saṅgha, and why do the monks not live in comfort?" he asked.

"Upāli, here in this teaching, the monks explain what is not Dhamma as Dhamma, and they explain what is Dhamma as not Dhamma. They explain what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, and they explain what is Vinaya as not Vinaya. They explain what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as prescribed by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as not prescribed by the Tathāgata. Upāli, because of these, quarrels, strife, contention, and disputes arise in the Saṅgha, and the monks do not live in comfort. This is the cause, this is the reason."

First Sutta.

## 2. Paṭhamavivādamūla Sutta

42. "Venerable sir, how many are the roots of dispute?" he asked. "Upāli, there are ten roots of dispute. What ten? Upāli, here in this teaching, the monks explain what is not Dhamma as Dhamma, and they explain what is Dhamma as not Dhamma. They explain what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, and they explain what is Vinaya as not Vinaya. They explain what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata. They explain what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as prescribed by the Tathāgata, and they explain what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as not prescribed by the Tathāgata. Upāli, these are the ten roots of dispute," (the Buddha) said.

Second Sutta.

## 3. Dutiyavivādamūla Sutta

43. "Venerable sir, how many are the roots of dispute?" he asked. "Upāli, there are ten roots of dispute. What ten? Upāli, here in this teaching, the monks explain what is not an offense as an offense,
318:
and they explain what is an offense as not an offense. They explain a light offense as a heavy offense, and they explain a heavy offense as a light offense. They explain a gross offense as a non-gross offense, and they explain a non-gross offense as a gross offense. They explain an offense with a remainder as an offense without a remainder, and they explain an offense without a remainder as an offense with a remainder. They explain a remediable offense as an irremediable offense, and they explain an irremediable offense as a remediable offense. Upāli, these are the ten roots of dispute," (the Buddha) said.

Third Sutta.

## 4. Kusināra Sutta

44. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusināra in the Baliharaṇa Wood. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks." "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, an accuser monk who wishes to accuse another should first reflect on five things within himself and establish five things within himself before accusing another. What five things should be reflected on within himself? Monks, an accuser monk who wishes to accuse another should reflect thus: 'Is my bodily conduct pure? Am I possessed of pure bodily conduct, which is unbroken, untarnished, and beyond reproach? Is this quality found in me or not?' Monks, if a monk's bodily conduct is not pure, if he is not possessed of pure bodily conduct, which is unbroken, untarnished, and beyond reproach, there will be those who say to him: 'Come now, venerable sir, train yourself first in bodily conduct.' Thus there will be those who speak to him.

Furthermore, monks, an accuser monk who wishes to accuse another should reflect thus: 'Is my verbal conduct pure? Am I possessed of pure verbal conduct, which is unbroken, untarnished, and beyond reproach? Is this quality found in me or not?'

Monks, if a monk's verbal conduct is not pure, if he is not possessed of pure verbal conduct, which is unbroken, untarnished, and beyond reproach, there will be those who say to him: 'Come now, venerable sir, train yourself first in verbal conduct.' Thus there will be those who speak to him. Furthermore, monks, an accuser monk who wishes to accuse another should reflect thus: 'Is a heart of loving-kindness, free from resentment, established in me toward my fellow practitioners? Is this quality found in me or not?' Monks, if a heart of loving-kindness, free from resentment, is not established in a monk toward his fellow practitioners, there will be those who say to him: 'Come now, venerable sir, first establish a heart of loving-kindness, free from resentment, toward your fellow practitioners.'",
319: Thus, there will be grounds for speaking to that monk. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a monk who wishes to accuse another should reflect thus: 'Am I one who has heard much, a bearer of what is heard, a storer of what is heard? Have I heard much of those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which proclaim the holy life in its meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure? Have I retained them in mind, practiced them verbally, pondered them in the heart, and well-penetrated them with wisdom? Is this quality found in me or not?' Bhikkhus, if a monk has not heard much, has not retained what is heard, has not stored what is heard, and has not heard much of those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which proclaim the holy life in its meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure; if he has not retained them in mind, practiced them verbally, pondered them in the heart, and well-penetrated them with wisdom, then there will be grounds for others to say to him: 'I urge you, venerable one, first master the scriptures.' Thus, there will be grounds for speaking to those monks. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a monk who wishes to accuse another should reflect thus: 'Are both Pātimokkhas known to me in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-settled, by way of the text and by way of the commentary? Is this quality found in me or not?' Bhikkhus, if both Pātimokkhas are not known to a monk in detail, not well-analyzed, not well-recited, and not well-settled, by way of the text and by way of the commentary, then when asked, 'Where, venerable one, was this training rule taught by the Blessed One?', he will not be able to answer correctly. Then there will be grounds for others to say to him: 'I urge you, venerable one, first train in the Vinaya.' Thus, there will be grounds for speaking to that monk. These five things should be reflected upon within oneself. What are the five things to be established within oneself? 'I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time. I will speak the truth, not what is false. I will speak gently, not harshly. I will speak what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial. I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred.' These five things should be established within oneself. Bhikkhus, a monk who wishes to accuse another, having reflected on these five things within himself and having established these five things within himself, should then accuse the other. (End of the fourth discourse.)
320:
The Fourth Sutta.

## 5 - Rāzantepurappavesanasutta

45. “Monks, there are these ten dangers in entering a king’s inner palace. What ten? Here, monks, a king is seated together with his chief queen. A monk enters there. Either the queen, seeing the monk, smiles, or the monk, seeing the queen, smiles. Thereupon, the king thinks: ‘Surely these two have committed [misconduct] or will commit it.’ Monks, this is the first danger in entering a king’s inner palace.

Furthermore, monks, a king is very busy and has much to do. After visiting a certain woman (a minor queen), he does not remember it. She becomes pregnant because of that visit. Thereupon, the king thinks: ‘No one else enters here except the renunciant. Could this be the renunciant’s doing?’ Monks, this is the second danger in entering a king’s inner palace.

Furthermore, monks, when a certain jewel is lost in the king’s inner palace, the king thinks: ‘No one else enters here except the renunciant. Could this be the renunciant’s doing?’ Monks, this is the third danger in entering a king’s inner palace.

Furthermore, monks, when secret consultations (palace affairs) within the king’s inner palace are leaked outside, the king thinks: ‘No one else enters here except the renunciant. Could this be the renunciant’s doing?’ Monks, this is the fourth danger in entering a king’s inner palace.

Furthermore, monks, in the king’s inner palace, either a father desires [to kill] his son or a son desires [to kill] his father. They think: ‘No one else enters here except the renunciant. Could this be the renunciant’s doing?’ Monks, this is the fifth danger in entering a king’s inner palace.

Furthermore, monks, a king appoints someone of low status to a high position. To those who are displeased by this, the thought occurs: ‘The king is intimate with the renunciant. Could this be the renunciant’s doing?’ Monks, this is the sixth danger in entering a king’s inner palace.”
321:
Furthermore, bhikkhus, a king demotes one of high rank to a low position. Those who are displeased by this think: 'The king is intimate with the ascetic. Could this be the ascetic's doing?' This, bhikkhus, is the seventh danger of entering the king's inner palace.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a king dispatches the army at an inappropriate time. Those who are displeased by this think: 'The king is intimate with the ascetic. Could this be the ascetic's doing?' This, bhikkhus, is the eighth danger of entering the king's inner palace.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a king dispatches the army at an appropriate time but has them return from midway. Those who are displeased by this think: 'The king is intimate with the ascetic. Could this be the ascetic's doing?' This, bhikkhus, is the ninth danger of entering the king's inner palace.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, the king's inner palace is crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots; there are also enticing sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches which are not suitable for an ascetic. This, bhikkhus, is the tenth danger of entering the king's inner palace. These, bhikkhus, are the ten dangers of entering the king's inner palace.

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Sakka Sutta

46. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha's Park. Then, on that Uposatha day, many Sakyan lay followers approached the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to him, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to them: "Sakyans, do you observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors?"

"Venerable sir, sometimes we observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, and sometimes we do not."

"It is a loss for you, Sakyans, it is ill-gotten for you, that while life is so full of sorrow and the fear of death, you only sometimes observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors and sometimes do not.

What do you think, Sakyans? Suppose a man here, without committing any unwholesome deed, were to earn half a kahāpaṇa in a day by some means of livelihood. Would he be called a skillful and energetic man?" "Yes, venerable sir."
322:
"What do you think, Sakyans? Suppose a man here, without committing any unwholesome deed, were to earn one kahāpaṇa in a day by some means of livelihood. Would he be called a skillful and energetic man?" "Yes, venerable sir."

"What do you think, Sakyans? Suppose a man here, without committing any unwholesome deed, were to earn in a day two kahāpaṇas... three kahāpaṇas... four kahāpaṇas... five kahāpaṇas... six kahāpaṇas... seven kahāpaṇas... eight kahāpaṇas... nine kahāpaṇas... ten kahāpaṇas... twenty kahāpaṇas... thirty kahāpaṇas... forty kahāpaṇas... fifty kahāpaṇas... a hundred kahāpaṇas. Would he be called a skillful and energetic man?" "Yes, venerable sir."

"What do you think, Sakyans? If that man, earning a hundred or a thousand kahāpaṇas every single day, living for a hundred years, and accumulating what he gained, were to acquire a great mass of wealth, would that be so?" "Yes, venerable sir."

"What do you think, Sakyans? Would that man, because of that wealth, on account of that wealth, by reason of that wealth, experience absolute happiness for a whole night, or a whole day, or even half a night or half a day?" "No, venerable sir." "Why is that?" "Because, venerable sir, sensual pleasures are impermanent, empty, false, and deceptive by nature."

"But here, Sakyans, if a disciple of mine, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute for ten years, practicing as I have instructed, he would experience absolute happiness for a hundred years, for ten thousand years, or for a hundred thousand years. And he would be a Sakadāgāmī, an Anāgāmī, or certainly a Sotāpanna. Let alone ten years, Sakyans.

If a disciple of mine, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute for nine years... eight years... seven years... six years... five years... four years... three years... two years... one year, practicing as I have instructed, he would experience absolute happiness for the next hundred years..."
323:
...would dwell experiencing true happiness for ten thousand years or for a hundred thousand years; such a person would be a Once-returner, or a Non-returner, or certainly a Stream-enterer. Let alone one year, O Sakyans. If a disciple of mine in this Dispensation dwells for ten months, diligent, ardent, and resolute, directing the mind [towards Nibbāna], and practicing as I have instructed, they would dwell experiencing true happiness for a hundred years, or for ten thousand years, or for a hundred thousand years; such a person would be a Once-returner, or a Non-returner, or certainly a Stream-enterer. Let alone ten months, O Sakyans. If a disciple of mine in this Dispensation [dwells for] nine months, eight months, seven months, six months, five months, four months, three months, two months, one month, or half a month, diligent, ardent, and resolute, directing the mind [towards Nibbāna], and practicing as I have instructed, they would dwell experiencing true happiness for a hundred years, or for ten thousand years, or for a hundred thousand years;

such a person would be a Once-returner, or a Non-returner, or certainly a Stream-enterer. Let alone half a month, O Sakyans. If a disciple of mine in this Dispensation dwells for ten days and nights, diligent, ardent, and resolute, directing the mind [towards Nibbāna], and practicing as I have instructed, they would dwell experiencing true happiness for a hundred years, or for ten thousand years, or for a hundred thousand years; such a person would be a Once-returner, or a Non-returner, or certainly a Stream-enterer. Let alone ten days and nights, O Sakyans. If a disciple of mine in this Dispensation [dwells for] nine days, eight days, seven days, six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, or one day, diligent, ardent, and resolute, directing the mind [towards Nibbāna], and practicing as I have instructed, they would dwell experiencing true happiness for a hundred years, or for ten thousand years, or for a hundred thousand years; such a person would be a Once-returner, or a Non-returner, or certainly a Stream-enterer. It is a loss for you, O Sakyans, it is poorly gained by you, that while life is fraught with the danger of sorrow and life is fraught with the danger of death, you sometimes observe the eight-factored Uposatha and sometimes do not." "Venerable Sir, from this day forward, we shall observe the eight-factored Uposatha." The sixth [sutta].
324:
The Sixth Sutta.
## 7. Mahāli Sutta
47. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Woods (Mahāvana), at the Hall with the Peaked Roof (Kūṭāgārasālā). Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One, and after approaching, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the performance of evil deeds, for the occurrence of evil deeds?" "Mahāli, greed (lobha) is the cause, greed is the condition for the performance of evil deeds, for the occurrence of evil deeds. Mahāli, hatred (dosa) is the cause, hatred is the condition for the performance of evil deeds, for the occurrence of evil deeds. Mahāli, delusion (moha) is the cause, delusion is the condition for the performance of evil deeds, for the occurrence of evil deeds. Mahāli, improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is the cause, improper attention is the condition for the performance of evil deeds, for the occurrence of evil deeds. Mahāli, a wrongly directed mind is the cause, a wrongly directed mind is the condition for the performance of evil deeds, for the occurrence of evil deeds. Mahāli, this is the cause, this is the condition for the performance of evil deeds, for the occurrence of evil deeds."

"Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the performance of noble deeds, for the occurrence of noble deeds?" "Mahāli, non-greed (alobha) is the cause, non-greed is the condition for the performance of noble deeds, for the occurrence of noble deeds. Mahāli, non-hatred (adosa) is the cause, non-hatred is the condition for the performance of noble deeds, for the occurrence of noble deeds. Mahāli, non-delusion (amoha) is the cause, non-delusion is the condition for the performance of noble deeds, for the occurrence of noble deeds. Mahāli, proper attention (yoniso manasikāra) is the cause, proper attention is the condition for the performance of noble deeds, for the occurrence of noble deeds. Mahāli, a rightly directed mind is the cause, a rightly directed mind is the condition for the performance of noble deeds, for the occurrence of noble deeds. Mahāli, this is the cause, this is the condition for the performance of noble deeds, for the occurrence of noble deeds.

Mahāli, if these ten things did not exist in the world, then 'unrighteous conduct, unbalanced conduct' or 'righteous conduct, balanced conduct' would not be known.
325:
“Mahāli, because these ten things exist in the world, ‘unrighteous conduct and unharmonious conduct’ as well as ‘righteous conduct and harmonious conduct’ are known.”

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Pabbajita-abhiṇha Sutta

48. “Monks, there are these ten things that one who has gone forth should frequently reflect upon. What ten? 

‘I have entered upon a state of changed appearance’—this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth. 

‘My livelihood is dependent on others’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘I must behave in a different manner (from laypeople)’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘Does my conscience not reproach me regarding my virtue?’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘Do my wise fellow practitioners, after examination, not reproach me regarding my virtue?’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘I will be separated and parted from all that is dear and beloved to me’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related to my actions, have my actions as my refuge. Whatever action I do, whether good or bad, I will be its heir’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘How are my nights and days passing?’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘Do I delight in empty places (seclusion)?’—this should be frequently reflected upon. 

‘Have I attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, such that I will not be embarrassed when questioned by my fellow practitioners in my final hours?’—this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth. 

Monks, these are the ten things that one who has gone forth should frequently reflect upon.”

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Sarīraṭṭhadhamma Sutta

49. “Monks, there are these ten things established in the body. What ten? Cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, restraint of body, restraint of speech, restraint of livelihood, and the formation of existence that leads to renewed existence—these, monks, are the ten things established in the body.”

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Bhaṇḍana Sutta

50. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
326:
At that time, many monks, after returning from their almsround and having finished their meal, assembled and sat together in the assembly hall. They became quarrelsome, contentious, and disputatious, and lived stabbing each other with the weapons of the tongue. 

Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and went to the assembly hall. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together here, and what was your discussion that was interrupted?”

“Venerable Sir, here, after returning from our almsround and having finished our meal, we assembled and sat together in the assembly hall. We became quarrelsome, contentious, and disputatious, and lived stabbing each other with the weapons of the tongue.”

“Monks, it is not fitting for you, sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, that you should live being quarrelsome, contentious, and disputatious, stabbing each other with the weapons of the tongue.

Monks, there are these ten things that lead to being remembered, to being loved, to being respected, to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity. What ten? 

Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them. Monks, that a monk is virtuous... (p) ...and trains in the rules of training—this thing also leads to being remembered, to being loved, to being respected, to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity. 

Furthermore, monks, a monk is one of great learning (bahussuta), a bearer of what he has heard, a storer of what he has heard. Those teachings which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which explain the holy life that is entirely complete and pure—such teachings he has heard much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, pondered over in the mind, and well-penetrated by view. Monks, that a monk is one of great learning... (p) ...and well-penetrated by view—this thing also leads to being remembered, to being loved, to being respected, to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.”
327:
Monks, furthermore, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates. Monks, the fact that a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts); it creates love and creates respect; it leads to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Monks, furthermore, a monk is easy to admonish and is endowed with qualities that make him easy to speak to; he is patient and receives instruction respectfully. Monks, the fact that a monk is easy to admonish, is endowed with qualities that make him easy to speak to, is patient, and receives instruction respectfully—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts); it creates love and creates respect; it leads to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Monks, furthermore, a monk is skillful and diligent in the various duties, great or small, to be done for his fellow monks; he is endowed with investigative wisdom regarding the means to those tasks, and is capable of doing them and organizing them. Monks, the fact that a monk is skillful and diligent in the various duties, great or small, to be done for his fellow monks, is not lazy, is endowed with investigative wisdom regarding the means to those tasks, and is capable of doing and organizing them—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts); it creates love and creates respect; it leads to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Monks, furthermore, a monk loves the Dhamma and is pleasant in speech; he feels great joy in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya. Monks, the fact that a monk loves the Dhamma, is pleasant in speech, and feels great joy in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts); it creates love and creates respect; it leads to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Monks, furthermore, a monk lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states; he is energetic, firm in effort, and does not shirk his responsibility regarding wholesome states. Monks, the fact that a monk lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states, is energetic, firm in effort, and does not shirk his responsibility regarding wholesome states—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts),
328:
creates love, creates respect, and leads to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Monks, furthermore, a monk is contented with whatever robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive. Monks, the fact that a monk is contented with whatever robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts). ... [Pe] ... it leads to unity.
