Monks, furthermore, a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and prudence, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago. Monks, the fact that a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and prudence, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts). ... [Pe] ... it leads to unity.

Monks, furthermore, a monk is wise, endowed with the noble penetrative wisdom that sees the arising and passing away of things and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. Monks, the fact that a monk is wise, endowed with the noble penetrative wisdom that sees the arising and passing away of things and leads to the complete destruction of suffering—this quality is also to be remembered (for as long as life lasts). ... [Pe] ... it leads to unity.

Monks, these ten qualities are to be remembered (for as long as life lasts), they create love and respect, and lead to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

The Tenth (Sutta).

## (6) 1. Sacittavagga
## 1. Sacitta Sutta
51. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks, "Monks." "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, if a monk is not skilled in the ways of others' minds, then you should train yourselves thus: 'I will be skilled in the ways of my own mind.'

"And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the ways of his own mind? Monks, it is just as if a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, were to examine their own facial reflection in a bright, clean mirror or in a bowl of clear water. If they see any dust or blemish there, they make an effort to remove that dust or blemish. But if they do not see any dust or blemish there, they are glad and satisfied on that account: 'It is a gain for me, I am indeed clean.'

"In the same way, monks, a monk's reflection (paccavekkhaṇā) is of great benefit in regard to wholesome states: 'Do I usually dwell full of covetousness or without covetousness? Do I usually dwell with a mind of ill will or without ill will? Do I usually dwell overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha) or free from sloth and torpor? Do I usually dwell restless or not restless? Do I usually dwell with doubt or having overcome doubt? Do I usually dwell angry or not angry? Do I usually dwell with a defiled mind or an undefiled mind? Do I usually dwell with a strained body or an unstrained body? Do I usually dwell lazy or with energy aroused? Do I usually dwell unconcentrated or concentrated?'"
330:
"Monks, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: 'I usually dwell full of covetousness, I usually dwell with a mind of ill will, I usually dwell overcome by sloth and torpor, I usually dwell restless, I usually dwell with doubt, I usually dwell angry, I usually dwell with a defiled mind, I usually dwell with a strained body, I usually dwell lazy, I usually dwell unconcentrated,' then, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, endeavor, zeal, unfaltering mindfulness (sati), and clear comprehension (sampajañña) for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.

"Monks, it is just as if one's clothes were on fire or one's head were on fire. To extinguish that fire on the clothes or the head, one would apply extraordinary desire, effort, endeavor, zeal, unfaltering mindfulness, and clear comprehension. In the same way, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, endeavor, zeal, unfaltering mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.

"But, monks, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: 'I usually dwell without covetousness, I usually dwell without ill will, I usually dwell free from sloth and torpor, I usually dwell not restless, I usually dwell having overcome doubt, I usually dwell not angry, I usually dwell with an undefiled mind, I usually dwell with an unstrained body, I usually dwell with energy aroused, I usually dwell concentrated,' then, monks, that monk, staying established in those very same wholesome states, should further apply effort for the destruction of the taints (āsavas)."

The first sutta.
## 2. Sāriputta Sutta
52. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks, "Friends, monks." "Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

"Friends, if a monk is not skilled in the ways of others' minds, then you should train yourselves thus: 'I will be skilled in the ways of my own mind.' And how, friends, is a monk skilled in the ways of his own mind?"
331:
“Friends, for example, a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, would examine their own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water. If they see a speck of dust or a blemish there, they strive to remove that speck of dust or blemish. If they do not see a speck of dust or a blemish there, they are delighted and their purpose is fulfilled, thinking: ‘It is a gain for me, I am truly clean.’

In the same way, friends, reflection is of great benefit to a monk regarding wholesome states: ‘Do I usually dwell full of covetousness, or do I usually dwell without covetousness? Do I usually dwell with a mind of ill-will, or do I usually dwell without a mind of ill-will? Do I usually dwell overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha), or do I usually dwell free from sloth and torpor? Do I usually dwell restless, or do I usually dwell without restlessness? Do I usually dwell with doubt, or do I usually dwell having crossed over doubt? Do I usually dwell angry, or do I usually dwell without anger? Do I usually dwell with a defiled mind, or do I usually dwell with an undefiled mind? Do I usually dwell with a fatigued body, or do I usually dwell without a fatigued body? Do I usually dwell lazy, or do I usually dwell with energetic effort? Do I usually dwell unconcentrated, or do I usually dwell concentrated?’

Friends, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: ‘I usually dwell full of covetousness... [pe] ...I usually dwell unconcentrated,’ then, friends, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness (sati), and clear comprehension (sampajañña) to abandon those very evil, unwholesome states.

Friends, for example, a person whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness (sati), and clear comprehension (sampajañña) to extinguish the fire on those clothes or that head. In the same way, friends, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness (sati), and clear comprehension (sampajañña) to abandon those very evil, unwholesome states.

Friends, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: ‘I usually dwell without covetousness... [pe] ... (I usually dwell without a mind of ill-will, I usually dwell free from sloth and torpor, I usually dwell without restlessness, I usually dwell having crossed over doubt,”
332:
I usually dwell without anger, I usually dwell with an undefiled mind, I usually dwell without a fatigued body, I usually dwell with energetic effort,) I usually dwell concentrated,’ then, friends, that monk, staying established in those very wholesome states, should further apply himself to the destruction of the taints (āsavas).”

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Ṭhiti Sutta

53. “Monks, I do not praise standing still in wholesome states, let alone decline. Monks, I praise only growth in wholesome states, not standing still, not decline.

And how, monks, is there decline in wholesome states, and not standing still or growth? Here, monks, a monk has a certain amount of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence; those states of his neither stand still nor grow. This, monks, I call decline in wholesome states, not standing still, not growth. In this way, monks, there is decline in wholesome states, and not standing still or growth.

And how, monks, is there standing still in wholesome states, and not decline or growth? Here, monks, a monk has a certain amount of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence; those states of his do not decline, but they do not grow. This, monks, I call standing still in wholesome states, not decline, not growth. In this way, monks, there is standing still in wholesome states, and not growth or decline.

And how, monks, is there growth in wholesome states, and not standing still or decline? Here, monks, a monk has a certain amount of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence; those states of his do not stand still and do not decline. This, monks, I call growth in wholesome states, not standing still, not decline. In this way, monks, there is growth in wholesome states, and not standing still or decline.

Monks, if a monk is not skilled in the ways of others' minds, then he should train himself thus: ‘I will be skilled in the ways of my own mind.’ This is how you should train, monks.”
333:
Monks, how is a monk skilled in the ways of his own mind? Monks, just as a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, would examine the reflection of their own face in a mirror that is clean, bright, and pure, or in a bowl of clear water; if they see dust or a blemish there, they make an effort to remove that dust or blemish. If they do not see any dust or blemish there, they are glad and satisfied on that account, thinking: 'It is a gain for me, I am indeed pure.'

In the same way, monks, a monk's reflection is of great benefit in regard to wholesome states: 'Do I often abide full of covetousness, or do I often abide without covetousness? Do I often abide with a mind of ill will, or do I often abide without ill will? Do I often abide overwhelmed by sloth and torpor (thina-middha), or do I often abide free from sloth and torpor? Do I often abide restless, or do I often abide not restless? Do I often abide full of doubt, or do I often abide having overcome doubt? Do I often abide angry, or do I often abide without anger? Do I often abide with a defiled mind, or do I often abide with an undefiled mind? Do I often abide with a fatigued body, or do I often abide with an unfatigued body? Do I often abide lazy, or do I often abide with energetic effort? Do I often abide concentrated, or do I often abide unconcentrated?'

Monks, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: 'I often abide full of covetousness, I often abide with a mind of ill will, I often abide overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, I often abide restless, I often abide full of doubt, I often abide angry, I often abide with a defiled mind, I often abide with a fatigued body, I often abide lazy, I often abide unconcentrated,' then, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness (sati), and clear comprehension (sampajañña) for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states. Monks, just as one whose clothes or head are on fire would apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish the fire on those clothes or that head; in the same way, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
334:
Monks, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: 'I often abide without covetousness, I often abide without ill will, I often abide free from sloth and torpor, I often abide not restless, I often abide having overcome doubt, I often abide without anger, I often abide with an undefiled mind, I often abide with an unfatigued body, I often abide with energetic effort, I often abide concentrated,' then, monks, that monk, being established in those very same wholesome states, should make further effort for the destruction of the taints (āsavas).

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Samatha Sutta

54. Monks, if a monk is not skilled in the ways of others' minds, then he should train himself thus: 'I will be skilled in the ways of my own mind.' Monks, how is a monk skilled in the ways of his own mind? Monks, just as a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, would examine the reflection of their own face in a mirror that is clean, bright, and pure, or in a bowl of clear water; if they see dust or a blemish there, they make an effort to remove that dust or blemish. If they do not see any dust or blemish there, they are glad and satisfied on that account, thinking: 'It is a gain for me, I am indeed pure.'

In the same way, monks, a monk's reflection is of great benefit in regard to wholesome states: 'Am I one who has gained internal serenity of mind (samatha), or am I one who has not gained internal serenity of mind? Am I one who has gained insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (adhipaññādhammavipassanā), or am I one who has not gained insight into phenomena through higher wisdom?'

Monks, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: 'I am one who has gained internal serenity of mind, but I am not one who has gained insight into phenomena through higher wisdom,' then, monks, that monk, being established in internal serenity of mind, should make an effort for the sake of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom.
335:
At another time, that bhikkhu becomes one who has gained internal serenity of mind and one who has gained insight into phenomena based on higher wisdom. Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, while reflecting, knows: 'I have gained insight into phenomena based on higher wisdom, but I have not gained internal serenity of mind,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu, established in insight into phenomena based on higher wisdom, should apply himself to gain internal serenity of mind. At another time, he becomes one who has gained insight into phenomena based on higher wisdom and one who has gained internal serenity of mind.

Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, while reflecting, knows: 'I have not gained internal serenity of mind, and I have not gained insight into phenomena based on higher wisdom,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremittingness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of gaining those very wholesome states. Bhikkhus, just as a person whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremittingness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish the fire on his clothes or head; even so, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremittingness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of gaining those very wholesome states. At another time, he becomes one who has gained internal serenity of mind and one who has gained insight into phenomena based on higher wisdom.

Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, while reflecting, knows: 'I have gained internal serenity of mind, and I have gained insight into phenomena based on higher wisdom,' then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu, established in those very wholesome states, should apply himself further for the destruction of the taints.

Bhikkhus, I say that robes are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with. Bhikkhus, I say that almsfood is of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with. Bhikkhus, I say that lodgings are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with. Bhikkhus, I say that villages and towns are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with. Bhikkhus, I say that regions are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with. Bhikkhus, I say that persons are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.

'Bhikkhus, I say that robes are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' Thus it was said. In reference to what was this said?
336:
Among those robes, if one knows of a robe: 'While I associate with this robe, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease,' then such a robe should not be associated with. Among those robes, if one knows of a robe: 'While I associate with this robe, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase,' then such a robe should be associated with. 'Bhikkhus, I say that robes are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' It is in reference to this that this was said.

'Bhikkhus, I say that almsfood is of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' Thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Among those kinds of almsfood, if one knows of almsfood: 'While I associate with this almsfood, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease,' then such almsfood should not be associated with. Among those kinds of almsfood, if one knows of almsfood: 'While I associate with this almsfood, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase,' then such almsfood should be associated with. 'Bhikkhus, I say that almsfood is of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' It is in reference to this that this was said.

'Bhikkhus, I say that lodgings are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' Thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Among those lodgings, if one knows of a lodging: 'While I associate with this lodging, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease,' then such a lodging should not be associated with. Among those lodgings, if one knows of a lodging: 'While I associate with this lodging, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase,' then such a lodging should be associated with. 'Bhikkhus, I say that lodgings are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' It is in reference to this that this was said.

'Bhikkhus, I say that villages and towns are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' Thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Among those villages and towns, if one knows of a village or town: 'While I associate with this village or town, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease,' then such a village or town should not be associated with.

Among those villages and towns, if one knows of a village or town: 'While I associate with this village or town, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase,' then such a village or town should be associated with. 'Bhikkhus, I say that villages and towns are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' It is in reference to this that this was said. Bhikkhus, I say that regions are of two kinds: those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.' Thus it was said. In reference to what was this said?
337:
Among those regions, if one knows of a region: 'While I frequent this region, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline,' then such a region should not be frequented. Among those regions, if one knows of a region: 'While I frequent this region, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase,' then such a region should be frequented. 'Monks, I say that a region is of two kinds: to be frequented and not to be frequented.' What was said was said in reference to this.

'Monks, I say that a person is of two kinds: to be frequented and not to be frequented.' In reference to what was this said? Among those persons, if one knows of a person: 'While I frequent this person, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline,' then such a person should not be frequented. Among those persons, if one knows of a person: 'While I frequent this person, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase,' then such a person should be frequented. 'Monks, I say that a person is of two kinds: to be frequented and not to be frequented.' What was said was said in reference to this.

Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Parihāna Sutta

55. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Friend,' those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

'Friends, it is said, "A person subject to decline, a person subject to decline." Friends, it is said, "A person not subject to decline, a person not subject to decline." Friends, to what extent is a person called one subject to decline by the Blessed One, and to what extent is a person called one not subject to decline by the Blessed One?'

'Friend, we have come from afar to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the meaning of this statement occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta himself. Having heard it from the Venerable Sāriputta, the monks will remember it.'
338:
'In that case, friends, listen and attend closely; I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

'Friends, to what extent is a person called one subject to decline by the Blessed One? Here, friends, a monk does not hear the Dhamma he has not heard before, and the Dhammas he has heard go to forgetfulness. Those Dhammas that were not previously contacted by his mind do not occur to him, and he does not understand what is not yet understood. To this extent, friends, a person is called one subject to decline by the Blessed One.

'And to what extent, friends, is a person called one not subject to decline by the Blessed One? Here, friends, a monk hears the Dhamma he has not heard before, and the Dhammas he has heard do not go to forgetfulness. Those Dhammas that were not previously contacted by his mind occur to him, and he understands what is not yet understood. To this extent, friends, a person is called one not subject to decline by the Blessed One.

'Friends, if a monk is not skilled in the ways of others' minds, then he should train himself thus: "I will be skilled in the ways of my own mind."

'Friends, how is a monk skilled in the ways of his own mind? Friends, just as a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, would examine their own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water; if they see any dust or blemish there, they make an effort to remove that dust or blemish. But if they do not see any dust or blemish there, they are glad and satisfied at that very fact: "It is a gain for me, I am clean."

'In the same way, friends, a monk's self-examination is very helpful for wholesome qualities: "Do I usually dwell without covetousness? Does this quality exist in me or not? Do I usually dwell with a mind free from ill will? Does this quality exist in me or not? Do I usually dwell free from sloth and torpor? Does this quality exist in me or not? Do I usually dwell without restlessness? Does this quality exist in me or not? Do I usually dwell having crossed over doubt? Does this quality exist in me or not? Do I usually dwell without anger?..."'
339:
"Do I often live having overcome doubt? Is this quality present in me or not? Do I often live without anger? Is this quality present in me or not? Do I often live with an undefiled mind? Is this quality present in me or not? Am I one who gains internal joy in the Dhamma? Is this quality present in me or not? Am I one who gains internal tranquility of mind? Is this quality present in me or not? Am I one who gains insight into phenomena through higher wisdom? Is this quality present in me or not?"—reflection in this way is of great benefit to a bhikkhu regarding wholesome states.

Friends, if a bhikkhu, while reflecting, does not see all these wholesome states within himself, then, friends, that bhikkhu should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremitting mindfulness, and clear comprehension to attain all these wholesome states. Friends, just as a person whose clothes or head are on fire would apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremitting mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish the fire on his clothes or head; even so, friends, that bhikkhu should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremitting mindfulness, and clear comprehension to attain all these wholesome states.

Friends, if a bhikkhu, while reflecting, sees some wholesome states within himself but does not see others, then, friends, that bhikkhu, having established himself in those wholesome states he sees within himself, should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremitting mindfulness, and clear comprehension to attain those wholesome states he does not see within himself. Friends, just as a person whose clothes or head are on fire would apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremitting mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish the fire on his clothes or head; even so, friends, that bhikkhu, having established himself in those states he sees within himself, should apply extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, unremitting mindfulness, and clear comprehension to attain those very states he does not see within himself.

Friends, if a bhikkhu, while reflecting, sees all these wholesome states within himself, then, friends, that bhikkhu, having established himself in all these wholesome states...
340:
...having established himself in those wholesome states, he should apply himself further for the destruction of the taints." (The Fifth Sutta.)

## 6. Paṭhama Saññā Sutta
56. "Bhikkhus, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and benefit; they plunge into the Deathless and end in the Deathless. What ten? The perception of unattractiveness (asubhasaññā), the perception of death (maraṇasaññā), the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), the perception of non-delight in the whole world (sabbaloke anabhiratisaññā), the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), the perception of suffering in the impermanent (anicce dukkhasaññā), the perception of non-self in suffering (dukkhe anattasaññā), the perception of abandoning (pahānasaññā), the perception of dispassion (virāgasaññā), and the perception of cessation (nirodhasaññā). Bhikkhus, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and benefit; they plunge into the Deathless and end in the Deathless." (The Sixth Sutta.)

## 7. Dutiya Saññā Sutta
57. "Bhikkhus, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and benefit; they plunge into the Deathless and end in the Deathless. What ten? The perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), the perception of non-self (anattasaññā), the perception of death (maraṇasaññā), the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), the perception of non-delight in the whole world (sabbaloke anabhiratisaññā), the perception of a skeleton (aṭṭhikasaññā), the perception of a worm-infested corpse (puḷuvakasaññā), the perception of a livid corpse (vinīlakasaññā), the perception of a fissured corpse (vicchiddakasaññā), and the perception of a bloated corpse (uddhumātakasaññā). Bhikkhus, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and benefit; they plunge into the Deathless and end in the Deathless." (The Seventh Sutta.)

## 8. Mūlaka Sutta
58. "Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask: 'Friends, in what are all things rooted? In what do all things originate? From what do all things arise? Where do all things meet? What is the head of all things? What is the authority over all things? What is the superior of all things? What is the essence of all things? Into what do all things plunge? What is the final end of all things?'—if asked thus, bhikkhus, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?"

"Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, Venerable Sir, if the meaning of this statement were to be clarified by the Blessed One himself. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it."
341:
The monks replied, "We will listen and bear it in mind, Bhante."

"Then, bhikkhus, listen and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask: 'Friends, what is the root of all things? What is the origin of all things? What is the source of all things? What is the meeting point of all things? What is the head of all things? What is the authority of all things? What is the supremacy of all things? What is the essence of all things? What is the immersion of all things? What is the conclusion of all things?' Being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way:

'Friends, all things are rooted in desire. All things originate from attention. All things have contact as their source. All things have feeling as their meeting point. All things have concentration as their head. All things have mindfulness as their authority. All things have wisdom as their supremacy. All things have liberation (the fruit of Arahantship) as their essence. All things are immersed in the Deathless. All things conclude in Nibbāna.' Being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way."

The eighth discourse.

## 9. Pabbajjā Sutta

59. "Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: 'Our minds will be well-cultivated in accordance with the going forth, and arisen evil unwholesome states will not remain obsessing the mind. Our minds will be well-cultivated with the perception of impermanence, our minds will be well-cultivated with the perception of non-self, our minds will be well-cultivated with the perception of foulness, our minds will be well-cultivated with the perception of danger. Knowing the evenness and unevenness of the world, our minds will be well-cultivated with that perception. Knowing the growth and decline of the world, our minds will be well-cultivated with that perception. Knowing the arising and passing away of the world, our minds will be well-cultivated with that perception. Our minds will be well-cultivated with the perception of abandoning, our minds will be well-cultivated with the perception of dispassion, and our minds will be well-cultivated with the perception of cessation.' Thus, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves."
342:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu's mind is well-cultivated in accordance with the going forth, and arisen evil unwholesome states do not remain obsessing the mind; when his mind is well-cultivated with the perception of impermanence, his mind is well-cultivated with the perception of non-self, his mind is well-cultivated with the perception of foulness, his mind is well-cultivated with the perception of danger; when, knowing the evenness and unevenness of the world, his mind is well-cultivated with that perception; when, knowing the growth and decline of the world, his mind is well-cultivated with that perception; when, knowing the arising and passing away of the world, his mind is well-cultivated with that perception; when his mind is well-cultivated with the perception of abandoning, his mind is well-cultivated with the perception of dispassion, and his mind is well-cultivated with the perception of cessation—then one of two fruits may be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or if there is a residue of clinging, the state of a non-returner."

The ninth discourse.

## 10. Girimānanda Sutta

60. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇ膽ika's Park. Now on that occasion, the Venerable Girimānanda was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, the Venerable Girimānanda is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, Bhante, if the Blessed One would visit the Venerable Girimānanda out of compassion."

"Ānanda, if you were to speak ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda, it is possible that having heard these ten perceptions, his affliction would immediately subside. What are the ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of foulness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of the undesirability of all conditioned things, and mindfulness of breathing.

And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, volitional formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.' Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates of clinging."
343:
Ānanda, this is called the perception of impermanence. (1)

Ānanda, what is the perception of non-self? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place, reflects thus: ‘The eye is non-self, forms are non-self; the ear is non-self, sounds are non-self; the nose is non-self, odors are non-self; the tongue is non-self, tastes are non-self; the body is non-self, tactile objects are non-self; the mind is non-self, mental phenomena are non-self.’ Thus he dwells observing non-self in these six internal and external sense bases. Ānanda, this is called the perception of non-self. (2)

Ānanda, what is the perception of unattractiveness? Here, Ānanda, a monk reviews this very body, upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the tips of the hairs, enclosed by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, gorge, dung, (brain), bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, skin-oil, saliva, mucus, fluid in the joints, and urine.’ Thus he dwells observing unattractiveness in this body. Ānanda, this is called the perception of unattractiveness. (3)

Ānanda, what is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place, reflects thus: ‘This body is full of suffering, full of danger; for various diseases arise in this body, such as: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, head-disease, ear-ache, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, lip-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning sensation, fever, stomach-disease, fainting, dysentery, piercing pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, nail-scratch, skin-disease, hemorrhage, diabetes, piles, carbuncle, fistula; diseases arising from bile, diseases arising from phlegm, diseases arising from wind, diseases arising from a combination of the humors (sannipāta), diseases arising from change of season, diseases arising from improper care, diseases arising from assault,
344:
diseases arising from the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination.’ Thus he dwells observing danger in this body. Ānanda, this is called the perception of danger. (4)

Ānanda, what is the perception of abandoning? Here, Ānanda, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will; he abandons it, dispels it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of harmfulness; he abandons it, dispels it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence. He does not tolerate any arisen evil unwholesome states; he abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, and brings them to non-existence. Ānanda, this is called the perception of abandoning. (5)

Ānanda, what is the perception of dispassion? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place, reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, Nibbāna.’ Ānanda, this is called the perception of dispassion. (6)

Ānanda, what is the perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place, reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Ānanda, this is called the perception of cessation. (7)

Ānanda, what is the perception of non-delight in the whole world? Here, Ānanda, a monk dwells having abandoned those clingings, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies in the world, not clinging to them. Ānanda, this is called the perception of non-delight in the whole world. (8)

Ānanda, what is the perception of dissatisfaction with all formations? Here, Ānanda, a monk is troubled by, ashamed of, and disgusted with all formations. Ānanda, this is called the perception of dissatisfaction with all formations. (9)

Ānanda, what is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place, sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him.
345:
Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows, 'I breathe in long'; or breathing out long, he knows, 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he knows, 'I breathe in short'; or breathing out short, he knows, 'I breathe out short.' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body (the beginning, middle, and end of the breath)'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation (the gross in-breath)'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation (the gross out-breath).' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in experiencing rapture'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out experiencing rapture.' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure.' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation (feeling and perception)'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation (feeling and perception).' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in calming the mental formation (the gross feeling and perception)'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out calming the mental formation (the gross feeling and perception).' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mind'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.' He trains himself, 'I shall breathe in gladdening the mind... [as before] ... steadying the mind... [as before] ... liberating the mind... [as before] ... contemplating impermanence... [as before] ... contemplating fading away... [as before] ... contemplating cessation... [as before] ... contemplating relinquishment'; he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.' Ānanda, this is called mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). (10)

Ānanda, if you were to speak these ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda, it is possible that when the bhikkhu Girimānanda hears these ten perceptions, his affliction will immediately subside.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having learned these ten perceptions from the Blessed One, went to the Venerable Girimānanda and spoke these ten perceptions to him. When the Venerable Girimānanda heard these ten perceptions, his affliction immediately subsided. The Venerable Girimānanda rose from that affliction, and that affliction of the Venerable Girimānanda was entirely abandoned.
346:
Tenth Sutta.
The first chapter, the Sacitta Vagga, is finished.

## (7) 2. Yamaka Vagga
## 1. Avijjā Sutta

61. "Bhikkhus, a first point of ignorance is not discerned, such that one could say: 'Before this, ignorance did not exist; then it came into being.' But even though this is said, bhikkhus, it is discerned: 'Ignorance has this as its condition (nutriment).'

Bhikkhus, I say that ignorance, too, has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: 'The five hindrances.' Bhikkhus, I say that the five hindrances, too, have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? It should be said: 'The three types of misconduct.' Bhikkhus, I say that the three types of misconduct, too, have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three types of misconduct? It should be said: 'Lack of sense restraint.'

Bhikkhus, I say that lack of sense restraint, too, has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of sense restraint? It should be said: 'Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension.' Bhikkhus, I say that lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension, too, has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension? It should be said: 'Improper attention.' Bhikkhus, I say that improper attention, too, has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for improper attention? It should be said: 'Lack of faith.' Bhikkhus, I say that lack of faith, too, has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of faith? It should be said: 'Not hearing the True Dhamma.' Bhikkhus, I say that not hearing the True Dhamma, too, has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for not hearing the True Dhamma? It should be said: 'Not associating with superior persons.'

Thus, bhikkhus, when the lack of association with superior persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the not hearing of the True Dhamma. When the not hearing of the True Dhamma is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of faith. When the lack of faith is fulfilled, it fulfills improper attention. When improper attention is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension. When the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of sense restraint. When the lack of sense restraint is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of misconduct."
347:
When the three types of misconduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the five hindrances; when the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance (avijjā). Thus is the nutriment for that ignorance, and thus is its fulfillment.

Monks, it is like when it rains in thick drops on a mountain top, and the water, flowing down according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. When the small pools are full, they fill the large pools. When the large pools are full, they fill the small rivers. When the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers. When the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean called Sāgara. Thus is the nutriment for that great ocean called Sāgara, and thus is its fulfillment.

Monks, in the same way, when non-association with superior persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the not hearing of the true Dhamma. When the not hearing of the true Dhamma is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of faith. When the lack of faith is fulfilled, it fulfills unwise attention. When unwise attention is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension. When the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of restraint of the sense faculties. When the lack of restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of misconduct. When the three types of misconduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the five hindrances. When the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance. Thus is the nutriment for that ignorance, and thus is its fulfillment.

Monks, I say that true knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti)¹ also has a nutriment; I do not say it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for true knowledge and liberation? It should be said: "The seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)." Monks, I say that the seven factors of enlightenment also have a nutriment; I do not say they are without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the seven factors of enlightenment? It should be said: "The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)." Monks, I say that the four foundations of mindfulness also have a nutriment; I do not say they are without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the four foundations of mindfulness? It should be said: "The three types of good conduct (sucarita)." Monks, I say that the three types of good conduct also have a nutriment; I do not say they are without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three types of good conduct? It should be said: "Restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara)." Monks, I say that restraint of the sense faculties also has a nutriment; I do not say it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for restraint of the sense faculties? It should be said: "Mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña)." Monks, I say that mindfulness and clear comprehension also have a nutriment; I do not say they are without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for mindfulness and clear comprehension? It should be said: "Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra)." Monks, I say that wise attention also has a nutriment; I do not say it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for wise attention? It should be said: "Faith (saddhā)." Monks, I say that faith also has a nutriment; I do not say it is without nutriment. What is the nutriment...
348:
...for faith? It should be said: "Hearing the true Dhamma (saddhamma-savana)." Monks, I say that hearing the true Dhamma also has a nutriment; I do not say it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for hearing the true Dhamma? It should be said: "Association with superior persons (sappurisa-saṃseva)."

Thus, monks, when association with superior persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the hearing of the true Dhamma. When the hearing of the true Dhamma is fulfilled, it fulfills faith. When faith is fulfilled, it fulfills wise attention. When wise attention is fulfilled, it fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension. When mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills restraint of the sense faculties. When restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of good conduct. When the three types of good conduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness. When the four foundations of mindfulness are fulfilled, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. When the seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation. Thus is the nutriment for that true knowledge and liberation, and thus is its fulfillment.

Monks, it is like when it rains in thick drops on a mountain top, and the water, flowing down according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. When the small pools are full, they fill the large pools. When the large pools are full, they fill the small rivers. When the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers. When the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean called Sāgara. Thus is the nutriment for that great ocean called Sāgara, and thus is its fulfillment.

Monks, in the same way, when association with superior persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the hearing of the true Dhamma. When the hearing of the true Dhamma is fulfilled, it fulfills faith. When faith is fulfilled, it fulfills wise attention. When wise attention is fulfilled, it fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension. When mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills restraint of the sense faculties. When restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of good conduct. When the three types of good conduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness. When the four foundations of mindfulness are fulfilled, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. When the seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation. Thus is the nutriment for that true knowledge and liberation, and thus is its fulfillment.

The First Sutta.

1. The knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship is called 'vijjā'; the remaining associated states are called 'vimutti'.

## 2. Taṇhā Sutta

62. “Monks, a first point of craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) is not discerned, such that one could say: 'Before this, craving for existence did not exist; then it came into being.' But, monks, though this is so, it is discerned: 'Craving for existence has this as its condition.'"
349:
Monks, I say that craving for existence has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for craving for existence? It should be said: 'Ignorance.' Monks, I say that ignorance has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: 'The five hindrances.' Monks, I say that the five hindrances have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? It should be said: 'The three types of misconduct.' Monks, I say that the three types of misconduct have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three types of misconduct? It should be said: 'Lack of sense restraint.' Monks, I say that the lack of sense restraint has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the lack of sense restraint? It should be said: 'Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension.' Monks, I say that the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension? It should be said: 'Improper attention.' Monks, I say that improper attention has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for improper attention? It should be said: 'Lack of faith.' Monks, I say that the lack of faith has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the lack of faith? It should be said: 'Not hearing the true Dhamma.' Monks, I say that not hearing the true Dhamma has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for not hearing the true Dhamma? It should be said: 'Not associating with good persons.'

Thus, monks, when association with bad persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the hearing of the false Dhamma. When the hearing of the false Dhamma is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of faith. When the lack of faith is fulfilled, it fulfills improper attention. When improper attention is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension. When the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of sense restraint. When the lack of sense restraint is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of misconduct. When the three types of misconduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the five hindrances. When the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance. When ignorance is fulfilled, it fulfills craving for existence. Thus is the nutriment for craving for existence, and thus is its fulfillment.

Monks, just as when rain falls heavily on a mountain top, the water flows down according to the slope and fills the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. When the small pools are full, they fill the large pools. When the large pools are full, they fill the small rivers.
350:
When the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers. When the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean called Sāgara. Thus is the nutriment for the great ocean called Sāgara, and thus is its fulfillment.

In the same way, monks, when association with bad persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the hearing of the false Dhamma. When the hearing of the false Dhamma is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of faith. When the lack of faith is fulfilled, it fulfills improper attention. When improper attention is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension. When the lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills the lack of sense restraint. When the lack of sense restraint is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of misconduct. When the three types of misconduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the five hindrances. When the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance. When ignorance is fulfilled, it fulfills craving for existence. Thus is the nutriment for craving for existence, and thus is its fulfillment.

Monks, I say that true knowledge and liberation have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for true knowledge and liberation? It should be said: 'The seven factors of enlightenment.' Monks, I say that the seven factors of enlightenment have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the seven factors of enlightenment? It should be said: 'The four foundations of mindfulness.' Monks, I say that the four foundations of mindfulness have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the four foundations of mindfulness? It should be said: 'The three types of good conduct.' Monks, I say that the three types of good conduct have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three types of good conduct? It should be said: 'Sense restraint.' Monks, I say that sense restraint has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for sense restraint? It should be said: 'Mindfulness and clear comprehension.' Monks, I say that mindfulness and clear comprehension have a nutriment; I do not say they are without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for mindfulness and clear comprehension? It should be said: 'Proper attention.' Monks, I say that proper attention has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for proper attention? It should be said: 'Faith.' Monks, I say that faith has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for faith? It should be said: 'Hearing the true Dhamma.' Monks, I say that hearing the true Dhamma has a nutriment; I do not say it is without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for hearing the true Dhamma? It should be said: 'Associating with good persons.'

Thus, monks, when association with good persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the hearing of the true Dhamma. When the hearing of the true Dhamma is fulfilled, it fulfills faith. When faith is fulfilled, it fulfills proper attention.
351:
When wise attention is fulfilled, it fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension. When mindfulness and clear comprehension are fulfilled, they fulfill the restraint of the senses. When the restraint of the senses is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of good conduct. When the three types of good conduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness. When the four foundations of mindfulness are fulfilled, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. When the seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled, they fulfill knowledge and liberation.

In this way, there is nutriment for that knowledge and liberation, and in this way, there is fulfillment. Monks, just as when it rains heavily on a mountain top, that water flows down to the lowlands... [etc.]... in this way, there is nutriment for that great ocean called Sāgara, and in this way, there is fulfillment. Monks, in the same way, when association with superior persons is fulfilled, it fulfills hearing the true Dhamma... [etc.]... in this way, there is nutriment for that knowledge and liberation, and in this way, there is fulfillment. (Thus he said).

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Niṭṭhaṅgata Sutta

63. "Monks, all those who have reached certainty in me are endowed with right view. Among those endowed with right view, five types attain final Nibbāna right here (in the sense-sphere), and five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here. Which five types attain final Nibbāna right here? The one who is a stream-enterer for seven times at most (sattakkhattuparama), the one who goes from family to family (kolaṃkola), the one who has only one more seed (ekabījī), the once-returner (sakadāgāmī), and the one who becomes an Arahant in this very life—these five types attain final Nibbāna right here. Which five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here? The one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), and the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī)—these five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here. Monks, all those who have reached certainty in me are endowed with right view. Among those endowed with right view, these five types attain final Nibbāna right here, and these five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here." (Thus he said).

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Aveccappasanna Sutta

64. "Monks, all those who have unwavering confidence in me are stream-enterers. Among those stream-enterers, five types attain final Nibbāna right here, and five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here. Which five types attain final Nibbāna right here? The one who is a stream-enterer for seven times at most, the one who goes from family to family, the one who has only one more seed, the once-returner, and the one who becomes an Arahant in this very life—these five types attain final Nibbāna right here. Which five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here? The one who attains Nibbāna in the interval, the one who attains Nibbāna upon landing, the one who attains Nibbāna without exertion, the one who attains Nibbāna with exertion, and the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm—these five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here. Monks, all those who have unwavering confidence in me are stream-enterers."
352:
"Among those stream-enterers, these five types attain final Nibbāna right here, and these five types attain final Nibbāna after leaving here." (Thus he said).

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Paṭhama Sukha Sutta

65. On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying in the village of Nālaka in the Magadha country. Then Sāmaṇḍakāni the wanderer approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. After finishing the polite and friendly conversation, he sat down at one side. While sitting there, he asked the Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, what is happiness and what is suffering?"

"Friend, rebirth (abhinibbatti) is suffering, and non-rebirth is happiness. Friend, when there is rebirth, this suffering can be expected: cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the need to defecate, the need to urinate, contact with fire, contact with sticks, contact with weapons, and the irritation caused by relatives and friends who come together. Friend, when there is rebirth, this suffering can be expected. Friend, when there is no rebirth, this happiness can be expected: no cold, no heat, no hunger, no thirst, no need to defecate, no need to urinate, no contact with fire, no contact with sticks, no contact with weapons, and no irritation caused by relatives and friends who come together. Friend, when there is no rebirth, this happiness can be expected." (Thus he said).

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Dutiya Sukha Sutta

66. On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying in the village of Nālaka in the Magadha country. Then Sāmaṇḍakāni the wanderer approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. After finishing the polite and friendly conversation, he sat down at one side. While sitting there, he asked the Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, in this Dhamma-Vinaya (Dispensation), what is happiness and what is suffering?"

"Friend, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, discontent (anabhirati) is suffering, and delight (abhirati) is happiness. Friend, when there is discontent, one finds no happiness or pleasure even while walking. Even while standing. Even while sitting. Even while lying down. Even while entering a village."
353:
...even when gone to the forest; even when gone to the root of a tree; even when gone to an empty place; even when gone to the open air; even when in the midst of monks, one does not find happiness or pleasure. Friends, when there is a lack of delight, this suffering is to be expected.

Friends, when there is delight, this happiness is to be expected—even when walking, one finds happiness and pleasure; even when standing; even when sitting; even when lying down; even when gone to a village; even when gone to the forest; even when gone to the root of a tree; even when gone to an empty place; even when gone to the open air; even when in the midst of monks, one finds happiness and pleasure. Friends, when there is delight, this happiness is to be expected.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Paṭhamanalakapāna Sutta

67. On one occasion, the Blessed One was wandering on a tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at a Kosalan town named Nalakapāna. There, the Blessed One stayed at Nalakapāna in the Palāsa grove. At that time, on the Uposatha day, the Blessed One was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. Then, having instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the monks with a Dhamma talk for much of the night, the Blessed One looked over the silent Saṅgha of monks and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:

"Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of monks is free from sloth and torpor (thina-middha). Sāriputta, let a Dhamma talk occur to you for the monks. My back is aching; I will stretch it."

"Yes, Bhante," the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe (saṅghāṭi) folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture (sīhaseyya), placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having attended to the thought of rising.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: "Friends, monks." "Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this: "Friends, for anyone who has no faith in wholesome states,"
354:
...who has no shame, no fear of wrongdoing, no energy, no wisdom in wholesome states—whether it be night or day that comes, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.

Friends, just as in the dark fortnight, whether it be night or day that comes to the moon, it wanes in beauty, wanes in its orb, wanes in its light, and wanes in its diameter and circumference; even so, friends, for anyone who has no faith in wholesome states, no shame, no fear of wrongdoing, no energy, no wisdom in wholesome states—whether it be night or day that comes, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.

"Friends, a person who is faithless"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who is shameless"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who is fearless of wrongdoing"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who is lazy"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who is unwise"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who is angry"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who is vengeful"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who is of evil desires"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who has bad friends"—this is a decline. "Friends, a person who has wrong view"—this is a decline.

Friends, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states, has shame, has fear of wrongdoing, has energy, has wisdom in wholesome states—whether it be night or day that comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. Friends, just as in the bright fortnight, whether it be night or day that comes to the moon, it waxes in beauty, waxes in its orb, waxes in its light, and waxes in its diameter and circumference; even so, friends, for anyone who has faith, shame, fear of wrongdoing, energy—only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
355:
"Friends, the statement 'a person who has faith' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has a sense of shame' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has fear of wrongdoing' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has aroused energy' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has wisdom' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who is without anger' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who is without malice' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has few wishes' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has good friends' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has right view' is a state of non-decline."

Then the Blessed One, having risen, addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: "Sadhu, sadhu, Sāriputta! Sāriputta, for anyone who has no faith in wholesome states, no sense of shame, no fear of wrongdoing, no energy, no wisdom in wholesome states, whatever night or day comes to him, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.

Sāriputta, just as in the dark fortnight, for the moon, whatever night or day comes, it wanes in color, wanes in its orb, wanes in brightness, and wanes in its diameter and circumference; even so, Sāriputta, for anyone who has no faith in wholesome states... [p]... no wisdom in wholesome states, whatever night or day comes... [p]... growth is not to be expected.

Sāriputta, the statement 'a person who is faithless' is a state of decline. 'A person who is shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, lazy, unwise, angry, malicious, of evil wishes, of evil friendship, a person who has wrong view' is a state of decline.

Sāriputta, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states, has a sense of shame, has fear of wrongdoing, has energy, has wisdom in wholesome states, whatever night or day comes to him, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. Sāriputta, just as in the bright fortnight, for the moon, whatever night or day comes, it waxes in color, waxes in its orb, waxes in brightness, and waxes in its diameter and circumference; even so, Sāriputta, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states, has a sense of shame, has fear of wrongdoing, has energy, has wisdom in wholesome states, whatever night or day comes to him, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected,"
356:
decline is not to be expected.

Sāriputta, the statement 'a person who has faith' is a state of non-decline. 'A person who has a sense of shame, fear of wrongdoing, aroused energy, wisdom, is without anger, without malice, has few wishes, has good friends, a person who has right view' is a state of non-decline," said the Blessed One.

The seventh discourse.

## 8. Second Naḷakapāna Sutta

68. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Naḷakapāna in the Palāsa Grove. At that time, the Blessed One was sitting surrounded by the community of monks on the Uposatha day. Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the monks with a Dhamma talk for much of the night, looked around at the silent community of monks and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:

"Sāriputta, the community of monks is free from sloth and torpor (thina-middha). Sāriputta, let a Dhamma talk occur to you for the monks. My back aches; I will stretch it."

"Yes, Bhante," the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the thought of rising.

Thereupon, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: "Friends, monks!"

"Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

"Friends, for anyone who has no faith in wholesome states, no sense of shame, no fear of wrongdoing, no energy, no wisdom, no listening (to the Dhamma), no retention of the Dhamma, no examination of the meaning, no practice in accordance with the Dhamma, no heedfulness in wholesome states, whatever night or day comes to him, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth. Friends, just as in the dark fortnight, for the moon, whatever night or day comes, it wanes in color, wanes in its orb, wanes in brightness, and wanes in its diameter and circumference; even so, friends, for anyone who has no faith in wholesome states, no sense of shame, no fear of wrongdoing, no energy, no wisdom, no listening, no retention of the Dhamma, no examination of the meaning, no practice in accordance with the Dhamma, no heedfulness in wholesome states, whatever night or day comes to him, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected,"
357:
growth is not to be expected.

Friends, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states, has a sense of shame, has fear of wrongdoing, has energy, has wisdom, has the habit of listening, has the quality of retaining the Dhamma, has the quality of examining the meaning, has the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, and has diligence in wholesome states—whether by night or by day, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.

Friends, just as in the bright fortnight, for the moon, whether by night or by day, it grows in beauty, grows in its orb, grows in radiance, and grows in height and circumference; even so, friends, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states... p... has diligence in wholesome states, whether by night or by day, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.

Then the Blessed One, having risen from his seclusion, addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: "Sadhu, sadhu, Sāriputta! For anyone, Sāriputta, who lacks faith in wholesome states, lacks a sense of shame, lacks fear of wrongdoing, lacks energy, lacks wisdom, lacks the habit of listening, lacks the quality of retaining the Dhamma, lacks the quality of examining the meaning, lacks the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, and lacks diligence in wholesome states—whether by night or by day, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth. Sāriputta, just as in the dark fortnight, for the moon, whether by night or by day, it wanes in beauty, wanes in its orb, wanes in radiance, and wanes in height and circumference; even so, Sāriputta, for anyone who lacks faith in wholesome states... p... lacks diligence in wholesome states, whether by night or by day, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.

Sāriputta, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states, has a sense of shame, has fear of wrongdoing, has energy, has wisdom, has the habit of listening, has the quality of retaining the Dhamma, has the quality of examining the meaning, has the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, and has diligence in wholesome states—whether by night or by day, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. Sāriputta, just as in the bright fortnight, for the moon, whether by night or by day, it grows in beauty, grows in its orb, grows in radiance, and grows in height and circumference;
358:
Sāriputta, even so, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states... p... has diligence in wholesome states, whether by night or by day, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline," so He said.

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Paṭhamakathāvatthu Sutta

69. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. At that time, many monks, after returning from their alms round after the meal, were sitting together in the assembly hall, engaged in various kinds of low talk (tiracchānakathā). These were: talk about kings, talk about thieves, talk about ministers, talk about armies, talk about dangers, talk about battles, talk about food, talk about drink, talk about clothing, talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about perfumes, talk about relatives, talk about vehicles, talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about districts, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about watering places, talk about the departed, miscellaneous talk, talk about the world, talk about the sea, and talk about success and failure.

Then the Blessed One, having emerged from His seclusion in the evening, went to the assembly hall and sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, for what kind of talk are you sitting together now? And what was the conversation that was interrupted?"

"Venerable Sir, after returning from our alms round after the meal, we were sitting together in the assembly hall engaged in various kinds of low talk. These talks were: talk about kings, talk about thieves... p... talk about success and failure; these were the topics," they replied.

"Monks, it is not fitting for you, sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, to engage in various kinds of low talk, such as: talk about kings, talk about thieves, talk about ministers, talk about armies, talk about dangers, talk about battles, talk about food, talk about drink, talk about clothing, talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about perfumes, talk about relatives, talk about vehicles, talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about districts, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about watering places, talk about the departed, miscellaneous talk, talk about the world, talk about the sea, and talk about success and failure.

Monks, there are these ten topics of conversation that lead to benefit and happiness."
359:
What are the ten? They are: talk on fewness of wishes, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on arousal of energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation (the fruit of arahantship), and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation. Monks, these are the ten topics of conversation that are the cause of welfare and happiness.

Monks, if you were to engage in conversation by repeatedly referring to these ten topics of conversation (which are the cause of welfare and happiness), you could outshine even the radiance of the sun and moon, which are so powerful and majestic, with your own radiance; what then to say of the wanderers of other sects?

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Dutiya Kathāvatthu Sutta

70. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. At that time, many monks, after returning from their alms round after the meal, were sitting together in the assembly hall, engaged in various kinds of lowly talk (contrary to the path). What were they? Talk about kings, talk about thieves, talk about ministers... [etc.] ...talk about prosperity and decline.

Monks, there are these ten praiseworthy grounds. What are the ten? Here, monks, a monk is himself one of few wishes and is one who speaks to the monks on fewness of wishes. 'The monk is of few wishes and speaks to the monks on fewness of wishes'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself contented and is one who speaks to the monks on contentment. 'The monk is contented and speaks to the monks on contentment'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself secluded and is one who speaks to the monks on seclusion. 'The monk is secluded and speaks to the monks on seclusion'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself non-associated and is one who speaks to the monks on non-association. 'The monk is non-associated and speaks to the monks on non-association'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself one of aroused energy and is one who speaks to the monks on the arousal of energy. 'The monk is of aroused energy and speaks to the monks on the arousal of energy'—this is a praiseworthy ground.
360:
He is himself possessed of virtue and is one who speaks to the monks on the attainment of virtue. 'The monk is possessed of virtue and speaks to the monks on the attainment of virtue'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself possessed of concentration and is one who speaks to the monks on the attainment of concentration. 'The monk is possessed of concentration and speaks to the monks on the attainment of concentration'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself possessed of wisdom and is one who speaks to the monks on the attainment of wisdom. 'The monk is possessed of wisdom and speaks to the monks on the attainment of wisdom'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself possessed of liberation (the fruit of arahantship) and is one who speaks to the monks on the attainment of liberation. 'The monk is possessed of liberation (the fruit of arahantship) and speaks to the monks on the attainment of liberation'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

He is himself possessed of the knowledge and vision of liberation (the fruit of arahantship) and is one who speaks to the monks on the attainment of the knowledge and vision of liberation. 'The monk is possessed of the knowledge and vision of liberation (the fruit of arahantship) and speaks to the monks on the attainment of the knowledge and vision of liberation'—this is a praiseworthy ground.

Monks, these are the ten praiseworthy grounds.

The Tenth Sutta.

The second Yamaka Vagga is finished.

Its summary:
Ignorance, craving, and the goal; verified confidence, two on happiness;
Two are spoken at Naḷakapāna, and two more on the topics of conversation.

## (C) 3. Ākaṅkha Vagga

## 1. Ākaṅkha Sutta

71. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks!' 'Venerable Sir!' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

Monks, dwell possessed of virtue...
361:
"Monks, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults. Having undertaken the rules of training, train yourselves in them.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be dear and agreeable to my companions in the holy life, respected and esteemed,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues, is devoted to internal serenity of mind, does not neglect meditation, is possessed of insight, and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues, is devoted to internal serenity of mind, does not neglect meditation, is possessed of insight, and frequents empty huts.
