If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May the services of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick I use be of great fruit and great benefit,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues... [...] and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May it be of great fruit and great benefit for those departed relatives and kinsmen who remember me with a confident heart,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues... [...] and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be one who is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick I receive,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues... [...] and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be one who endures cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; ill-spoken, unwelcome words; and arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, displeasing, and life-threatening,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues... [...] and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be a conqueror of aversion and delight, may aversion and delight not conquer me, and may I dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen aversion and delight,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues... [...] and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be a conqueror of fear and dread,
362:
may fear and dread not conquer me, and may I dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen fear and dread,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues... [...] and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I be one who obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues... [...] and frequents empty huts.

If a bhikkhu should desire: 'May I, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life, realize for myself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues, is devoted to internal serenity of mind, does not neglect meditation, is possessed of insight, and frequents empty huts.

'Monks, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults. Having undertaken the rules of training, train yourselves in them.' Thus, what was said was said in reference to this."

The First Sutta.

## 2. Kaṇṭaka Sutta

72. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof together with many well-known elder disciples—with the Venerable Cāla, the Venerable Upacāla, the Venerable Kukkuṭa, the Venerable Kaḷimbha, the Venerable Nikaṭa, the Venerable Kaṭissaha, and other well-known elder disciples.

At that time, many well-known Licchavis were entering the Great Wood in magnificent vehicles, one after another, with great noise and din, to see the Blessed One. Then those Venerables had this thought: "Many well-known Licchavis are entering the Great Wood in magnificent vehicles, one after another, with great noise and din, to see the Blessed One. The Blessed One has said: 'Sounds are thorns to the jhānas.'"
363:
"It would be good if we were to go to the Gosiṅga Sāla forest and dwell there in comfort, with little noise and few distractions." (This was their thought). Then those venerable ones went to the Gosiṅga Sāla forest and dwelt there in comfort, with little noise and few distractions.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, where is Cāla? Where is Upacāla? Where is Kukkuṭa? Where is Kaḷimbha? Where is Nikaṭa? Where is Kaṭissaha? Monks, where have those elder disciples gone?"

"Venerable Sir, those venerable ones had this thought: 'Many famous Licchavīs are entering the Mahāvana in fine vehicles, one after another, with loud and great noise to see the Blessed One. The Blessed One has said: "Noise is a thorn to jhāna." It would be good if we were to go to the Gosiṅga Sāla forest and dwell there in comfort, with little noise and few distractions.' Venerable Sir, then those venerable ones went to the Gosiṅga Sāla forest and are now dwelling there in comfort, with little noise and few distractions."

"Sadhu, sadhu, monks. As those great disciples would rightly answer, so they have answered. It is true, monks, I have said: 'Noise is a thorn to jhāna.' Monks, there are these ten thorns. What ten? Delight in company is a thorn to one who delights in solitude. Devotion to the sign of beauty is a thorn to one devoted to the sign of foulness. Watching shows, which is like a thorn (to the Dispensation), is a thorn to one who guards the sense doors. Proximity to women is a thorn to the holy life. Noise is a thorn to the first jhāna. Thought and examination are thorns to the second jhāna. Rapture is a thorn to the third jhāna. In-breathing and out-breathing are thorns to the fourth jhāna. Both perception and feeling are thorns to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Lust is a thorn, hatred is a thorn, and delusion is a thorn.

Monks, dwell without thorns."
364:
"Monks, dwell without thorns. Monks, dwell free from thorns. Monks, dwell without thorns and free from thorns. Monks, Arahants are without thorns. Monks, Arahants are free from thorns. Monks, Arahants are without thorns and free from thorns."

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Iṭṭhadhamma Sutta

73. "Monks, these ten things in the world are desirable, liked, charming, and rare. What ten? Wealth in the world is desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Beauty in the world is desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Health in the world is desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Virtue in the world is desirable, liked, charming, and rare. The holy life in the world is desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Friends in the world are desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Great learning in the world is desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Wisdom in the world is desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Teachings in the world are desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Heavens in the world are desirable, liked, charming, and rare.

Monks, there are ten obstacles to these ten things in the world that are desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Laziness and lack of effort are obstacles to wealth. Lack of grooming and adornment is an obstacle to beauty. Unsuitable behavior (regarding health) is an obstacle to health. Having bad friends is an obstacle to virtue. Lack of sense restraint is an obstacle to the holy life. Deception (lying) is an obstacle to friends. Lack of recitation is an obstacle to great learning. Lack of desire to listen and lack of inquiring are obstacles to wisdom. Lack of application and lack of reflection are obstacles to the teachings. Wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavens. Monks, these are the ten obstacles to these ten things in the world that are desirable, liked, charming, and rare.

Monks, there are ten causes for these ten things in the world that are desirable, liked, charming, and rare. Effort and non-laziness are the causes of wealth. Grooming and adornment are the causes of beauty. Doing what is suitable (regarding health) is the cause of health. Having good friends is the cause of virtue. Sense restraint is the cause of the holy life. Non-deception (not lying) is the cause of friends. Recitation is the cause of great learning. The desire to listen and inquiring are the causes of wisdom. Application and reflection are the causes of the teachings,"
365:
Right practice is the cause for the heavenly realms. Monks, these ten things are the causes for these ten desirable, pleasant, agreeable, and rare things in the world.

The third discourse.

## 4. Vaḍḍhi Sutta

74. Monks, a noble disciple who grows in ten ways grows with the noble growth, taking the essence and taking the best of the body. In what ten ways? He grows in fields and lands; he grows in wealth and grain; he grows in children and wives; he grows in slaves, workers, and men; he grows in four-footed animals; he grows in faith; he grows in virtue; he grows in learning; he grows in generosity; and he grows in wisdom. Monks, a noble disciple who grows in these ten ways grows with the noble growth, taking the essence and taking the best of the body.

"One who grows here in wealth and grain,
In children, wives, and four-footed animals,
Becomes wealthy, famous, and honored
By relatives, friends, and even by kings.

One who grows here in faith and virtue,
In wisdom, generosity, and learning—both,
Such a virtuous person, being discerning,
Grows in both ways in this very life."

The fourth discourse.

## 5. Migasālā Sutta

75. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery. Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and outer robe, approached the residence of the laywoman Migasālā and sat down on the prepared seat. Then the laywoman Migasālā approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the laywoman Migasālā said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how is this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be understood, when one who leads the holy life and one who does not lead the holy life will both have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter? Venerable sir, my father Purāṇa led the holy life; he lived apart from it, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the village practice.
366:
When my father died, the Blessed One declared: 'He is a Once-returner who has been reborn in the Tusita heaven.' Venerable sir, my grandfather Isidatta was one who did not lead the holy life, but was content with his own wife. When he died, the Blessed One also declared: 'He is a Once-returner who has been reborn in the Tusita heaven.'

"Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how is this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be understood, when one who leads the holy life and one who does not lead the holy life will both have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter?"

"Sister, it was indeed declared so by the Blessed One."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received almsfood at the residence of the laywoman Migasālā, rose from his seat and departed. Then, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, in the morning, having dressed and taking my bowl and outer robe, I approached the residence of the laywoman Migasālā and sat down on the prepared seat. Then, venerable sir, the laywoman Migasālā approached me, paid homage to me, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the laywoman Migasālā said this to me:

'Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how is this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be understood, when one who leads the holy life and one who does not lead the holy life will both have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter? Venerable sir, my father Purāṇa led the holy life; he lived apart from it, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the village practice. When my father died, the Blessed One declared: "He is a Once-returner who has been reborn in the Tusita heaven." Venerable sir, my grandfather Isidatta was one who did not lead the holy life, but was content with his own wife. When he died, the Blessed One also declared: "He is a Once-returner who has been reborn in the Tusita heaven."

'Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how is this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be understood, when one who leads the holy life and one who does not lead the holy life will both have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter?' Venerable sir, when she said this, I answered the laywoman Migasālā: 'Sister, it was indeed declared so by the Blessed One.'"
367:
Who is Migasālā the laywoman, Ānanda? She is but a foolish, unskilled woman, with only a woman’s wisdom. And what is the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of persons [Indriyaparopariya Ñāṇa]? (Only the Buddhas, whose knowledge is unobstructed, possess it.)

Ānanda, these ten types of persons are found existing in the world. What are the ten? Ānanda, here a certain person is immoral. He does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—the 'Fruition of Arahantship'—wherein that immorality ceases without remainder. He has not done what should be done through hearing, nor through learning, nor has he penetrated it with wisdom. He does not attain even temporary liberation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds toward decline, not toward excellence; he is one who goes to decline, not one who goes to excellence. (1)

Ānanda, here another person is immoral. But he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—the 'Fruition of Arahantship'—wherein that immorality ceases without remainder. He has done what should be done through hearing, and through learning, and has penetrated it with wisdom. He attains temporary liberation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds toward excellence, not toward decline; he is one who goes to excellence, not one who goes to decline. (2)

In this case, Ānanda, those who measure [judge] say: 'This person has these same qualities, and the other person also has these same qualities. Why then, among these two, is one inferior and the other superior?' Ānanda, such measuring [judging] will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Ānanda, of these two persons, the one who is immoral but understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—the 'Fruition of Arahantship'—wherein that immorality ceases without remainder; who has done what should be done through hearing, and through learning, and has penetrated it with wisdom; and who attains temporary liberation—Ānanda, this person is more excellent and more refined than the former person. Why is that? Ānanda, it is because the stream of Dhamma [insight] carries this person [to the stage of the Noble Ones]. Who else could know this difference except the Tathāgata? Therefore, Ānanda, do not be measurers of persons; do not take measures of persons. Ānanda, one who takes measures of persons digs [a pit for himself].
368:
Ānanda, either I or one like me may take the measure of persons.

Ānanda, here a certain person is virtuous. But he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—the 'Fruition of Arahantship'—wherein that virtue ceases without remainder. He has not done what should be done through hearing, nor through learning, nor has he penetrated it with wisdom. He does not attain even temporary liberation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds toward decline, not toward excellence; he is one who goes to decline, not one who goes to excellence. (3)

Ānanda, here another person is virtuous. And he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—the 'Fruition of Arahantship'—wherein that virtue ceases without remainder. He has done what should be done through hearing, and through learning, and has penetrated it with wisdom. He attains temporary liberation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds toward excellence, not toward decline; he is one who goes to excellence, not one who goes to decline. (4)

In this case, Ānanda, those who measure say... [as before]... Ānanda, either I or one like me may take the measure of persons.

Ānanda, here a certain person has intense passion. But he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—the 'Fruition of Arahantship'—wherein that passion ceases without remainder. He has not done what should be done through hearing, nor through learning, nor has he penetrated it with wisdom. He does not attain even temporary liberation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds toward decline, not toward excellence; he is one who goes to decline, not one who goes to excellence. (5)

Ānanda, here another person has intense passion. But he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—the 'Fruition of Arahantship'—wherein that passion ceases without remainder. He has done what should be done through hearing, and through learning, and has penetrated it with wisdom. He attains temporary liberation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds toward excellence, not toward decline; he is one who goes to excellence, not one who goes to decline. (6)

In this case, Ānanda, those who measure say... [as before]... Ānanda, either I or one like me may take the measure of persons.
369:
“Ānanda, here some person is prone to anger. He does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom (the fruit of Arahatship) where that anger ceases without remainder. He has not done what should be done through hearing, nor has he done what should be done through great learning, nor has he penetrated what should be known through wisdom, nor does he attain temporary liberation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he heads for decline, not for distinction; he is one who goes to decline, not one who goes to distinction. (7)

“Ānanda, here some person is prone to anger. But he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom (the fruit of Arahatship) where that anger ceases without remainder. He has done what should be done through hearing, he has done what should be done through great learning, he has penetrated what should be known through wisdom, and he attains temporary liberation (vimutti) from time to time. With the breakup of the body, after death, he heads for distinction, not for decline; he is one who goes to distinction, not one who goes to decline. (8)

“Ānanda, regarding those two persons, those who measure (judge) others compare them... [as before]... Ānanda, either I or one like me may take the measure of persons. Ānanda, here some person is restless. He does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom (the fruit of Arahatship) where that restlessness ceases without remainder. He has not done what should be done through hearing, nor has he done what should be done through great learning, nor has he penetrated what should be known through wisdom, nor does he attain temporary liberation (vimutti). With the breakup of the body, after death, he heads for decline, not for distinction; he is one who goes to decline, not one who goes to distinction. (9)

“Ānanda, here some person is restless. But he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom (the fruit of Arahatship) where that restlessness ceases without remainder. He has done what should be done through hearing, he has done what should be done through great learning, he has penetrated what should be known through wisdom, and he attains temporary liberation (vimutti) from time to time. With the breakup of the body, after death, he heads for distinction, not for decline; he is one who goes to distinction, not one who goes to decline. (10)

“Ānanda, regarding those two persons, those who measure (judge) others say: 'This person has these same qualities, and the other person also has these same qualities.
370:
and the other person also has these same qualities; why then is one of them low (in quality) and the other excellent?' Thus they judge. Ānanda, such judging leads to their harm and suffering for a long time. Ānanda, of those two persons, the one who is restless but understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom (the fruit of Arahatship) where that restlessness ceases without remainder; who has done what should be done through hearing, through great learning, has penetrated it through wisdom, and attains temporary liberation (vimutti) from time to time—Ānanda, this person is more excellent and more refined than the former person. Why is that? Ānanda, it is because the stream of Dhamma (insight) carries this person along (to the stage of the Noble Ones). Who else could know that reason except the Tathāgata? Therefore, Ānanda, do not be measurers of persons; do not take the measure of persons. Ānanda, one who takes the measure of persons digs up (destroys) himself. Either I, Ānanda, or one like me may take the measure of persons. Ānanda, who is the laywoman Migasālā? She is just a foolish, incompetent woman with a woman's wisdom. And who are those (the Buddhas) who possess the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of persons (indriyaparopariyañāṇa) without any obstruction? Ānanda, these ten types of persons are found existing in the world. Ānanda, if Isidatta had been possessed of the same kind of virtue that Purāṇa was possessed of, then Purāṇa would not have even known Isidatta's destination. Ānanda, if Purāṇa had been possessed of the same kind of wisdom that Isidatta was possessed of, then Isidatta would not have even known Purāṇa's destination. Thus, Ānanda, both these persons were deficient in one factor."
The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Tayodhamma Sutta
76. "Monks, if these three things did not exist in the world, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, would not arise in the world, and the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata would not shine in the world. What are the three? Birth, aging, and death. Monks, if these three things did not exist in the world, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, would not arise in the world, and the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata would not shine in the world."
371:
Bhikkhus, it is only because these three things exist in the world that the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arises in the world, and the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata shine in the world. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death. What are the three? They are: lust, hatred, and delusion. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death. (1)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion. What are the three? They are: identity view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion. (2)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning identity view, abandoning doubt, and abandoning misapprehension of precepts and observances. What are the three? They are: unwise attention, following a wrong path, and sluggishness of mind. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning identity view, abandoning doubt, and abandoning misapprehension of precepts and observances. (3)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning unwise attention, abandoning the following of a wrong path, and abandoning sluggishness of mind. What are the three? They are: forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction of mind. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning unwise attention, abandoning the following of a wrong path, and abandoning sluggishness of mind. (4)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning forgetfulness, abandoning the lack of clear comprehension, and abandoning distraction of mind. What are the three? They are: no desire to see the Noble Ones, no desire to hear the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and a fault-finding mind. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning forgetfulness, abandoning the lack of clear comprehension, and abandoning distraction of mind. (5)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones, abandoning the lack of desire to hear the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and abandoning a fault-finding mind. What are the three? They are: restlessness, lack of restraint, and immorality.
372:
Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones, abandoning the lack of desire to hear the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and abandoning a fault-finding mind. (6)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning restlessness, abandoning the lack of restraint, and abandoning immorality. What are the three? They are: lack of faith, unresponsiveness to what is said, and laziness. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning restlessness, abandoning the lack of restraint, and abandoning immorality. (7)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning the lack of faith, abandoning unresponsiveness to what is said, and abandoning laziness. What are the three? They are: disrespect, being difficult to admonish, and having bad friends. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning the lack of faith, abandoning unresponsiveness to what is said, and abandoning laziness. (8)

Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning being difficult to admonish, and abandoning having bad friends. What are the three? They are: shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, and heedlessness. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning being difficult to admonish, and abandoning having bad friends. (9)

Bhikkhus, one who is shameless and fearless of wrongdoing is heedless. Being heedless, he is incapable of abandoning disrespect, being difficult to admonish, and having bad friends. Having bad friends, he is incapable of abandoning the lack of faith, unresponsiveness to what is said, and laziness. Being lazy, he is incapable of abandoning restlessness, the lack of restraint, and immorality. Being immoral, he is incapable of abandoning the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones, the lack of desire to hear the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and a fault-finding mind. Having a fault-finding mind, he is incapable of abandoning forgetfulness, the lack of clear comprehension, and distraction of mind. Having a distracted mind, he is incapable of abandoning unwise attention, the following of a wrong path, and sluggishness of mind. Having a sluggish mind, he is incapable of abandoning identity view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances. Having doubt, he is incapable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion.
373:
Without abandoning lust, without abandoning hatred, and without abandoning delusion, one is incapable of abandoning birth, incapable of abandoning aging, and incapable of abandoning death. (10)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death. What three? Lust, hatred, and delusion. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death. (1)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion. What three? Self-identity view, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion. (2)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning self-identity view, abandoning doubt, and abandoning attachment to rites and rituals. What three? Unwise attention, following a wrong path, and sluggishness of mind. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning self-identity view, abandoning doubt, and abandoning attachment to rites and rituals. (3)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning unwise attention, abandoning following a wrong path, and abandoning sluggishness of mind. What three? Forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction of mind. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning unwise attention, abandoning following a wrong path, and abandoning sluggishness of mind. (4)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning forgetfulness, abandoning lack of clear comprehension, and abandoning distraction of mind. What three? Unwillingness to see the Noble Ones, unwillingness to hear the Noble Dhamma, and a fault-finding mind. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning forgetfulness, abandoning lack of clear comprehension, and abandoning distraction of mind. (5)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning the unwillingness to see the Noble Ones, abandoning the unwillingness to hear the Noble Dhamma, and abandoning a fault-finding mind. What three? Restlessness, lack of restraint, and immorality.
374:
Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning the unwillingness to see the Noble Ones, abandoning the unwillingness to hear the Noble Dhamma, and abandoning a fault-finding mind. (6)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning restlessness, abandoning lack of restraint, and abandoning immorality. What three? Lack of faith, unreceptiveness, and laziness. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning restlessness, abandoning lack of restraint, and abandoning immorality. (7)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning lack of faith, abandoning unreceptiveness, and abandoning laziness. What three? Disrespect, recalcitrance, and evil friendship. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning lack of faith, abandoning unreceptiveness, and abandoning laziness. (8)

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning recalcitrance, and abandoning evil friendship. What three? Lack of shame, lack of moral dread, and heedlessness. Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning recalcitrance, and abandoning evil friendship. (9)

Monks, one who possesses shame and moral dread is heedful. Being heedful, he is capable of abandoning disrespect, recalcitrance, and evil friendship. Having good friendship, he is capable of abandoning lack of faith, unreceptiveness, and laziness. Being energetic, he is capable of abandoning restlessness, lack of restraint, and immorality. Being virtuous, he is capable of abandoning the unwillingness to see the Noble Ones, the unwillingness to hear the Noble Dhamma, and a fault-finding mind. Without a fault-finding mind, he is capable of abandoning forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction of mind. With an undistracted mind, he is capable of abandoning unwise attention, following a wrong path, and sluggishness of mind. With an unsluggish mind, he is capable of abandoning self-identity view, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals. Being without doubt, he is capable of abandoning lust, hatred, and delusion.
375:
If that person abandons lust, abandons hatred, and abandons delusion, he is fit to abandon birth, to abandon aging, and to abandon death.

Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Kāka Sutta
77. "Monks, a crow is possessed of ten unwholesome qualities. What ten? It is destructive, impudent, full of craving, gluttonous, harsh, merciless, weak, noisy, forgetful, and non-storing. Monks, a crow is possessed of these ten unwholesome qualities. In the same way, monks, a wicked monk is possessed of ten unwholesome qualities. What ten? He is destructive, impudent, full of craving, gluttonous, harsh, merciless, weak, noisy, forgetful, and non-storing. Monks, a wicked monk is possessed of these ten unwholesome qualities."

Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Nigaṇṭha Sutta
78. "Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas (Jain ascetics) are possessed of ten unwholesome qualities. What ten? Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas are faithless. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas are immoral. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas are shameless. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas are fearless (of wrongdoing). Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas associate with bad people. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas exalt themselves and disparage others. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas misinterpret according to their own views, hold onto them firmly, and relinquish them with difficulty. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas act pretentiously. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas have evil desires. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas have evil friends. Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas are possessed of these ten unwholesome qualities."

Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Āghātavatthu Sutta
79. "Monks, there are these ten grounds for resentment. What ten? One harbors resentment, thinking: 'He has done me harm'; one harbors resentment, thinking: 'He is doing me harm'; one harbors resentment, thinking: 'He will do me harm.' One harbors resentment, thinking: 'He has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me... [pe] ...is doing harm... [pe] ...will do harm.' One harbors resentment, thinking: 'He has done a favor to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me... [pe] ...is doing a favor... [pe] ...'
376:
...will do a favor'; and one gets angry at improper things. Monks, these are the ten grounds for resentment."

Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta
80. "Monks, there are these ten ways of removing resentment. What ten? One removes resentment, thinking: 'He has done me harm, but what can be done about it?'; one removes resentment, thinking: 'He is doing me harm, but what can be done about it?'; one removes resentment, thinking: 'He will do me harm, but what can be done about it?'; one removes resentment, thinking: 'He has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me... [pe] ...is doing harm... [pe] ...will do harm, but what can be done about it?'; one removes resentment, thinking: 'He has done a favor to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me... [pe] ...is doing a favor... [pe] ...will do a favor, but what can be done about it?'; and one does not get angry at improper things. Monks, these are the ten ways of removing resentment."

Tenth Sutta.

The third chapter, Ākaṅkha Vagga, is finished.

## (9) 4. Thera Vagga
## 1. Vāhana Sutta
81. On one occasion, the Blessed One was staying in the city of Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond. Then the Venerable Vāhana approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Vāhana said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, from how many things has the Tathāgata emerged, being detached and released from them, so that he dwells with a mind free from boundaries?"

"Vāhana, the Tathāgata has emerged from ten things, being detached and released from them, so that he dwells with a mind free from boundaries. What ten? Vāhana, the Tathāgata has emerged from form, being detached and released from it, so that he dwells with a mind free from boundaries."
377:
Vāhana, from feeling... [pe]... Vāhana, from perception. Vāhana, from formations. Vāhana, from consciousness. Vāhana, from birth. Vāhana, from aging. Vāhana, from death. Vāhana, from sufferings. Vāhana, from defilements, the Tathāgata has emerged, is detached, and is released; he dwells with a mind free from boundaries. Vāhana, just as a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus, born in the water, grown in the water, having risen above the water, stands unsoiled by the water; even so, Vāhana, having emerged from these ten things, detached and released from them, the Tathāgata dwells with a mind free from boundaries.

The First Sutta.

## 2. Ānanda Sutta

“Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being faithless, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (1)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being immoral, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (2)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being of little learning, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (3)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being difficult to admonish, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (4)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, having evil friends, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (5)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being lazy, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (6)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being forgetful, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya.”
378:
(7)
Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being discontented, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (8)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, having evil desires, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (9)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, having wrong view, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (10)

Ānanda, it is impossible for that monk, being possessed of these ten things, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya.

Ānanda, it is possible for that monk, being faithful, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (1)

Ānanda, it is possible for that monk, being virtuous, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (2)

Ānanda, it is possible for that monk, having good friends, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (5)

Ānanda, it is possible for that monk, being energetic, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (6)

Ānanda, it is possible for that monk, being established in mindfulness, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (7)

Ānanda, it is possible for that monk, being contented, to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. (8)

379:
(9)
Ānanda, it is possible that a monk, being one of right view, will arrive at growth, increase, and expansion in this Dhamma-Vinaya.

(10)

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Punniya Sutta

83. Then the Venerable Punniya approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Punniya said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why sometimes the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata occurs [to the mind], and sometimes it does not occur?"

"Punniya, a monk may have faith, but he does not approach [the teacher]; in that case, the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata does not yet occur. But, Punniya, when a monk has faith and also approaches, then the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata occurs.

"Punniya, a monk may have faith and approach, but he does not attend [upon the teacher]... (p)... he attends, but he does not ask questions... he asks questions, but he does not listen to the Dhamma with an attentive ear... he listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, but having heard it, he does not remember the Dhamma... he remembers the Dhamma, but he does not examine the meaning of the teachings he has remembered... he examines the meaning of the teachings he has remembered, but knowing the meaning and the text, he does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma... he knows the meaning and the text and practices in accordance with the Dhamma, but he is not a good speaker, not one with a good delivery, not endowed with speech that is polite, clear, faultless, and capable of conveying the meaning... he is a good speaker, one with a good delivery, endowed with speech that is polite, clear, faultless, and capable of conveying the meaning, but he is not one who instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens his fellow monks [with a Dhamma talk]. In that case, the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata does not yet occur.

"Punniya, when a monk has faith, approaches, attends, asks questions, listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, remembers the Dhamma he has heard, and examines the meaning of the teachings he has remembered...
380:
...examines the meaning of the teachings he has remembered, and knowing the meaning and the text, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma; he is a good speaker, one with a good delivery, endowed with speech that is polite, clear, faultless, and capable of conveying the meaning; and he is one who instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens his fellow monks. In such a case, the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata occurs. Punniya, when one is endowed with these ten qualities, the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata certainly occurs [to the mind]."

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Vyākaraṇa Sutta

84. There the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the monks: "Friends, monks."

"Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:

"Friends, here in this teaching, a monk declares final knowledge (arahattaphala): 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state.' Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in [reading] the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, examines him, probes him, and questions him. When he is examined, probed, and questioned by the Tathāgata or by a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in [reading] the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, he comes to a void, he comes to a loss [of virtue], he comes to misfortune, he comes to ruin, he comes to misfortune and ruin. Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in [reading] the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, reflects on that monk's mind with his own mind: 'Why does this venerable one declare final knowledge, saying: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state"?'

Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in [reading] the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, understands by encompassing [that monk's] mind with his own mind:"
381:
A disciple of the Blessed One, who is possessed of jhāna, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, discerns with his own mind the mind of another thus:
'This venerable one is angry; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by anger. This being overwhelmed by anger is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is malicious; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by malice. This being overwhelmed by malice is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is a disparager; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by disparaging. This being overwhelmed by disparaging is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is domineering; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by domineering. This being overwhelmed by domineering is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is envious; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by envy. This being overwhelmed by envy is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is miserly; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by miserliness. This being overwhelmed by miserliness is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is crafty; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by craftiness. This being overwhelmed by craftiness is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is deceitful; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by deceit. This being overwhelmed by deceit is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one has evil wishes; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by evil wishes.'
382:
'This being overwhelmed by evil wishes is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one, while there is still more to be done, has come to a standstill halfway because of some insignificant distinction. This coming to a standstill halfway is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
Indeed, friends, it is impossible for that bhikkhu, without abandoning these ten things, to reach growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. Indeed, friends, it is possible for that bhikkhu, having abandoned these ten things, to reach growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya.
Fourth Sutta.
## 5. Katthī Sutta
85. On one occasion, the Venerable Mahācunda was staying among the Cetis at Sahajāti. There, the Venerable Mahācunda addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus!" "Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahācunda. The Venerable Mahācunda said this:
"Friends, here a bhikkhu is a boaster, a vaunter regarding attainments, saying: 'I enter and emerge from the first jhāna; I enter and emerge from the second jhāna; I enter and emerge from the third jhāna; I enter and emerge from the fourth jhāna; I enter and emerge from the base of the infinity of space; I enter and emerge from the base of the infinity of consciousness; I enter and emerge from the base of nothingness; I enter and emerge from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; I enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling.'
Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is possessed of jhāna, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, examines him, investigates him, and questions him. When he is examined, investigated, and questioned by the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata... he comes to ruin, he comes to destruction, he comes to misfortune, he comes to disaster, he comes to misfortune and disaster."
383:
Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is possessed of jhāna, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, reflects on him, discerning his mind with his own mind: 'Why does this venerable one boast and vaunt regarding attainments, saying: "I enter and emerge from the first jhāna... I enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling"?'
Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is possessed of jhāna, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, discerns with his own mind the mind of that person thus:
'For a long time, this venerable one has been one who acts inconsistently, acts with holes, acts with spots, acts with blotches regarding the precepts; he is not one who acts continuously, not one of continuous conduct in virtue. This venerable one is immoral. This immorality is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is faithless. This lack of faith is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is of little learning and of improper conduct. This lack of learning and improper conduct is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is difficult to admonish. This difficulty in being admonished is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one has evil friends. This having evil friends is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is lazy. This laziness is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is muddle-minded. This muddle-mindedness is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is a deceiver. This deceit is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
'This venerable one is difficult to support. This difficulty in being supported is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.'
384:
“This venerable one is unwise; this lack of wisdom is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

“Friends, it is like a friend who says to another friend: ‘Friend, whenever you have a need for wealth, ask me for wealth; I will give it to you.’ When some need for wealth arises, that friend says to the other: ‘Friend, I have a need for wealth. Give me wealth.’ He says: ‘Well then, friend, dig here.’ Digging there, he finds nothing. He says: ‘Friend, you spoke falsely to me; friend, you spoke in vain to me, saying “dig here”.’ He says: ‘Friend, I did not speak falsely to you, nor did I speak in vain. Well then, friend, dig here.’ Digging there too, he finds nothing. He says: ‘Friend, you spoke falsely to me; friend, you spoke in vain to me, saying “dig here”.’ He says: ‘Friend, I did not speak falsely to you, nor did I speak in vain. Well then, friend, dig here.’ Digging there too, he finds nothing. He says: ‘Friend, you spoke falsely to me; friend, you spoke in vain to me, saying “dig here”.’ He says: ‘Friend, I did not speak falsely to you, nor did I speak in vain. Rather, I myself have reached madness and derangement of mind.’

“In the same way, friends, a monk is a boaster and a braggart regarding attainments, saying: ‘I enter and emerge from the first jhāna; I enter and emerge from the second jhāna; I enter and emerge from the third jhāna; I enter and emerge from the fourth jhāna; I enter and emerge from the base of infinite space; I enter and emerge from the base of infinite consciousness; I enter and emerge from the base of nothingness; I enter and emerge from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; I enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling.’

“Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others' minds, examines him, scrutinizes him, and questions him. When he is examined, scrutinized, and questioned by the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others' minds, he reaches emptiness, he reaches vanity, he reaches ruin, he reaches disaster, he reaches ruin and disaster.”
385:
“Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others' minds, reflects on him, encompassing his mind with their own: ‘Why does this venerable one boast and brag about attainments, saying: “I enter and emerge from the first jhāna... (as before) ... up to ... I enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling”?’

“Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the ways of others' minds, understands by encompassing his mind with their own:

‘For a long time, this venerable one has been one who acts with breaks, with holes, with spots, with blotches in his virtue; he is not one who acts consistently, not one of consistent conduct in the precepts.

‘This venerable one is immoral; immorality is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

‘This venerable one is faithless; lack of faith is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

‘This venerable one is of little learning and of bad conduct; little learning is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

‘This venerable one is difficult to admonish; being difficult to admonish is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

‘This venerable one has evil friends; having evil friends is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

‘This venerable one is lazy; laziness is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

‘This venerable one is muddle-minded; muddle-mindedness is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

‘This venerable one is a deceiver; deceit is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.’"
386:
“This venerable one is difficult to support; this difficulty in being supported is a cause of decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

This venerable one is unwise; this lack of wisdom is a cause of decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata” (thus he knows by distinguishing).

“Indeed, friends, it is impossible for that bhikkhu, without abandoning these ten things, to reach growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya. Indeed, friends, it is possible for that bhikkhu, by abandoning these ten things, to reach growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya” (thus he says).

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Adhimāna Sutta

86. At one time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. There, the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahākassapa. The Venerable Mahākassapa said this:

“Friends, here a bhikkhu declares final knowledge: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others’ minds, examines him, scrutinizes him, and questions him. When he is examined, scrutinized, and questioned by the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others’ minds, he comes to emptiness, he comes to a state devoid of virtue, he comes to misfortune, he comes to ruin, he comes to misfortune and ruin. Then the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others’ minds, reflects on that bhikkhu’s mind with his own mind: ‘Why does this venerable one declare final knowledge: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being”?’ (thus he reflects).
387:
Then the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others’ minds, understands by encompassing that bhikkhu’s mind with his own:

‘This venerable one is one who overestimates himself, one whose truth is overestimation; he has the perception of attainment in what is not attained, the perception of having done in what is not done, the perception of realization in what is not realized. Through overestimation, he declares final knowledge: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.”’ Then the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others’ minds, reflects on that bhikkhu’s mind with his own mind: ‘Depending on what does this venerable one have such overestimation, whose truth is overestimation, having the perception of attainment in what is not attained, the perception of having done in what is not done, the perception of realization in what is not realized, and declare final knowledge through overestimation: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being”?’ (thus he reflects).

Then the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others’ minds, understands by encompassing that bhikkhu’s mind with his own:

‘This venerable one is very learned, a bearer of what he has heard, a storer of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings have been much heard by him, retained, recited, mentally pondered, and well-penetrated by view. Therefore, this venerable one is one who overestimates himself, one whose truth is overestimation, having the perception of attainment in what is not attained, the perception of having done in what is not done, the perception of realization in what is not realized, and declares final knowledge through overestimation: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.”’ Then the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, skilled in the ways of others’ minds, understands by encompassing that bhikkhu’s mind with his own:

‘This venerable one is full of covetousness; he dwells with a mind frequently obsessed by covetousness. This obsession with covetousness is a cause of decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.’
388:
This venerable one is full of covetousness; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by covetousness. This being overwhelmed by covetousness is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one is full of anger; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by anger. This being overwhelmed by anger is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one is full of sloth and torpor (thina-middha); he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by sloth and torpor. This being overwhelmed by sloth and torpor is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one is restless; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by restlessness. This being overwhelmed by restlessness is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one is full of doubt; he dwells frequently with a mind overwhelmed by doubt. This being overwhelmed by doubt is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one delights in activities, rejoices in activities, and is devoted to delighting in activities. This delighting in activities is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one delights in talk, rejoices in talk, and is devoted to delighting in talk. This delighting in talk is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one delights in sleep, rejoices in sleep, and is devoted to delighting in sleep. This delighting in sleep is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one delights in company, rejoices in company, and is devoted to delighting in company. This delighting in company is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one, while there is still more to be done in the higher training, comes to a standstill mid-way (reaches an end) upon attaining some mere insignificant distinction. This coming to a standstill mid-way is a decline in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. 
Friends, it is impossible for that monk, without abandoning these ten things, to reach growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya.
389:
Friends, it is possible for that monk, by abandoning these ten things, to reach growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma-Vinaya.
The Sixth Sutta.
## 7. Nappiya Sutta
87. On that occasion, the Blessed One, concerning a monk who had passed away, addressed the monks: "Monks." "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
"Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk is a maker of disputes and does not speak in praise of the settlement of disputes. Monks, this quality of being a maker of disputes and not speaking in praise of the settlement of disputes does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to being developed, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk does not desire the training and does not speak in praise of undertaking the training. Monks, this quality of not desiring the training and not speaking in praise of undertaking the training does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to being developed, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has evil desires and does not speak in praise of the removal of evil desires. Monks, this quality of having evil desires and not speaking in praise of the removal of evil desires does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to being developed, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is denigrating and does not speak in praise of the removal of denigration. Monks, this quality of being denigrating and not speaking in praise of the removal of denigration does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to being developed, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is deceitful,"
390:
...and does not speak in praise of the removal of deceit. Monks, this quality of being deceitful and not speaking in praise of the removal of deceit does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is fraudulent and does not speak in praise of the removal of fraud. Monks, this quality of being fraudulent and not speaking in praise of the removal of fraud does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is not one who listens carefully to the teachings and does not speak in praise of listening carefully to the teachings. Monks, this quality of not listening carefully to the teachings and not speaking in praise of listening carefully to the teachings does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is not fond of seclusion and does not speak in praise of seclusion. Monks, this quality of not being fond of seclusion and not speaking in praise of seclusion does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is not hospitable toward his fellow practitioners and does not speak in praise of hospitality. Monks, this quality of not being hospitable and not speaking in praise of hospitality does not lead to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.

Monks, such a monk might have this wish: 'Oh, that my fellow practitioners would honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me!' Yet, his fellow practitioners do not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate him. Why is that? Because, monks, wise fellow practitioners see those evil, unwholesome qualities that have not been abandoned in him.

Monks, it is like a bad, wild horse that might have this wish: 'Oh, that people would treat me as a noble thoroughbred, feed me the food of a thoroughbred, and groom me as they groom a thoroughbred!' Yet, people do not treat that bad horse as a thoroughbred, nor do they feed it the food of a thoroughbred...
391:
...nor do they groom it as they groom a thoroughbred. Why is that? Because, monks, wise people see those qualities of deceit, fraud, crookedness, and craftiness that have not been abandoned in that horse. In the same way, monks, such a monk might have this wish: 'Oh, that my fellow practitioners would honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me!' Yet, his fellow practitioners do not honor, respect, esteem, or venerate him. Why is that? Because, monks, wise fellow practitioners see those evil, unwholesome qualities that have not been abandoned in him.

But here, monks, a monk is not a maker of disputes and speaks in praise of the settling of disputes. Monks, this quality of not being a maker of disputes and speaking in praise of the settling of disputes leads to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is desirous of the training and speaks in praise of undertaking the training. Monks, this quality of being desirous of the training and speaking in praise of undertaking the training leads to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk has few wishes and speaks in praise of the removal of evil wishes. Monks, this quality of having few wishes and speaking in praise of the removal of wishes leads to... [as above] ...and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is without anger and speaks in praise of the removal of anger. Monks, this quality of being without anger and speaking in praise of the removal of anger leads to... [as above] ...and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is not disparaging and speaks in praise of the removal of disparagement. Monks, this quality of not being disparaging and speaking in praise of the removal of disparagement leads to... [as above] ...and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is not deceitful and speaks in praise of the removal of deceit. Monks, this quality of not being deceitful and speaking in praise of the removal of deceit leads to... [as above] ...and to unity.
392:
Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not deceitful and speaks in praise of the removal of deceit. This quality, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is not deceitful and speaks in praise of the removal of deceit, also ... leads to unity.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who listens attentively to the Dhamma and speaks in praise of listening attentively to the Dhamma. This quality, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu listens attentively to the Dhamma and speaks in praise of listening attentively to the Dhamma, also ... leads to unity.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who resorts to seclusion and speaks in praise of seclusion. This quality, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu resorts to seclusion and speaks in praise of seclusion, also ... leads to unity.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is hospitable to his fellow practitioners and speaks in praise of hospitality. This quality, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is hospitable and speaks in praise of hospitality, leads to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the state of a recluse, and to unity.

Bhikkhus, in such a bhikkhu, even if the wish does not arise: 'Oh, may my fellow practitioners honor, respect, revere, and venerate me,' yet his fellow practitioners do honor, respect, revere, and venerate him. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, wise fellow practitioners see that those evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned in him.

Bhikkhus, just as in a noble thoroughbred horse, even if the wish does not arise: 'Oh, may people place me in the position of a thoroughbred, feed me thoroughbred food, and groom me with thoroughbred grooming,' yet people do place him in the position of a thoroughbred, feed him thoroughbred food, and groom him with thoroughbred grooming. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, wise people see that those instances of deceit, craftiness, deviousness, and crookedness have been abandoned in him.

In the same way, bhikkhus, in such a bhikkhu, even if the wish does not arise: 'Oh, may my fellow practitioners honor, respect, revere, and venerate me,' yet his fellow practitioners do honor, respect, revere, and venerate him. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, wise fellow practitioners see that those evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned in him." (The Seventh Sutta).

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8 - Akkosaka Sutta
88. Bhikkhus, it is to be expected that a bhikkhu who insults and reviles his fellow practitioners, and who is an accuser of the Noble Ones (with a charge of the ultimate offense), will meet with one of ten types of ruin. What ten?

He does not attain the unattained distinction; he falls away from the distinction he has attained; his good qualities do not become purified; or he becomes over-conceited regarding the True Dhamma; or he lives the holy life dissatisfied; or he falls into some defiling offense; or he suffers a severe, incurable disease; or he falls into madness and mental derangement; or he dies confused; and with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell.

Bhikkhus, it is to be expected that a bhikkhu who insults and reviles his fellow practitioners, and who is an accuser of the Noble Ones, will meet with one of these ten types of ruin. (The Eighth Sutta).

## 9 - Kokālika Sutta
89. Then the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the bhikkhu Kokālika said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have come under the influence of evil desires."

"Do not say so, Kokālika! Do not say so, Kokālika! Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, Kokālika. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are lovers of virtue."

A second time, the bhikkhu Kokālika said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, although the Blessed One is my trustworthy and reliable authority, yet Sāriputta and Moggallāna indeed have evil desires; they have come under the influence of evil desires."

"Do not say so, Kokālika! Do not say so, Kokālika! Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, Kokālika. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are lovers of virtue."

A third time, the bhikkhu Kokālika said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, although the Blessed One is my trustworthy and reliable authority, yet Sāriputta and Moggallāna indeed have evil desires; they have come under the influence of evil desires."

"Do not say so, Kokālika! Do not say so, Kokālika! Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, Kokālika..."
394:
(The Buddha said,) "Sāriputta and Moggallāna are lovers of virtue."

Then the monk Kokālika rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, performed a circumambulation, and departed. Not long after he had left, Kokālika's whole body became covered with boils the size of mustard seeds. From the size of mustard seeds, they became the size of mung beans; from the size of mung beans, they became the size of chickpeas; from the size of chickpeas, they became the size of jujube stones; from the size of jujube stones, they became the size of jujube fruits; from the size of jujube fruits, they became the size of emblic myrobalans; from the size of emblic myrobalans, they became the size of tinduka fruits; from the size of tinduka fruits, they became the size of young bel fruits; from the size of young bel fruits, they became the size of mature bel fruits. Having become the size of mature bel fruits, they burst, and pus and blood flowed out. That Kokālika lay on banana leaves like a fish that had swallowed poison.

Then the Pacceka-Brahmā named Turu approached the monk Kokālika and, standing in the air, said to him: "Kokālika, settle your mind with confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are lovers of virtue."

"Who are you, friend?" (Kokālika asked). "I am the Pacceka-Brahmā named Turu," (he replied).

"Friend, were you not declared an Anāgāmī by the Blessed One? If so, why have you come here? Look at this fault of yours (coming to the human world despite being an Anāgāmī)," (Kokālika said).

Then the Pacceka-Brahmā named Turu addressed the monk Kokālika with verses:

"When a man is born, an axe is born in his mouth,
With which the fool cuts himself while speaking harsh words.

He who praises the blameworthy, or blames the praiseworthy,
Accumulates evil with his mouth; because of that evil, he finds no happiness.

Small is the loss of wealth through gambling, even if one loses everything including oneself;
Far greater is the evil of harboring ill-will towards the Well-Gone Ones (Arahants).
Having set one's speech and mind..."
395:
"...and mind on evil, he who reviles the Noble Ones goes to hell for a period of one hundred thousand Nirabbudas, thirty-six Nirabbudas, and five Abbudas."

Then the monk Kokālika died of that very illness. Having died, the monk Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma Hell because of the ill-will he harbored towards Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

Then, when the night was far spent, Brahmā Sahampati, of magnificent appearance, illuminating the entire Jetavana, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side. Standing there, Brahmā Sahampati said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the monk Kokālika has died. Having died, Venerable Sir, the monk Kokālika has been reborn in the Paduma Hell because of the ill-will he harbored towards Sāriputta and Moggallāna."

Brahmā Sahampati said this, paid homage to the Blessed One, performed a circumambulation, and vanished right there.

Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, last night, when the night was far spent, Brahmā Sahampati, of magnificent appearance, illuminating the entire Jetavana, approached me, paid homage, and stood to one side. Standing there, monks, Brahmā Sahampati said to me: 'Venerable Sir, the monk Kokālika has died. Having died, Venerable Sir, the monk Kokālika has been reborn in the Paduma Hell because of the ill-will he harbored towards Sāriputta and Moggallāna.' Monks, Brahmā Sahampati said this, paid homage to me, performed a circumambulation, and vanished right there."

When this was said, a certain monk asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, how long is the lifespan in the Paduma Hell?"

"Monk, the lifespan in the Paduma Hell is long. It is not easy to count it as 'so many years,' 'so many hundreds of years,' 'so many thousands of years,' or 'so many hundreds of thousands of years.'"

"Venerable Sir, is it possible to give a simile?"

"It is possible, monk," the Blessed One said. "Monk, suppose there were a Kosalan cartload of twenty khārīs of sesame seeds. And a man were to take out a single seed once every hundred years. Monk, that Kosalan cartload of twenty khārīs of sesame seeds would be exhausted and depleted more quickly by this effort..."
396:
One Abbuda hell does not reach an end [so quickly].

Monks, twenty Abbuda hells are equal to one Nirabbuda hell. Twenty Nirabbuda hells are equal to one Ababa hell. Twenty Ababa hells are equal to one Aṭaṭa hell. Twenty Aṭaṭa hells are equal to one Ahaha hell. Twenty Ahaha hells are equal to one Kumuda hell. Twenty Kumuda hells are equal to one Sogandhika hell. Twenty Sogandhika hells are equal to one Uppalaka hell. Twenty Uppalaka hells are equal to one Puṇḍarīka hell. Twenty Puṇḍarīka hells are equal to one Paduma hell. Monks, the monk Kokālika has arisen in the Paduma hell because he harbored malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Fortunate One (Sugata), the Teacher, further said this:

“When a man is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which the fool cuts himself when speaking ill.

“He who praises the blameworthy, or blames the praiseworthy, accumulates bad luck with his mouth; because of that bad luck, he finds no happiness.

“Small is this bad luck, the loss of wealth at dice, even with all one's possessions and oneself; this indeed is a greater bad luck: to harbor ill-will toward the Well-Gone Ones (Sugatas).

“For one hundred thousand Nirabbudas, and thirty-six plus five Abbudas, he who reviles the Noble Ones (Ariyas) goes to hell, having directed evil speech and mind.”

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10 - Khīṇāsavabala Sutta

90. Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down at one side. To the Venerable Sāriputta who was seated at one side, the Blessed One said: “Sāriputta, how many are the powers of a monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava),
397:
by which powers a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints, saying: ‘My taints are destroyed’?”

“Venerable Sir, there are ten powers of a monk whose taints are destroyed, by which powers a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints, saying: ‘My taints are destroyed.’ What are the ten? Venerable Sir, here, all conditioned things (saṅkhāras) are clearly seen as they really are with right wisdom by a monk whose taints are destroyed as impermanent (anicca). Venerable Sir, that all conditioned things are clearly seen as they really are with right wisdom as impermanent by a monk whose taints are destroyed—this is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, based on which power a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints, saying: ‘My taints are destroyed.’ (1)

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, sensual pleasures (kāmas) are clearly seen as they really are with right wisdom by a monk whose taints are destroyed as being like a pit of glowing coals. Venerable Sir, that sensual pleasures are clearly seen as they really are with right wisdom as being like a pit of glowing coals by a monk whose taints are destroyed—this is also a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, based on which power a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints, saying: ‘My taints are destroyed.’ (2)

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the mind of a monk whose taints are destroyed inclines toward seclusion, leans toward seclusion, tends toward seclusion, delights in renunciation (nekkhamma), and is entirely free from things that are the basis for taints. Venerable Sir, that the mind of a monk whose taints are destroyed inclines, leans, and tends toward seclusion, delights in renunciation, and is entirely free from things that are the basis for taints—this is also a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, based on which power a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints, saying: ‘My taints are destroyed.’ (3)

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed. Venerable Sir, that the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed—this is also a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, based on which power a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints, saying: ‘My taints are destroyed.’ (4)

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) have been developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed.
398:
...has been well developed. [Pe] ... has developed the four bases of power; they have been well developed. [Pe] ... has developed the five faculties; they have been well developed. ... has developed the five powers; they have been well developed. ... has developed the seven factors of enlightenment; they have been well developed. ... has developed the Noble Eightfold Path; it has been well developed. Venerable sir, that a monk whose taints are destroyed has developed the Noble Eightfold Path, has well developed it—this also is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, by means of which power a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints: 'My taints are destroyed.' (5-10)

Venerable sir, these are the ten powers of a monk whose taints are destroyed, possessed of which a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints: 'My taints are destroyed,'" (he said).

Householder, these ten types of enjoyers of sense pleasures are found existing in the world.
