Householder, among these ten types of enjoyers of sense pleasures, the one who seeks wealth righteously and without violence; having sought wealth righteously and without violence, makes himself happy and pleased, shares it and performs meritorious deeds, and enjoys that wealth without being attached, infatuated, or greedy, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape—this one is the foremost, the best, the chief, the supreme, and the most excellent among these ten types of enjoyers of sense pleasures. Householder, just as from a cow comes milk, from milk curds, from curds butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee, and the cream of ghee is reckoned the best of them; even so, householder, among these ten types of enjoyers of sense pleasures, the one who seeks wealth righteously and without violence; having sought wealth righteously and without violence, makes himself happy and pleased, and is satisfied,"
404:
He shares [with others] and performs meritorious deeds. He enjoys those riches without being greedy, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. Among these ten types of sensual consumers, he is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent.” Thus he said.

First Sutta.

## 2. Bhaya Sutta

92. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Householder, when the five fears and enmities are stilled in a noble disciple, and he is endowed with the four factors of stream-entry, and the noble method is well seen and well penetrated by him through wisdom, he may, if he wishes, declare of himself: ‘I am finished with hell, finished with the animal realm, finished with the sphere of hungry ghosts, finished with the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. I am a stream-enterer, no longer bound for the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination.’

What are the five fears and enmities that are stilled? Householder, whatever fear and enmity one who kills living beings produces in this life as a result of killing, and whatever fear and enmity he produces in the future life, and whatever mental pain and grief he experiences—for one who abstains from killing living beings, that fear and enmity is stilled. Householder, whatever fear and enmity one who takes what is not given... [as above]... one who engages in sexual misconduct... one who speaks falsehood... one who drinks fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence produces in this life as a result of drinking fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence, and whatever fear and enmity he produces in the future life, and whatever mental pain and grief he experiences—for one who abstains from drinking fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence, that fear and enmity is stilled. These five fears and enmities are stilled.

With what four factors of stream-entry is he endowed? Householder, here a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an Arahant... [etc.]... the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ He is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is well-expounded,
405:
visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ He is endowed with verified confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, the straight way, the true way, the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ He is endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. He is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry.

And what is the noble method that is well seen and well penetrated by him through wisdom? Householder, here a noble disciple reflects thus:

“When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: with ignorance (avijjā) as condition, volitional formations (saṅkhāra) [come to be]; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence (bhava); with existence as condition, birth (jāti); with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance through the path of Arahantship comes the cessation of volitional formations... [etc.]... Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.” This is the noble method that is well seen and well penetrated by him through wisdom.

Householder, when these five fears and enmities are stilled in a noble disciple, and he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry,
406:
That noble disciple has well seen this noble method with wisdom and well penetrated it. At that time, if that noble disciple so desires, he may declare of himself by himself: 'Destroyed for me is hell, destroyed is the animal realm, destroyed is the realm of ghosts, destroyed are the states of deprivation, the bad destination, and perdition. I am a Stream-enterer, no longer bound for the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination.'

Second Sutta.

## 3 - Kiṃdiṭṭhika Sutta

93. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder left Sāvatthī in the middle of the day to see the Blessed One. Then it occurred to Anāthapiṇḍika the householder: "It is not the right time to see the Blessed One; the Blessed One is in seclusion. It is also not the right time to see the monks who are worthy of esteem; the monks who are worthy of esteem are in seclusion. What if I were to approach the park of the wanderers of other sects?"

Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. At that time, the wanderers of other sects had gathered and assembled, and were sitting together making a great noise, a loud din, engaged in various kinds of low conversation. Those wanderers of other sects saw Anāthapiṇḍika the householder coming from afar. Seeing him, they cautioned one another: "Be quiet, sirs! Do not make a noise, sirs! This Anāthapiṇḍika the householder, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming to the park. Among the white-robed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama living in Sāvatthī, this Anāthapiṇḍika the householder is one of them. These venerable ones desire quietness, are disciplined in quietness, and speak in praise of quietness. Perhaps if he knows the assembly is quiet, he might think it fit to approach."

Then those wanderers of other sects became silent. Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder approached those wanderers of other sects, and having approached, he exchanged greetings with them. When they had finished the polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. As Anāthapiṇḍika the householder was sitting to one side, the wanderers of other sects asked him: "Tell us, householder, what view does the ascetic Gotama hold?" "Venerable sirs, I do not know all the views of the Blessed One."
407:
"Householder, if you say you do not know all the views of the ascetic Gotama, tell us then, what views do the monks hold?" "Venerable sirs, I do not know all the views of the monks either."

"So, householder, you say you do not know all the views of the ascetic Gotama, nor do you know all the views of the monks. Tell us then, householder, what view do you hold?"

"Venerable sirs, it is not difficult for us to explain what view we hold. I would like to urge the venerable ones to first explain their own views, and afterwards it will not be difficult for us to explain what view we hold."

When this was said, one wanderer said to Anāthapiṇḍika the householder: "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is futile. This is the view I hold, householder." Another wanderer said to Anāthapiṇḍika the householder: "The world is not eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is futile. This is the view I hold, householder." Another wanderer said to Anāthapiṇḍika the householder: "The world is finite... (p)... The world is infinite. The soul is the same as the body. The soul is one thing and the body another. The Tathāgata exists after death. The Tathāgata does not exist after death. The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death. The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, everything else is futile. This is the view I hold, householder."

When this was said, Anāthapiṇḍika the householder said to those wanderers: "Venerable sirs, as to this venerable one who says: 'The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is futile. This is the view I hold, householder'—this view of this venerable one has arisen either because of his own improper attention or because of the voice of another. That view is indeed produced, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen. All things belonging to the three planes of existence are produced, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen. All those things are impermanent. Whatever is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering, to that this venerable one clings, that this venerable one has arrived at. Venerable sirs, as to this venerable one who says: 'The world is not eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is futile. This is the view I hold, householder'—this view of this venerable one also has arisen either because of his own improper attention or because of the voice of another."
408:
That view has arisen. It is conditioned, intended, and dependently originated. Whatever has come to be [pertaining to the three planes of existence] is conditioned, intended, and dependently originated; all that is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering, that is what this venerable one clings to, that is what this venerable one adheres to.

"Venerable sirs, 'The world is finite... the world is infinite... the soul and the body are the same... the soul is one thing and the body another... the Tathāgata exists after death... the Tathāgata does not exist after death... the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, any other view is empty.' Householder, I hold such a view."

This view of the venerable one also arises because of his own improper attention or because of the voice of another. That view has arisen; it is conditioned, intended, and dependently originated. Whatever has come to be [pertaining to the three planes of existence] is conditioned, intended, and dependently originated; all that is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering, that is what this venerable one clings to, that is what this venerable one adheres to.

When this was said, those wanderers said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika: "Householder, we have all explained our respective views. Tell us, householder, what view do you hold?"

"Venerable sirs, whatever has come to be [pertaining to the three planes of existence] is conditioned, intended, and dependently originated; all that is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. 'What is suffering—that is not mine, that I am not, that is not my self.' Venerable sirs, I hold such a view."

"Householder, whatever has come to be [pertaining to the three planes of existence] is conditioned, intended, and dependently originated; all that is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering, that is what you, householder, cling to, that is what you, householder, adhere to."

"Venerable sirs, whatever has come to be [pertaining to the three planes of existence] is conditioned, intended, and dependently originated; all that is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. 'What is suffering—that is not mine, that I am not,
409:
that is not my self'—thus I see this with right wisdom as it really is. And I know the escape from it as it really is."

When this was said, those wanderers sat silent, confounded, with shoulders drooping and heads down, brooding, speechless. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, knowing that those wanderers were silent, confounded, with shoulders drooping and heads down, brooding, and speechless, rose from his seat and went to the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat to one side. Sitting there, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with those wanderers of other sects.

"Excellent, householder, excellent! In this way, householder, those hollow men should be well refuted with the Dhamma from time to time."

Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with a Dhamma talk. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed.

Soon after the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had left, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, even a monk who has been ordained for a hundred years in this Dhamma and Vinaya should refute those wanderers of other sects with the Dhamma just as they were refuted by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika."

The third sutta.

## 4. Vajjiyamāhita Sutta

94. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Campā on the bank of the Gargarā Lake. Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita left Campā during the day to see the Blessed One. Then it occurred to the householder Vajjiyamāhita: "It is not the right time to see the Blessed One. The Blessed One is in seclusion. It is also not the right time to see the monks who develop the mind; the monks who develop the mind are also in seclusion."
410:
It occurred to me: 'It would be good if I were to approach the park of the wanderers of other sects.' Then Vajjiyamāhita the householder approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. At that time, those wanderers of other sects had gathered and assembled, sitting together making a great noise and din, engaging in various kinds of lowly talk. Those wanderers of other sects saw Vajjiyamāhita the householder coming from afar. Seeing him, they cautioned one another: 'Be quiet, sirs! Do not make a noise, sirs! This Vajjiyamāhita the householder, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming. Among the white-clothed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama living in Campā, this Vajjiyamāhita the householder is one of them. These venerable ones desire little noise, are trained in little noise, and speak in praise of little noise. Perhaps, knowing the assembly to be quiet, he might think it fit to approach.'

Then those wanderers became silent. Then Vajjiyamāhita the householder approached those wanderers of other sects. Having approached, he exchanged friendly and courteous greetings with them and sat down to one side. As Vajjiyamāhita the householder was sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said to him: 'Is it true, householder, that the ascetic Gotama condemns all asceticism, and that he categorically upbraids and blames every ascetic who lives a harsh life?'

'Venerable sirs, the Blessed One does not condemn all asceticism, nor does he categorically upbraid and blame every ascetic who lives a harsh life. Venerable sirs, the Blessed One condemns what is blameworthy and praises what is praiseworthy. Venerable sirs, because the Blessed One condemns what is blameworthy and praises what is praiseworthy, the Blessed One is one who speaks after making a distinction (vibhajjavādī). In this matter, the Blessed One does not speak categorically.'

When this was said, one of the wanderers said to Vajjiyamāhita the householder: 'Wait a moment, householder! You speak in praise of that ascetic Gotama, but the ascetic Gotama is a nihilist (venayika) and one who does not prescribe anything.'

'Venerable sirs, in this matter too, I will speak to the venerable ones with reason. Venerable sirs, the Blessed One has prescribed: "This is wholesome." Venerable sirs, the Blessed One has prescribed: "This is unwholesome."'
411:
'Since the Blessed One prescribes wholesome and unwholesome states in this way, the Blessed One is indeed one who prescribes. That Blessed One is not a nihilist nor one who does not prescribe.'

When this was said, those wanderers sat silent, crestfallen, with shoulders drooping and heads down, brooding and speechless. Then Vajjiyamāhita the householder, knowing that those wanderers were silent, crestfallen, with shoulders drooping and heads down, brooding and speechless, rose from his seat and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with those wanderers of other sects.

'Good, good, householder! In this way, householder, those foolish men should be well-refuted with reason from time to time. Householder, I do not say that all asceticism should be practiced, nor do I say that all asceticism should not be practiced. Householder, I do not say that all undertakings should be undertaken, nor do I say that all undertakings should not be undertaken. Householder, I do not say that all exertions should be made, nor do I say that all exertions should not be made. Householder, I do not say that all relinquishments should be relinquished, nor do I say that all relinquishments should not be relinquished. Householder, I do not say that all mental applications should be applied, nor do I say that all mental applications should not be applied.

Householder, it is true: when one practices a certain kind of asceticism, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; I say that such asceticism should not be practiced. But, householder, when one practices a certain kind of asceticism, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; I say that such asceticism should be practiced. Householder, when one undertakes a certain kind of undertaking, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; I say that such undertaking should not be undertaken. But, householder, when one undertakes a certain kind of undertaking, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; I say that such undertaking should be undertaken. Householder, when one makes a certain kind of exertion, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; I say that such exertion should not be made. But, householder, when one makes a certain kind of exertion, unwholesome states decline...'
412:
Wholesome states increase. I say such practice 'should be practiced.' Householder, for one who gives up a certain giving up, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline. I say such giving up 'should not be given up.' Householder, for one who gives up a certain giving up, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase. I say such giving up 'should be given up.'

Householder, for one who attends to a certain attention, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline. I say such attention 'should not be attended to.' Householder, for one who attends to a certain attention, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase. I say such attention 'should be attended to.'

Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita, having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a talk on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then, not long after the householder Vajjiyamāhita had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, even a bhikkhu who has for a long time had little dust in his eyes in this Dhamma-Vinaya should likewise well refute the wanderers of other sects with reasons, just as they were refuted by the householder Vajjiyamāhita."

The fourth sutta.

## 5. Uttiya Sutta

95. Then the wanderer Uttiya approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Uttiya said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, is the world eternal? Is only this true and everything else false?" "Uttiya, I have not declared that the world is eternal, and that only this is true and everything else is false."

"Master Gotama, then is the world not eternal? Is only this true and everything else false?" "Uttiya, I have not declared that either, that the world is not eternal, and that only this is true and everything else is false."

"Master Gotama, is the world finite? ... Is the world infinite? ... Is the soul the same as the body? ... Is the soul one thing and the body another? ... Does the Tathāgata exist after death? ... Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? ... Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? ...
413:
...both exist and not exist. Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death? Is only this true and everything else false?" "Uttiya, I have not declared that either, that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death, and that only this is true and everything else is false."

"When asked, 'Master Gotama, is the world eternal? Is only this true and everything else false?' you say, 'Uttiya, I have not declared that the world is eternal, and that only this is true and everything else is false.' When asked, 'Master Gotama, then is the world not eternal? Is only this true and everything else false?' you say, 'Uttiya, I have not declared that either, that the world is not eternal, and that only this is true and everything else is false.' Master Gotama, is the world finite? ... Is the world infinite? ... Is the soul the same as the body? ... Is the soul one thing and the body another? ... Does the Tathāgata exist after death? ... Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? ... Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? ... Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death? Is only this true and everything else false? When asked thus, you say, 'Uttiya, I have not declared that either, that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death, and that only this is true and everything else is false.' If that is so, then what has been declared by Master Gotama?"

"Uttiya, having directly known it, I teach the Dhamma to my disciples for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method (the Path), and for the realization of Nibbāna."

"Master Gotama, when you teach the Dhamma having directly known it for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna, is the whole world led out by that Dhamma, or half of it, or a third of it?"

When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.
414:
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.

Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: "Let not the wanderer Uttiya acquire a harmful wrong view, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama, when asked a question of supreme importance, falters and does not answer; surely he is unable to.' That would be for the wanderer Uttiya's harm and suffering for a long time."

Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the wanderer Uttiya: "In that case, friend Uttiya, I will give you a simile. For by means of a simile, some wise people understand the meaning of what is said. Friend Uttiya, suppose there is a king's frontier city with strong foundations, strong walls, ramparts, and a single gate. There is a gatekeeper there, wise, competent, and intelligent, who keeps out strangers and lets in those who are known. As he patrols the path around the city, he would not see a gap in the wall or an opening in the wall, not even one large enough for a cat to pass through. He does not have the knowledge: 'So many living beings enter or leave this city.' Rather, he has this thought: 'Whatever large living beings enter or leave this city, they all enter or leave through this gate.'

In the same way, friend Uttiya, the Tathāgata is not concerned whether the whole world is led out [to liberation] by this Dhamma, or half of it, or a third of it. Rather, the Tathāgata has this thought: 'Whoever has been led out, is being led out, or will be led out from the world, all of them have done so by abandoning the five hindrances, the defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, with their minds well established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are. In this way, they have been led out, are being led out, or will be led out from the world.' Friend Uttiya, the very question you asked the Blessed One before, you have now asked the Blessed One in another way. That is why the Blessed One did not answer your question."

The fifth discourse.
415:
The fifth discourse.

## 6. Kokanuda Sutta

96. On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Rājagaha in the Tapodā monastery. Then, having risen early at the time of dawn, the Venerable Ānanda went to the Tapodā River to bathe his limbs. Having bathed his limbs in the Tapodā River and come out, he stood in a single robe, letting his limbs dry. The wanderer Kokanuda also, having risen early at the time of dawn, went to the Tapodā River to bathe his limbs. The wanderer Kokanuda saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar. Having seen him, he said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Who is there, friend?" "I am a monk, friend."

"Of which monks, friend?" "Of the ascetics who are sons of the Sakyans, friend."

"We would like to ask the venerable one a certain point, if the venerable one would grant the opportunity for the answering of a question." "Ask, friend; having heard it, we shall know."

"Sir, do you have this view: 'The world is eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile'?" "Friend, I do not have this view: 'The world is eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile'."

"Sir, do you have this view: 'The world is not eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile'?" "Friend, I do not have this view: 'The world is not eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile'."

"Sir, do you have this view: 'The world is finite... (etc.) ...the world is infinite... the soul and the body are the same... the soul is one thing and the body another... the Tathāgata exists after death... the Tathāgata does not exist after death... the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; only this is true, anything else is futile'?"

"Friend, I do not have this view: 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; only this is true, anything else is futile'."
416:
"In that case, does the venerable one not know, does he not see?" (they asked). "Friend, it is not that I do not know, it is not that I do not see. I know, friend, I see," he said. "Venerable sir, do you have the view: 'The world is eternal, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'?" When asked thus, he said: "Friend, I do not have the view: 'The world is eternal, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'." "Venerable sir, do you have the view: 'The world is not eternal, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'?" When asked thus, he said: "Friend, I do not have the view: 'The world is not eternal, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'." "Venerable sir, 'The world is finite... p ... The world is infinite... The soul is the same as the body... The soul is one thing and the body another... The Tathāgata exists after death... The Tathāgata does not exist after death... The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death... The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'—do you have such a view?" When asked thus, he said: "Friend, I do not have the view: 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'." "In that case, does the venerable one not know, does he not see?" When asked thus, he said: "Friend, it is not that I do not know, it is not that I do not see. Friend, I know, I see." "Friend, in what way should the meaning of this statement be understood?" (they asked).

"Friend, the statement 'The world is eternal, this alone is the truth, any other is empty' is a speculative view. 'Friend, the world is not eternal, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'—this statement is a speculative view. 'Friend, the world is finite... p ... The world is infinite... The soul is the same as the body... The soul is one thing and the body another... The Tathāgata exists after death... The Tathāgata does not exist after death... The Tathāgata both exists and..."
417:
...does not exist. 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death, this alone is the truth, any other is empty'—this statement is a speculative view. Friend, as far as there are views, the grounds for views, the standpoints of views, the obsession with views, the origin of views, and the uprooting of views—all that I know, all that I see. Knowing that, seeing that, why should I say, 'I do not know, I do not see'? Friend, I know, I see," (he said).

"What is the venerable one's name? How do your fellow practitioners know the venerable one?" (they asked). "Friend, my name is Ānanda. My fellow practitioners know me as Ānanda," (he replied). "Friends, we were conversing with a great teacher and did not know it was the Venerable Ānanda! Indeed, if we had known, 'This is the Venerable Ānanda,' we would not have spoken even this much. May the Venerable Ānanda forgive us," they said.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Āhuneyya Sutta

97. "Monks, a monk possessed of ten qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What ten?

Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, is perfect in conduct (ācara) and resort (gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults, and trains in the training rules. He is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, a storehouse of learning. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has heard much of, retained, recited, mentally pondered, and well-penetrated by view. He has good friends, good companions, good associates. He has right view, is possessed of right vision. He experiences the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, enclosures, and mountains as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though in water;"
418:
He walks on water without breaking through, as if on land. He travels through the air cross-legged like a winged bird. He touches and strokes with his hand the moon and the sun, so mighty and powerful. He exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.

With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds: divine and human, whether far or near.

He understands the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with his own mind. He understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust, and a mind without lust as a mind without lust. He understands a mind with hatred... a mind without hatred... a mind with delusion... a mind without delusion... a contracted mind as a contracted mind (saṅkhitta)... a distracted mind as a distracted mind (vikkhitta)... an exalted mind as an exalted mind (mahaggata)... an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind (amahaggata)... a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind (sa-uttara)... an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind (anuttara)... a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind (samāhita)... an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind (asamāhita)... a liberated mind as a liberated mind (vimutta)... and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind (avimutta).

He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion, thus: 'In such a place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn in such a place, and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus, with their aspects and details, he recollects his manifold past lives.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: 'These beings, sirs, were endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind; they were revilers of noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.'
419:
'With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell. But these beings, sirs, were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; they were not revilers of noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

Through the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself in this very life through direct knowledge. Monks, a monk endowed with these ten qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Thera Sutta

98. Monks, an elder monk endowed with ten qualities lives happily wherever he dwells. What ten? (1) He is an elder, of long standing, long ordained, and of great seniority. (2) He is virtuous... he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. (3) He is very learned... and has penetrated well with wisdom. (4) Both Pātimokkhas have been handed down to him in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, and well settled, according to the rules and their context. (5) He is skilled in taking up and settling legal issues that have arisen. (6) He is a lover of the Dhamma, pleasant in speech, and possesses great joy in the Abhidhamma and Abhivinaya. (7) He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. (8) He is graceful in approaching and departing, and is well-restrained when sitting in the village. (9) He obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life. (10) Through the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself in this very life through direct knowledge.
420:
“Monks, a senior monk endowed with these ten qualities dwells at ease in whatever direction he stays.”

Eighth Sutta

## 9. Upāli Sutta

99. Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One, and after approaching, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat at one side. Sitting at one side, the Venerable Upāli said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, I wish to resort to remote lodgings in forest and jungle thickets.”

“Upāli, remote lodgings in forest and jungle thickets are difficult to endure. Seclusion is hard to practice, and it is difficult to find delight in solitude. The forests, as it were, carry away the mind of a monk who has not attained concentration. Upāli, if anyone should say, ‘Without having attained concentration, I will resort to remote lodgings in forest and jungle thickets,’ it is to be expected of him that he will either sink or float.

“Upāli, suppose there were a large lake. Then a great bull elephant, seven or seven and a half cubits tall, would come. This thought would occur to him: ‘What if I were to plunge into this lake and play the game of washing my ears and play the game of washing my back? Having played the game of washing my ears and the game of washing my back, having bathed and drunk, I would then come out and go wherever I wish.’ He would plunge into that lake and play the game of washing his ears and play the game of washing his back. Having played the game of washing his ears and the game of washing his back, having bathed and drunk, he would then come out and go wherever he wished. Why is that? Upāli, a large physical frame finds a footing in deep water.

“Then a hare or a cat would come. This thought would occur to it: ‘What is the difference between me and a great bull elephant? What if I were to plunge into this lake and play the game of washing my ears and play the game of washing my back? Having played the game of washing my ears and the game of washing my back, having bathed and drunk, I would then come out and go wherever I wish.’ It would hastily plunge into that lake without reflection. It is to be expected of it that it will either sink or float. Why is that? Upāli, a small physical frame cannot find a footing in deep water. In the same way, Upāli, if anyone should say, ‘Without having attained concentration, I will resort to remote lodgings in forest and jungle thickets,’ it is to be expected of him that he will either sink or float. Upāli, for example, a young infant lying on its back plays with its own excrement and urine. Upāli, what do you think?
421:
Is not this child's play complete in every way?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.”

“Upāli, when that child has grown up and his faculties have matured, he plays with such toys as are for children, namely: toy ploughs, tip-cat, somersaults, toy windmills, toy measures, toy carts, and toy bows. Upāli, what do you think? Is not this play more advanced and more refined than the previous play?”

“Yes, Venerable Sir.”

“Upāli, when that child has grown up and his faculties have matured, being endowed and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure, he enjoys himself with forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; with sounds cognizable by the ear... with smells cognizable by the nose... with tastes cognizable by the tongue... with tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Upāli, what do you think? Is not this enjoyment more advanced and more refined than the previous forms of play?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.”

“Upāli, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sublime One, a knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Having realized it through his own direct knowledge, he makes known this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. He reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure.

“A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other clan, hears that Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata. Possessing that faith, he reflects: ‘Household life is confined, a path for the dust of passion. Going forth is like the open air. It is not easy for one living at home to practice this holy life in all its fullness and purity, polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?’”
422:
Later, giving up a small amount of wealth or a large amount of wealth, giving up a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth, he dwells possessed of the monks' training and system of life (sājīva), abstaining from taking life; he has laid aside the rod and the sword; he is conscientious, kind, and dwells compassionate for the welfare of all living beings. Abstaining from taking what is not given, he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a pure heart, not stealing.

Giving up unchastity, he lives a life of celibacy, dwelling apart, abstaining from the common practice of sexual intercourse. Giving up false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to truth, is reliable, trustworthy, and not a deceiver of the world.

Giving up malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to cause division from these people, nor does he repeat to these people what he has heard elsewhere in order to cause division from those people. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of those who are united; he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks words that create concord. Giving up harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks words that are blameless, pleasing to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, liked by many, and agreeable to many. Giving up idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks what is Dhamma, speaks what is Vinaya; at the right time he speaks words worth treasuring, reasoned, moderate, and connected with the goal.

That monk abstains from damaging seeds and plants. He eats only one meal a day, abstaining from eating at night and from eating at the wrong time (after noon). He abstains from dancing, singing, music, and unseemly shows which are thorns to the Dhamma. He abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and beautifying himself with ointments. He abstains from high and large beds.
423:
He abstains from accepting gold and silver. He abstains from accepting raw grain. He abstains from accepting raw meat. He abstains from accepting women and girls. He abstains from accepting male and female slaves. He abstains from accepting goats and sheep. He abstains from accepting poultry and pigs. He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mules. He abstains from accepting fields and land. He abstains from running errands and messages. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from cheating with scales, coins, and measures. He abstains from the crooked ways of bribery, deception, and fraud. He abstains from wounding, killing, binding, highway robbery, plundering, and violence.

That monk is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with only its wings as its burden, so too, a monk is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Possessed of this noble aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.

On seeing a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the eye-faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and grief (domanassa) might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye-faculty and achieves restraint over the eye-faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear... on smelling an odor with the nose... on tasting a flavor with the tongue... on touching a tangible object with the body... on cognizing a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the mind-faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the mind-faculty and achieves restraint over the mind-faculty. Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara), he experiences within himself an unalloyed happiness. He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning.
424:
He acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, bowl, and robes; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

Possessing this noble aggregate of virtue, possessing this noble restraint of the senses, and possessing this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, the open air, or a heap of straw.

Having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to a secluded place, he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Having abandoned ill will and malice, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and malice. Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly stilled; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having transcended doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind from doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and pleasure (sukha) born of seclusion. "What do you think, Upāli? Is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?" "Yes, Bhante." "Upāli, my disciples, seeing this state within themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle thickets, yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal (the fruit of Arahantship)."
425:
By that much, they have not yet reached the goal they aspire to (the fruit of Arahantship).

Furthermore, Upāli, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna. "What do you think, Upāli? Is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?" "Yes, Bhante." "Upāli, my disciples, seeing this state within themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle thickets, yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal (the fruit of Arahantship)."

Furthermore, Upāli, with the fading away of rapture... he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. "What do you think, Upāli? Is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?"

"Yes, Bhante."

"Upāli, my disciples, seeing this state within themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle thickets, yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal (the fruit of Arahantship)."

Furthermore, Upāli, with the abandoning of pleasure... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. ...

Furthermore, Upāli, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. "What do you think, Upāli? Is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?" "Yes, Bhante." "Upāli, my disciples, seeing this state within themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle thickets, yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal (the fruit of Arahantship)."

Furthermore, Upāli, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. ...

By completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing,' he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. ...

By completely surmounting the base of nothingness, aware that 'this is peaceful, this is sublime,' he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "What do you think, Upāli? Is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?"
426:
"It is so, Bhante." "Upāli, my disciples, seeing this quality in themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forest wilds; yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal (the fruit of Arahantship).

Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. What do you think, Upāli? Is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?" "It is so, Bhante."

"Upāli, my disciples, seeing this quality in themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forest wilds and dwell having attained their own goal (the fruit of Arahantship). Come now, Upāli, dwell in the Saṅgha. Dwelling in the Saṅgha will be comfortable for you."

Ninth Sutta.

## 10-Abbhabba Sutta

100. "Bhikkhus, without abandoning these ten things, one is incapable of realizing the fruit of Arahantship. Which ten? Lust, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, envy, stinginess, and conceit. Bhikkhus, without abandoning these ten things, one is incapable of realizing the fruit of Arahantship.

Bhikkhus, by abandoning these ten things, one is capable of realizing the fruit of Arahantship. Which ten? Lust, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, envy, stinginess, and conceit. Bhikkhus, by abandoning these ten things, one is capable of realizing the fruit of Arahantship."

Tenth Sutta.

The fifth chapter, the Upāli Vagga, is finished.

The second fifty suttas are finished.
427:
## 3-Tatiya Paṇṇāsaka

3-The Third Fifty Suttas

## (11) 1-Samaṇasaññā Vagga

## 1-Samaṇasaññā Sutta

101. "Bhikkhus, these three perceptions of a recluse, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven qualities. Which three? 'I have reached a state of altered appearance.' 'My livelihood is dependent on others.' 'I must behave in a manner different [from a layperson].' Bhikkhus, these three perceptions of a recluse, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven qualities.

Which seven? One is constant in practice and constant in conduct regarding the precepts; one is not covetous; one is without ill-will; one is not overly conceited; one is desirous of training; one reflects on the requisites of life, 'It is for this purpose'; and one dwells with aroused energy. Bhikkhus, these three perceptions of a recluse, when developed and cultivated, fulfill these seven qualities."

First Sutta.

## 2-Bojjhaṅga Sutta

102. "Bhikkhus, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the three knowledges. Which seven? The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Bhikkhus, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the three knowledges.

Which three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births... thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of human beings... he understands beings faring according to their kamma. With the destruction of the taints... he dwells having realized it for himself. Bhikkhus, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill these three knowledges."
428:
Second Sutta.

## 3. Micchatta Sutta

103. Monks, based on wrongness, there is failure, not success. And how, monks, is there failure and not success based on wrongness? For one of wrong view, monks, wrong intention originates. For one of wrong intention, wrong speech originates. For one of wrong speech, wrong action originates. For one of wrong action, wrong livelihood originates. For one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort originates. For one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness originates. For one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration originates. For one of wrong concentration, wrong knowledge originates. For one of wrong knowledge, wrong liberation originates. In this way, monks, based on wrongness, there is failure, not success.

Monks, based on rightness, there is success, not failure. And how, monks, is there success and not failure based on rightness? For one of right view, monks, right intention originates. For one of right intention, right speech originates. For one of right speech, right action originates. For one of right action, right livelihood originates. For one of right livelihood, right effort originates. For one of right effort, right mindfulness originates. For one of right mindfulness, right concentration originates. For one of right concentration, right knowledge originates. For one of right knowledge, right liberation originates. In this way, monks, based on rightness, there is success, not failure.

Third Sutta.

## 4. Bīja Sutta

104. Monks, for a person of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation, whatever bodily action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever verbal action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever mental action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever intention (cetanā), whatever aspiration (patthanā), whatever resolve (paṇidhi), and whatever volitional formations (saṅkhārā)—all those things lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, unbeneficial, and to suffering. Why is that? Because, monks, the view is evil.

Monks, it is like a seed of neem, a seed of a bitter creeper, or a seed of a bitter gourd planted in moist soil. Whatever taste of the earth it absorbs and whatever taste of the water it absorbs, all that leads to bitterness, pungency, and disagreeableness. Why is that?
429:
Because, monks, the seed is bad. In the same way, monks, for a person of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation, whatever bodily action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever verbal action... whatever mental action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever intention (cetanā), whatever aspiration (patthanā), whatever resolve (paṇidhi), and whatever volitional formations (saṅkhārā)—all those things lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, unbeneficial, and to suffering. Why is that? Because, monks, the view is evil.

Monks, for a person of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation, whatever bodily action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever verbal action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever mental action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever intention (cetanā), whatever aspiration (patthanā), whatever resolve (paṇidhi), and whatever volitional formations (saṅkhārā)—all those things lead to what is desirable, lovely, pleasant, beneficial, and to happiness. Why is that? Because, monks, the view is good.

Monks, it is like a seed of sugarcane, a seed of hill rice, or a seed of grape planted in moist soil. Whatever taste of the earth it absorbs and whatever taste of the water it absorbs, all that leads to agreeableness, sweetness, and an exquisite state. Why is that? Because, monks, the seed is good. In the same way, monks, for a person of right view... (pe)... right liberation, whatever bodily action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever verbal action... whatever mental action is undertaken and completed in accordance with that view, whatever intention (cetanā), whatever aspiration (patthanā), whatever resolve (paṇidhi), and whatever volitional formations (saṅkhārā)—all those things lead to what is desirable, lovely, pleasant, beneficial, and to happiness. Why is that? Because, monks, the view is good.

Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Vijjā Sutta

105. Monks, ignorance (avijjā) is the precursor to the attainment of unwholesome states; lack of shame (ahirika) and lack of moral dread (anottappa) follow it. Monks, for an ignorant, unwise person, wrong view originates. For one of wrong view, wrong intention originates. For one of wrong intention, wrong speech originates. For one of wrong speech, wrong action originates,
430:
For one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises. For one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises. For one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises. For one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises. For one of wrong concentration, wrong knowledge arises. For one of wrong knowledge, wrong liberation arises.

"Monks, knowledge (vijjā) is the precursor to the attainment of wholesome states; shame and dread (hiri-ottappa) follow it. Monks, for one who is wise and possessed of knowledge, right view arises. For one of right view, right intention arises. For one of right intention, right speech arises. For one of right speech, right action arises. For one of right action, right livelihood arises. For one of right livelihood, right effort arises. For one of right effort, right mindfulness arises. For one of right mindfulness, right concentration arises. For one of right concentration, right knowledge arises. For one of right knowledge, right liberation arises."

The fifth sutta.

## 6. Nijjara Sutta

106. "Monks, there are these ten bases for wearing away (nijjara). What ten? Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is worn away (effaced). And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right view as condition.

Monks, for one of right intention, wrong intention is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong intention as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right intention as condition.

Monks, for one of right speech, wrong speech is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong speech as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right speech as condition.

Monks, for one of right action, wrong action is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong action as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right action as condition."
431:
Monks, for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong livelihood as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right livelihood as condition.

Monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong effort as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right effort as condition.

Monks, for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong mindfulness as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right mindfulness as condition.

Monks, for one of right concentration, wrong concentration is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong concentration as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right concentration as condition.

Monks, for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong knowledge as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right knowledge as condition.

Monks, for one of right liberation, wrong liberation is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong liberation as condition are also worn away. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right liberation as condition. Monks, these are the ten bases for wearing away."

The sixth sutta.

## 7. Dhovana Sutta

107. "Monks, in the Southern districts, there is a ceremony called 'Washing' (dhovana). In that ceremony, there is rice, drink, snacks, food, things to be licked, things to be drunk, dancing, singing, and music. Monks, that ceremony exists; I do not say it does not. But, monks, that ceremony is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial."
432:
It is not the work of the Noble Ones; it is connected with what is not beneficial; it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to liberation (from craving), or to Nibbāna.

"Monks, I will teach the Noble Washing, which leads certainly to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to liberation (from craving), and to Nibbāna. By means of this washing, beings subject to birth are freed from birth; beings subject to aging are freed from aging; beings subject to death are freed from death; beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak."

"Yes, Bhante," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"And what, monks, is the Noble Washing, which leads certainly to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to liberation (from craving), and to Nibbāna; by means of which washing, beings subject to birth are freed from birth, beings subject to aging are freed from aging, beings subject to death are freed from death, and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?

"Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is washed away. And whatever various evil unwholesome states arise with wrong view as condition, those too are washed away for him. And with right view as condition, various wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.

"Monks, for one of right intention, wrong intention is washed away... [Pe] ...

"Monks, for one of right speech, wrong speech is washed away. Monks, for one of right action, wrong action is washed away. Monks, for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is washed away. Monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort is washed away. Monks, for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is washed away. Monks, for one of right concentration, wrong concentration is washed away. Monks, for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is washed away... [Pe] ..."
433:
"Monks, for one of right liberation, wrong liberation is washed away. And whatever various evil unwholesome states arise with wrong liberation as condition, those too are washed away for him. And with right liberation as condition, various wholesome states reach fulfillment by development. Monks, this is the Noble Washing which leads certainly to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to liberation (from craving), and to Nibbāna. By means of this washing, beings subject to birth are freed from birth; beings subject to aging are freed from aging; beings subject to death are freed from death; and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."

The seventh sutta.

## 8. Tikicchaka Sutta

108. "Monks, physicians give a purgative for the purpose of curing diseases originating from bile, for the purpose of curing diseases originating from phlegm, and for the purpose of curing diseases originating from wind. Monks, there is such a purgative; I do not say it does not exist. But, monks, that purgative sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails.

"But, monks, I will teach the Noble Purgative which expels faults, which only succeeds and never fails. By means of this purgative, beings subject to birth are freed from birth; beings subject to aging are freed from aging; beings subject to death are freed from death; and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Listen to those teachings, pay close attention, I will speak."

"Yes, Bhante," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught this Dhamma:

"And what, monks, is that Noble Purgative which only succeeds and never fails; by means of which purgative, beings subject to birth are freed from birth, beings subject to aging are freed from aging, beings subject to death are freed from death, and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair? Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is purged. And whatever various evil unwholesome states arise with wrong view as condition, those too are purged for him. And with right view as condition, various wholesome states reach fulfillment by development."
434:
“Monks, for one of right intention, wrong intention is purged... [p]... Monks, for one of right speech, wrong speech is purged. Monks, for one of right action, wrong action is purged. Monks, for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is purged. Monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort is purged. Monks, for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is purged. Monks, for one of right concentration, wrong concentration is purged. Monks, for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is purged... [p]...

“Monks, for one of right liberation, wrong liberation is purged. Many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong liberation as a condition are purged for him. And many wholesome states conditioned by right liberation reach fulfillment through development. Monks, this is the noble purgative. This purgative is always successful, never unsuccessful. By means of this purgative, beings subject to birth are freed from birth... [p]... beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Vamana Sutta

109. “Monks, physicians give an emetic to cure illnesses arising from bile, to cure illnesses arising from phlegm, and to cure illnesses arising from wind. Monks, there is such an emetic; I do not say it does not exist. But, monks, that emetic is sometimes successful and sometimes unsuccessful.

“But I, monks, will teach the noble emetic, which is always successful and never unsuccessful. By means of this emetic, beings subject to birth are freed from birth; beings subject to aging are freed from aging; beings subject to death are freed from death; beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Listen to that... [p]...

“And what, monks, is the noble emetic that is always successful and never unsuccessful, by means of which beings subject to birth are freed from birth... [p]... beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?”
435:
“Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is vomited up. Many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as a condition are vomited up for him. And many wholesome states conditioned by right view reach fulfillment through development. Monks, for one of right intention, wrong intention is vomited up... [p]...

“Monks, for one of right speech, wrong speech is vomited up. Monks, for one of right action, wrong action is vomited up. Monks, for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is vomited up.

“Monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort is vomited up. Monks, for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is vomited up. Monks, for one of right concentration, wrong concentration is vomited up. Monks, for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is vomited up... [p]...

“Monks, for one of right liberation, wrong liberation is vomited up. Many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong liberation as a condition are vomited up for him. And many wholesome states conditioned by right liberation reach fulfillment through development. Monks, this is the noble emetic. This noble emetic is always successful, never unsuccessful. By means of this emetic, beings subject to birth are freed from birth... [p]... are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Niddhamanīya Sutta

110. “Monks, there are these ten things to be expelled. What ten? Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is expelled. Many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as a condition are expelled for him. And many wholesome states conditioned by right view reach fulfillment through development. Monks, for one of right intention, wrong intention is expelled... [p]...

“Monks, for one of right speech, wrong speech is expelled. Monks, for one of right action, wrong action is expelled. Monks, for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is expelled. Monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort is expelled. Monks, for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is expelled. Monks, for one of right concentration, wrong concentration is expelled. Monks, for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is expelled... [p]...”
436:
Monks, for one who has right liberation, wrong liberation is expelled. Many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong liberation as a condition are expelled for him. And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right liberation as a condition. Monks, these are the ten things to be expelled.

The Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Pathama Asekha Sutta

111. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, that monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is said, 'An Asekha, an Asekha.' To what extent, venerable sir, is a monk an Asekha?"

"Here, monk, a monk is possessed of the right view of an Asekha, the right intention of an Asekha, the right speech of an Asekha, the right action of an Asekha, the right livelihood of an Asekha, the right effort of an Asekha, the right mindfulness of an Asekha, the right concentration of an Asekha, the right knowledge of an Asekha, and the right liberation of an Asekha. In this way, monk, a monk is an Asekha."

The Eleventh Sutta.

## 12. Dutiya Asekha Sutta

112. "Monks, there are these ten qualities of an Asekha. Which ten? The right view of an Asekha, the right intention of an Asekha, the right speech of an Asekha, the right action of an Asekha, the right livelihood of an Asekha, the right effort of an Asekha, the right mindfulness of an Asekha, the right concentration of an Asekha, the right knowledge of an Asekha, and the right liberation of an Asekha. Monks, these are the ten qualities of an Asekha."

The Twelfth Sutta.

The first chapter, the Samaṇasaññā Vagga, is finished.

Its summary:
Perception, factors of enlightenment, wrongness, seed, knowledge, wearing away, washing, medicine, vomiting, expelling, and two on the Asekha.
437:
The Twelfth Sutta.

The first chapter, the Samaṇasaññā Vagga, is finished.

## (12) 2. Paccorohaṇi Vagga

## 1. Pathama Adhamma Sutta

113. "Monks, non-Dhamma should be known and harm should be known; Dhamma should be known and benefit should be known. Having known non-Dhamma and harm, and having known Dhamma and benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit."

"And what, monks, is non-Dhamma and what is harm? Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation. This, monks, is called non-Dhamma and harm."

"And what, monks, is Dhamma and what is benefit? Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation. This, monks, is called Dhamma and benefit."

"'Monks, non-Dhamma should be known and harm should be known; Dhamma should be known and benefit should be known. Having known non-Dhamma and harm, and having known Dhamma and benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit.' What was said thus was said in reference to this."

The First Sutta.

## 2. Dutiya Adhamma Sutta

114. "Monks, non-Dhamma should be known and Dhamma should be known; harm should be known and benefit should be known. Having known non-Dhamma and Dhamma, and having known harm and benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit."

"And what, monks, is non-Dhamma, what is Dhamma, what is harm, and what is benefit?"

"Wrong view, monks, is non-Dhamma; right view is Dhamma. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as a condition—this is harm. And the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development with right view as a condition—this is benefit."
438: Bhikkhus, wrong intention is not the Dhamma; right intention is the Dhamma. And because of wrong intention, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of right intention, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit. Bhikkhus, wrong speech is not the Dhamma; right speech is the Dhamma. And because of wrong speech, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of right speech, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit. Bhikkhus, wrong action is not the Dhamma; right action is the Dhamma. And because of wrong action, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of right action, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit. Bhikkhus, wrong livelihood is not the Dhamma; right livelihood is the Dhamma. And because of wrong livelihood, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of right livelihood, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit. Bhikkhus, wrong effort is not the Dhamma; right effort is the Dhamma. And because of wrong effort, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of right effort, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit. Bhikkhus, wrong mindfulness is not the Dhamma; right mindfulness is the Dhamma. And because of wrong mindfulness, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of right mindfulness, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit. Bhikkhus, wrong concentration is not the Dhamma; right concentration is the Dhamma. And because of wrong concentration, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of right concentration, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit. Bhikkhus, wrong knowledge is not the Dhamma; right knowledge is the Dhamma. And because of wrong knowledge, many evil unwholesome states arise,
439:
This is harm. And because of right knowledge, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit.

Monks, wrong liberation is not the Dhamma; right liberation is the Dhamma. Because of wrong liberation, many evil, unwholesome states arise; this is harm. Because of right liberation, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit.

'Monks, what is not the Dhamma should be known, and what is the Dhamma should be known; what is harm should be known, and what is benefit should be known. Having known what is not the Dhamma and what is the Dhamma, having known what is harm and what is benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit.' What was said was said in reference to this.

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Third Adhamma Sutta

115. Monks, what is not the Dhamma should be known, and what is the Dhamma should be known; what is harm should be known, and what is benefit should be known. Having known what is not the Dhamma and what is the Dhamma, having known what is harm and what is benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, those monks thought: 'Friends, the Blessed One has given us this brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail: "Monks, what is not the Dhamma should be known, and what is the Dhamma should be known; what is harm should be known, and what is benefit should be known. Having known what is not the Dhamma and what is the Dhamma, having known what is harm and what is benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit."
