Who could explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One?'

Then those monks thought: 'This Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One. What if we approach Venerable Ānanda and ask him about this meaning? As Venerable Ānanda explains it to us, so we shall remember it.'
440:
Then those monks approached the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, they exchanged friendly and courteous greetings with the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting there, those monks said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One, having given a brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: 'What is not-Dhamma should be known... [and so on]... one should practice according to the benefit.'

Friend, not long after the Blessed One had left, we thought: 'Friends, the Blessed One has given this brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and left. Who could explain in detail the meaning of this summary given by the Blessed One?'

Friend, we then thought: 'This Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. The Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this summary given by the Blessed One. If we were to approach the Venerable Ānanda and ask him about this meaning, and if we were to remember it as the Venerable Ānanda explains it to us, that would be good for us.' May the Venerable Ānanda please explain it."

Friends, it is as if a man seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass by the root and the trunk of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, and think that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves. Even so is this completion (of the simile); you, venerable sirs, think that I should be asked about this meaning, bypassing the Blessed One when you were in his very presence. Friends, that Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become the Eye, become Knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of the meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata. You should have approached the Blessed One himself and asked him about this meaning.
441:
"You should remember it as the Blessed One explains it to you; this is the time for such asking and remembering."

"Certainly, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become the Eye, become Knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of the meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata. This would indeed be the time for us to approach the Blessed One and ask him about this meaning, and as the Blessed One explains it, so would we remember it. However, the Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. The Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this summary given by the Blessed One. May the Venerable Ānanda explain it without regarding it as a burden."

"In that case, friends, listen and pay close attention; I will speak."

"Yes, friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda said this:

"Friends, the Blessed One, having given a brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: 'Monks, what is not-Dhamma should be known, and what is Dhamma should be known; what is harmful (anattha) should be known, and what is beneficial (attha) should be known. Having known what is not-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having known what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit.' Friends, what is not-Dhamma? What is Dhamma? What is the harmful? What is the beneficial?

Friends, wrong view is not-Dhamma; right view is Dhamma. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise because of wrong view—this is the harmful. And the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development because of right view—"
442: This is the benefit. Friends, wrong intention is not the Dhamma; right intention is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong speech is not the Dhamma; right speech is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong action is not the Dhamma; right action is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong livelihood is not the Dhamma; right livelihood is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong effort is not the Dhamma; right effort is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong mindfulness is not the Dhamma; right mindfulness is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong concentration is not the Dhamma; right concentration is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong knowledge is not the Dhamma; right knowledge is the Dhamma. Friends, wrong liberation is not the Dhamma; right liberation is the Dhamma. Due to wrong liberation as a condition, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is the harm. Due to right liberation as a condition, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit. Friends, the Blessed One, having given this brief summary: 'Bhikkhus, the non-Dhamma should be known and the Dhamma should be known... [and so on]... one should practice accordingly,' rose from his seat and entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail. Friends, I understand the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, which was not explained in detail, in this way. If you wish, friends, you may approach the Blessed One himself and ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it. 'Yes, friend,' those bhikkhus replied. Rejoicing and appreciating the words of the Venerable Ānanda, they rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, the Blessed One, having given us this brief summary: "Bhikkhus, the non-Dhamma should be known... [and so on]... one should practice accordingly," rose from his seat and entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail. Venerable Sir, soon after the Blessed One had departed, it occurred to us: "Friends, the Blessed One, having given this brief summary... [and so on]... rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Who could explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, which was not explained in detail?"'
443:
"...what is the Dhamma should be known. [etc.] ...one should practice according to the benefit." Having given this brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. We then thought: "Who could explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One?" Venerable Sir, it then occurred to us: "This Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One. What if we approach Venerable Ānanda and ask him about this meaning? As Venerable Ānanda explains it to us, so we shall remember it." Venerable Sir, then we approached Venerable Ānanda and asked him about the meaning. Venerable Sir, Venerable Ānanda has well explained the meaning to us with these aspects, these terms, and these expressions.'

'It is well, monks, it is well! Monks, Ānanda is wise; monks, Ānanda has great wisdom. Monks, if you had approached me and asked about this meaning, I would have explained it in the same way that Ānanda has explained it. This is indeed its meaning, and so you should remember it.'

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Ajita Sutta

116. Then Ajita the wanderer approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Ajita the wanderer said to the Blessed One:

'Venerable Gotama, we have a companion in the holy life named Paṇḍita. He has thought of five hundred points of mental states, by which other sectarians, being refuted, realize they have been refuted.' Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, remember the "Paṇḍita-vatthu" (the grounds of being wise).' Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One would teach...
444:
"It is the time for this, Blessed One; it is the time for this, Sublime One, that the Blessed One should speak. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it."

"Then listen, monks, and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Here, monks, some person suppresses an unrighteous view with an unrighteous view, and with that, he delights an unrighteous assembly. Because of that, that unrighteous assembly makes a loud noise and a great shout: 'Oh, how wise! Oh, how wise!'

"Here again, monks, some person suppresses a righteous view with an unrighteous view, and with that, he delights an unrighteous assembly. Because of that, that unrighteous assembly makes a loud noise and a great shout: 'Oh, how wise! Oh, how wise!'

"Here again, monks, some person suppresses both a righteous view and an unrighteous view with an unrighteous view, and with that, he delights an unrighteous assembly. Because of that, that unrighteous assembly makes a loud noise and a great shout: 'Oh, how wise! Oh, how wise!'

"Monks, what is not-Dhamma should be known, and what is Dhamma should be known; what is harmful should be known, and what is beneficial should be known. Having known what is not-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having known what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit.

"And what, monks, is not-Dhamma, what is Dhamma, what is harmful, and what is beneficial? Monks, wrong view is not-Dhamma, right view is Dhamma. Many evil, unwholesome states that arise because of wrong view—this is harmful. Many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development because of right view—this is beneficial.

"Monks, wrong intention is not-Dhamma, right intention is Dhamma... Monks, wrong speech is not-Dhamma, right speech is Dhamma... Monks, wrong action is not-Dhamma, right action is Dhamma... Monks, wrong livelihood is not-Dhamma, right livelihood is Dhamma."
445:
Monks, wrong effort is not-Dhamma, right effort is Dhamma. Monks, wrong mindfulness is not-Dhamma, right mindfulness is Dhamma. Monks, wrong concentration is not-Dhamma, right concentration is Dhamma. Monks, wrong knowledge is not-Dhamma, right knowledge is Dhamma. Monks, wrong liberation is not-Dhamma, right liberation is Dhamma. Many evil, unwholesome states that arise because of wrong liberation—this is harmful. Many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development because of right liberation—this is beneficial.

"'Monks, what is not-Dhamma should be known, and what is Dhamma should be known; what is harmful should be known, and what is beneficial should be known. Having known what is not-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having known what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit.' This which was said, was said in reference to this."

The Fourth Discourse.

## 5. Saṅgārava Sutta

117. Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One and exchanged friendly and courteous greetings with him. After finishing the exchange of greetings, he sat down at one side. While sitting at one side, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, what is the hither shore, and what is the further shore?"

"Brahmin, wrong view is the hither shore, right view is the further shore. Wrong intention is the hither shore, right intention is the further shore. Wrong speech is the hither shore, right speech is the further shore. Wrong action is the hither shore, right action is the further shore. Wrong livelihood is the hither shore, right livelihood is the further shore. Wrong effort is the hither shore, right effort is the further shore. Wrong mindfulness is the hither shore, right mindfulness is the further shore. Wrong concentration is the hither shore, right concentration is the further shore. Wrong knowledge is the hither shore, right knowledge is the further shore. Wrong liberation is the hither shore, right liberation is the further shore. Brahmin, this is the hither shore, and this is the further shore."

"Few are those among humans,
Who reach the further shore;
The rest of the people,
Only run along the hither shore.

But those who practice according to the Dhamma,
In the well-expounded Dhamma,
Those people will cross over the realm of Death,
So difficult to cross, and reach the further shore.

A wise person should abandon the dark states,
And develop the bright states;"
446:
Focusing on the non-attachment (Nibbāna) from the place of attachment (Saṃsāra), in that seclusion which is hard to enjoy, one should seek great delight there, having abandoned sensual pleasures and being without possessions. The wise one should cleanse oneself from the defilements of the mind. Those whose minds are well-developed in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas), who, without clinging, delight in the relinquishment of grasping (Nibbāna), those with taints destroyed (khīṇāsavā) and of great radiance, have attained Parinibbāna in this world.

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Orimatīra Sutta

118. "Monks, I will teach you the near shore and the far shore. Listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: 

"Monks, what is the near shore and what is the far shore? Wrong view is the near shore, right view is the far shore... [and so on]... Wrong liberation is the near shore, right liberation is the far shore. Monks, this is the near shore, this is the far shore."

"Few are those among humans who reach the far shore (Nibbāna); the rest of these people only run along the near shore (self-identity view). But those who practice according to the Dhamma in the well-expounded Dhamma, those people will reach the far shore, having crossed the realm of Death (Saṃsāra) which is so difficult to cross. 

The wise one, having abandoned the dark (unwholesome) path, should develop the bright (wholesome) path. Focusing on the non-attachment (Nibbāna) from the place of attachment (Saṃsāra), in that seclusion which is hard to enjoy, one should seek great delight there, having abandoned sensual pleasures and being without possessions. The wise one should cleanse oneself from the defilements of the mind. Those whose minds are well-developed in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas), who, without clinging, delight in the relinquishment of grasping (Nibbāna), those with taints destroyed and of great radiance, have attained Parinibbāna in this world."

The Sixth Sutta.
447:
## 7. Paṭhama Paccorohaṇī Sutta

119. At that time, the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, having washed his head and bathed on that Uposatha day, wearing a pair of new linen clothes and holding a handful of wet kusa grass, stood at a certain place near the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, who had washed his head and bathed on that Uposatha day, wearing a pair of new linen clothes and holding a handful of wet kusa grass, standing at a certain place. Having seen him, He said to the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: "Brahmin, why have you washed your head and bathed on this Uposatha day, wearing a pair of new linen clothes and holding a handful of wet kusa grass, standing at a certain place? Brahmin, what is the occasion for the Brahmin community today?"

"Master Gotama, today is the day of the descent (Paccorohaṇī) for the Brahmin community."

"But Brahmin, in what way is the descent of the Brahmins performed?"

"Master Gotama, here, the Brahmins, having washed their heads and bathed on the Uposatha day, wearing a pair of new linen clothes, smear the ground with fresh cow dung, spread green kusa grass, and make their beds between the sand-mound and the fire chamber. That night, they rise three times and, with palms joined, they worship the fire, saying: 'We descend to you, Master; we descend to you, Master.' They also satiate the fire with plenty of ghee, oil, and fresh butter. When that night has passed, they satisfy the Brahmins with choice food and snacks. Master Gotama, in this way, the descent of the Brahmins is performed."

"Brahmin, the descent of the Brahmins is one thing, but the descent in the Noble One's Discipline (Ariya Vinaya) is another."

"Master Gotama, how is the descent in the Noble One's Discipline? It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma on how the descent is performed in the Noble One's Discipline."

"In that case, Brahmin, listen, pay close attention, I will speak."

"Yes, Master," the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
448: Brahmin, here a noble disciple reflects thus: 'The result of wrong view is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong view; he descends from wrong view. 'The result of wrong intention is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong intention; he descends from wrong intention. 'The result of wrong speech is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong speech; he descends from wrong speech. 'The result of wrong action is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong action; he descends from wrong action. 'The result of wrong livelihood is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong livelihood; he descends from wrong livelihood. 'The result of wrong effort is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong effort; he descends from wrong effort. 'The result of wrong mindfulness is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong mindfulness; he descends from wrong mindfulness. 'The result of wrong concentration is evil in both the present life and the future life.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong concentration; he descends from wrong concentration. 'The result of wrong knowledge is evil in both the present life and the future life,' he reflects.
449:
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong knowledge; he sheds wrong knowledge. He reflects: "The result of wrong liberation is evil, both in this present life and in the life to come." Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong liberation; he sheds wrong liberation. In this way, Brahmin, there is the shedding in the Noble One's discipline."

"Master Gotama, the shedding of the Brahmins is one thing, and the shedding in the Noble One's discipline is quite another. Master Gotama, the shedding of the Brahmins is not worth a sixteenth part of this shedding in the Noble One's discipline. Excellent, Master Gotama! ... Let Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The seventh sutta.

## 8. Dutiya Paccorohaṇī Sutta

120. "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Noble Shedding. Listen to that... And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Shedding? ## (17) 2. Jāṇussoṇi Vagga

## 1. Brāhmaṇapaccorohaṇī Sutta
167. At that time, the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, having washed his head and bathed on that Uposatha day, wearing a new pair of linen clothes and holding a handful of wet kusa grass, stood at a certain place not far from the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, who had washed his head and bathed on that Uposatha day, wearing a new pair of linen clothes and holding a handful of wet kusa grass, standing at a certain place. Having seen him, He said to the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: "Brahmin, why have you washed your head and bathed on this Uposatha day, wearing a new pair of linen clothes and holding a handful of wet kusa grass, standing at a certain place? Brahmin, what is the occasion for the Brahmin community today?"

"Master Gotama, today is the 'Descent' (Paccorohaṇī—the ritual of expelling evil) for the Brahmin community."

"But in what way, Brahmin, is the 'Descent' of the Brahmins performed?"

"Here, Master Gotama, on the Uposatha day, the Brahmins wash their heads and bathe, wear a new pair of linen clothes, smear the ground with fresh cow dung, spread green kusa grass, and make their beds between the sand-pile and the fire-hall. That night, they rise three times and, with joined palms, worship the fire, saying: 'We expel (evil) unto you, Master; we expel (evil) unto you, Master.' They also satiate the fire with much ghee, oil, and fresh butter. When the night has passed, they satisfy the Brahmins with choice food and drinks. In this way, Master Gotama, is the 'Descent' of the Brahmins performed."

"Brahmin, the 'Descent' of the Brahmins is one thing, but the 'Descent' in the Noble One's Discipline (Ariya Vinaya) is quite another." (Thus He said.)
460:
"Master Gotama, how is there the descent in the Discipline of the Noble One? I ask you, Master Gotama, please teach me the Dhamma on how there is the descent in the Discipline of the Noble One."

"In that case, Brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I will speak."

"Yes, sir," the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Here, Brahmin, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'The result of killing living beings is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons killing living beings; he descends from killing living beings.

'The result of taking what is not given is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons taking what is not given; he descends from taking what is not given.

'The result of sexual misconduct is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons sexual misconduct; he descends from sexual misconduct.

'The result of false speech is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons false speech; he descends from false speech.

'The result of slanderous speech is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons slanderous speech; he descends from slanderous speech.

'The result of harsh speech is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons harsh speech; he descends from harsh speech.

'The result of frivolous chatter is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons frivolous chatter; he descends from frivolous chatter. 'In this life and...
461:
...in the life to come, the result of covetousness (abhijjhā) is evil.' Having reflected thus, he abandons covetousness; he descends from covetousness. 'The result of ill will (byāpāda) is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons ill will; he descends from ill will. 'The result of wrong view is evil, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong view; he descends from wrong view. In this way, Brahmin, there is the descent in the Discipline of the Noble One."

"Master Gotama, the descent of the Brahmins is one thing, and the descent in the Discipline of the Noble One is another. Master Gotama, the descent of the Brahmins is not worth a sixteenth part of this descent in the Discipline of the Noble One. Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama regard me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

First Sutta.

## 2. Ariyapaccorohaṇī Sutta

168. "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the noble descent. Listen to it and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"And what, bhikkhus, is the noble descent? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'The result of killing living beings is evil and wicked, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons killing living beings; he descends from killing living beings. 'The result of taking what is not given is evil and wicked, both in this life and in the life to come.'

Having reflected thus, he abandons taking what is not given; he descends from taking what is not given."
462:
...The result of sexual misconduct is evil and bad. ... [He] casts off sexual misconduct. The result of false speech is evil and bad. ... [He] casts off false speech. The result of slanderous speech is evil. ... [He] casts off slanderous speech. The result of harsh speech is evil and bad. ... [He] casts off harsh speech. The result of idle chatter is evil and bad. ... [He] casts off idle chatter. The result of covetousness (abhijjhā) is evil and bad. ... [He] casts off covetousness. The result of ill will (byāpāda) is evil and bad. ... [He] casts off ill will. He reflects: 'The result of wrong view is evil and bad, both in this life and in the life to come.' Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong view; he casts off wrong view. Monks, this is called the Noble Casting Off.

Second Sutta.

## 3. Saṅgārava Sutta

169. Then the Brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One and exchanged friendly and courteous greetings with him. After concluding the greetings, he sat to one side. While sitting there, the Brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, what is the near shore, and what is the far shore?"

Brahmin, killing living beings is the near shore; abstaining from killing living beings is the far shore. Taking what is not given is the near shore; abstaining from taking what is not given is the far shore. Sexual misconduct is the near shore; abstaining from sexual misconduct is the far shore. False speech is the near shore; abstaining from false speech is the far shore. Slanderous speech is the near shore; abstaining from slanderous speech is the far shore. Harsh speech is the near shore; abstaining from harsh speech is the far shore. Idle chatter is the near shore; abstaining from idle chatter is the far shore. Covetousness (abhijjhā) is the near shore; non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) is the far shore. Ill will (byāpāda) is the near shore; non-ill will (abyāpāda) is the far shore. Wrong view is the near shore; right view is the far shore. Brahmin, this is the near shore, and this is the far shore.

Few are those among humans who reach the far shore (Nibbāna); the rest of this population only runs along the near shore (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
463:
Those who practice according to the Dhamma well-proclaimed, those people will cross the realm of Death (vaṭṭa) so hard to cross and reach the far shore (Nibbāna).

The wise person, having abandoned the dark states, should develop the bright states. Having gone from home to homelessness, in the seclusion where it is hard to find delight,

there he should seek delight, having abandoned sensual pleasures and having no impediments. The wise person should cleanse himself from the defilements of the mind.

Those whose minds are well-developed in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), who, without clinging, delight in the relinquishing of attachment, they, with taints destroyed and full of radiance, are fully extinguished (parinibbuta) in this world.

Third Sutta.

## 4. Orima Sutta

170. "Monks, I will teach you the near shore and the far shore. Listen to that... Monks, what is the near shore, and what is the far shore? Monks, killing living beings is the near shore; abstaining from killing living beings is the far shore. Taking what is not given is the near shore; abstaining from taking what is not given is the far shore. Sexual misconduct is the near shore; abstaining from sexual misconduct is the far shore. False speech is the near shore; abstaining from false speech is the far shore. Slanderous speech is the near shore; abstaining from slanderous speech is the far shore. Harsh speech is the near shore; abstaining from harsh speech is the far shore. Idle chatter is the near shore; abstaining from idle chatter is the far shore. Covetousness (abhijjhā) is the near shore; non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) is the far shore. Ill will (byāpāda) is the near shore; non-ill will (abyāpāda) is the far shore. Wrong view is the near shore; right view is the far shore. Monks, this is the near shore, and this is the far shore."

Few are those among humans who reach the far shore (Nibbāna); the rest of this population only runs along the near shore (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). Those who practice according to the Dhamma well-proclaimed, those people will cross the realm of Death (vaṭṭa) so hard to cross and reach the far shore (Nibbāna).
464:
The wise person, abandoning the dark states, should develop the bright. Having gone from home to homelessness, in seclusion where it is hard to find delight, there he should seek delight. Having abandoned sensual pleasures, possessing nothing, the wise person should cleanse himself from the defilements of the mind. Those whose minds are well-developed in the factors of enlightenment, who, without clinging, delight in the relinquishment of grasping, they, with taints destroyed and full of radiance, are fully extinguished in the world.

Fourth Sutta.

## 5-Paṭhama Adhamma Sutta

171. Bhikkhus, what is not Dhamma should be known, and what is not the goal should be known; Dhamma should be known, and the goal should be known. Having known what is not Dhamma and what is not the goal, and having known Dhamma and the goal, one should practice according to Dhamma and according to the goal. Bhikkhus, what is not Dhamma and what is not the goal? Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness (abhijjhā), ill will (byāpāda), and wrong view—this, bhikkhus, is called what is not Dhamma and what is not the goal.

Bhikkhus, what is Dhamma and what is the goal? Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter, non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), non-ill will (abyāpāda), and right view—this, bhikkhus, is called Dhamma and the goal. "Bhikkhus, what is not Dhamma should be known, and what is not the goal should be known; Dhamma should be known, and the goal should be known. Having known what is not Dhamma and what is not the goal, and having known Dhamma and the goal, one should practice according to Dhamma and according to the goal." It is in reference to this that this was said.

Fifth Sutta.

## 6-Dutiya Adhamma Sutta

172. Bhikkhus, what is not Dhamma should be known, and Dhamma should be known; what is not the goal should be known, and the goal should be known. Having known what is not Dhamma and Dhamma, and having known what is not the goal and the goal...
465: ...and what is benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Fortunate One (Sugata) rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.  Soon after the Blessed One had left, those bhikkhus thought: 'Friends, the Blessed One has entered his dwelling after giving this brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail: "Bhikkhus, what is not-Dhamma should be known, and what is Dhamma should be known; what is harm should be known, and what is benefit should be known. Having known what is not-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having known what is harm and what is benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit." Now, who could explain in detail the meaning of this summary given by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been explained in detail?'  Then those bhikkhus thought: 'This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this summary given by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been explained in detail. Suppose we approach Venerable Mahākaccāna and ask him about this meaning. As Venerable Mahākaccāna explains it to us, so shall we remember it.'  Then those bhikkhus approached Venerable Mahākaccāna and exchanged greetings with him. After exchanging friendly and polite greetings, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said to Venerable Mahākaccāna:  'Friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One has entered his dwelling after giving this brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail: "Bhikkhus, what is not-Dhamma should be known, and what is Dhamma should be known; what is harm should be known, and what is benefit should be known. Having known what is not-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having known what is harm and what is benefit, one should practice according to the Dhamma and according to the benefit."  Soon after the Blessed One had left, we thought: "Friends, the Blessed One has entered his dwelling... Who could explain in detail the meaning of this summary...?"  Friend, then we thought: "This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life..."'
466:
“Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this summary which the Blessed One has stated in brief but has not explained the meaning in detail. It would be good if we were to approach Venerable Mahākaccāna and ask him about this meaning. We will remember it just as Venerable Mahākaccāna explains it to us.” (They requested:) “May Venerable Mahākaccāna explain it.”

“Friends, it is as if a man seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass over the root and pass over the trunk of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, and think that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves. So it is with the venerable ones: though the Blessed One is present, you pass over the Blessed One and think that we should be asked about this meaning. Friends, that Blessed One knows what should be known, sees what should be seen; he has become the Eye, become Knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of the meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. That was the time when you should have approached the Blessed One himself and asked about this meaning. As the Blessed One explained it to you, so you should have remembered it.”

“Certainly, friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One knows what should be known, sees what should be seen; he has become the Eye, become Knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of the meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. That was indeed the time when we should have approached the Blessed One himself and asked about this meaning. As the Blessed One explained it to us, so we should have remembered it. However, Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by wise fellow-practitioners. Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this summary which the Blessed One has stated in brief but has not explained the meaning in detail. May Venerable Mahākaccāna explain it without making it a burden.” (Mahākaccāna replied:) “Friends, if that is so, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.”
467:
“Yes, friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Mahākaccāna. Then Venerable Mahākaccāna said this:

“Friends, as to that summary which the Blessed One stated in brief and, without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: ‘Monks, what is not-Dhamma should be known... (etc.) ...thus should you practice.’

“And what, friends, is not-Dhamma? What is Dhamma? What is harm? What is benefit? Friends, killing living beings is not-Dhamma. Abstaining from killing living beings is Dhamma. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise because of killing living beings—this is harm. And the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through cultivation because of abstaining from killing living beings—this is benefit.

“Friends, taking what is not given is not-Dhamma. Abstaining from taking what is not given is Dhamma. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise because of taking what is not given—this is harm. And the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through cultivation because of abstaining from taking what is not given—this is benefit.

“Friends, sexual misconduct is not-Dhamma. Abstaining from sexual misconduct is Dhamma. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise because of sexual misconduct—this is harm. And the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through cultivation because of abstaining from sexual misconduct—this is benefit.

“Friends, false speech is not-Dhamma. Abstaining from false speech is Dhamma. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise because of false speech—this is harm. And the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through cultivation because of abstaining from false speech—this is benefit.

“Friends, slanderous speech is not-Dhamma. Abstaining from slanderous speech is Dhamma. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise because of slanderous speech—this is harm.”
468:
Because of abstaining from slanderous speech, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.

Friends, harsh speech is non-Dhamma; abstaining from harsh speech is Dhamma. Because of harsh speech, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is the harm. Because of abstaining from harsh speech, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.

Friends, idle chatter is non-Dhamma; abstaining from idle chatter is Dhamma. Because of idle chatter, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is the harm. Because of abstaining from idle chatter, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.

Friends, covetousness (abhijjhā) is non-Dhamma; non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) is Dhamma. Because of covetousness, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is the harm. Because of non-covetousness, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.

Friends, ill will (byāpāda) is non-Dhamma; non-ill will (avyāpāda) is Dhamma. Because of ill will, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is the harm. Because of non-ill will, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.

Friends, wrong view is non-Dhamma; right view is Dhamma. Because of wrong view, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is the harm. Because of right view, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.

Friends, the Blessed One, having given this brief summary and without explaining its meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: "Monks, non-Dhamma should be known... [etc.] ...it should be practiced accordingly."
469:
Friends, I understand the meaning of this summary, which the Blessed One gave in brief without explaining its meaning in detail, in this way. If you wish, friends, you may approach the Blessed One himself and ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it.

"Yes, friend," those monks replied. Delighting and rejoicing in the Venerable Mahākaccāna’s words, they rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those monks said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One, having given a brief summary and without explaining its meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: 'Monks, non-Dhamma should be known... [etc.] ...it should be practiced accordingly.'

Venerable sir, soon after the Blessed One had left, we thought: 'Friends, the Blessed One has given this brief summary and without explaining its meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: "Monks, non-Dhamma should be known... [etc.] ...it should be practiced accordingly." Who could explain in detail the meaning of this summary given in brief by the Blessed One?'

Venerable sir, we then thought: 'This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this summary given in brief by the Blessed One. What if we were to approach Venerable Mahākaccāna and ask him about this matter? As Venerable Mahākaccāna explains it to us, so shall we remember it.'

Then, venerable sir, we approached Venerable Mahākaccāna and asked him about this matter. Venerable sir, the meaning was well explained to us by Venerable Mahākaccāna with these terms, these phrases, and these expressions."

"Sadhu, sadhu, monks! Mahākaccāna is wise, monks. Mahākaccāna has great wisdom, monks. If you had approached me and asked about this matter, I would have explained it in exactly the same way as Mahākaccāna has explained it. This is indeed its meaning, and so should you remember it."
470:
Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Third Adhamma Sutta

173. Monks, unrighteousness should be known, and righteousness should be known; harm should be known, and benefit should be known. Having known unrighteousness and righteousness, and having known harm and benefit, one should practice according to righteousness and according to benefit.

Monks, what is unrighteousness? What is righteousness? What is harm? What is benefit?

Monks, taking life is unrighteousness; abstaining from taking life is righteousness. And because of taking life as a cause, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. And because of abstaining from taking life as a cause, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit.

Monks, taking what is not given is unrighteousness; abstaining from taking what is not given is righteousness. Monks, sexual misconduct is unrighteousness; abstaining from sexual misconduct is righteousness. Monks, false speech is unrighteousness; abstaining from false speech is righteousness. Monks, divisive speech is unrighteousness; abstaining from divisive speech is righteousness. Monks, harsh speech is unrighteousness; abstaining from harsh speech is righteousness. Monks, idle chatter is unrighteousness; abstaining from idle chatter is righteousness. Monks, covetousness (abhijjhā) is unrighteousness; non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) is righteousness. Monks, ill will (byāpāda) is unrighteousness; non-ill will (abyāpāda) is righteousness. Monks, wrong view is unrighteousness; right view is righteousness. Because of wrong view as a cause, many evil unwholesome states arise; this is harm. Because of right view as a cause, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is benefit.

"Monks, unrighteousness should be known, and righteousness should be known; harm should be known, and benefit should be known. Having known unrighteousness and righteousness, and having known harm and benefit, one should practice according to righteousness and according to benefit"—it is in reference to this that this was said.

Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Kammanidāna Sutta

174. Monks, I declare that taking life is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion.
471:
Monks, I declare that taking what is not given is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Monks, I declare that sexual misconduct is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion.

Monks, I declare that false speech is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Monks, I declare that divisive speech is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Monks, I declare that harsh speech is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Monks, I declare that idle chatter is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Monks, I declare that covetousness (abhijjhā) is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Monks, I declare that ill will (byāpāda) is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion. Monks, I declare that wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is of three kinds: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion.

Thus, monks, greed is a cause for the origin of kamma; hatred is a cause for the origin of kamma; delusion is a cause for the origin of kamma. With the destruction of greed, the cause of kamma is destroyed; with the destruction of hatred, the cause of kamma is destroyed; with the destruction of delusion, the cause of kamma is destroyed.

Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Parikkamana Sutta

175. Monks, this Dhamma is with a way of avoiding; this Dhamma is not without a way of avoiding. And how, monks, is this Dhamma with a way of avoiding and not without a way of avoiding?

Monks, for one who habitually takes life, abstaining from taking life is the way of avoiding. Monks, for one who habitually takes what is not given, abstaining from taking what is not given is the way of avoiding. Monks, for one who habitually engages in sexual misconduct, abstaining from sexual misconduct is the way of avoiding. Monks, for one who habitually speaks falsely, abstaining from false speech is the way of avoiding.
472:
“Monks, for one who speaks slanderous speech, abstaining from slanderous speech is the way of avoidance. Monks, for one who speaks harsh speech, abstaining from harsh speech is the way of avoidance. Monks, for one who speaks idle chatter, abstaining from idle chatter is the way of avoidance. Monks, for one who is covetous, non-covetousness is the way of avoidance. Monks, for one who has a mind of ill will, non-ill will is the way of avoidance. Monks, for one who holds wrong view, right view is the way of avoidance. Monks, in this way, this Dhamma is with avoidance; this Dhamma is not without avoidance.”

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Cunda Sutta

176. Thus have I heard—At one time the Blessed One was staying at Pāvā in the mango grove of Cunda the smith’s son. Then Cunda the smith’s son approached the Blessed One, and after approaching, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to Cunda the smith’s son: “Cunda, whose purifications do you approve of?”

“Venerable Sir, the Brahmins of the Western lands—those who carry water-jugs, wear garlands of water-plants, tend the fire, and descend into the water—prescribe purifications. I approve of their purifications.”

“In what way, Cunda, do the Brahmins of the Western lands—those who carry water-jugs, wear garlands of water-plants, tend the fire, and descend into the water—prescribe purifications?”

“Venerable Sir, here the Brahmins of the Western lands—those who carry water-jugs, wear garlands of water-plants, tend the fire, and descend into the water—enjoin a disciple thus: ‘Come, good man, rising early from your bed, touch the earth. If you do not touch the earth, touch moist cow dung. If you do not touch moist cow dung, touch green grass. If you do not touch green grass, tend the fire. If you do not tend the fire, worship the sun with joined palms. If you do not worship the sun with joined palms, descend into the water for the third time in the evening.’ Venerable Sir, in this way the Brahmins of the Western lands—those who carry water-jugs, wear garlands of water-plants, tend the fire, and descend into the water—prescribe purifications.”
473:
“I approve of their purifications.”

“Cunda, the purification of the Brahmins of the Western lands—those who carry water-jugs, wear garlands of water-plants, tend the fire, and descend into the water—is one thing, but purification in the Discipline of the Noble One is quite another.”

“Venerable Sir, how is there purification in the Discipline of the Noble One? It would be good, Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma on how there is purification in the Discipline of the Noble One.”

“Then listen, Cunda, and pay close attention; I will speak.”

“Yes, Venerable Sir,” Cunda the smith’s son replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Cunda, there are three kinds of bodily impurity, four kinds of verbal impurity, and three kinds of mental impurity.

And how, Cunda, are there three kinds of bodily impurity? Here, Cunda, someone is one who takes life; he is cruel, bloody-handed, given to striking and killing, and merciless to living beings.

He is one who takes what is not given. He takes, with the intention of stealing, the wealth and property of others, whether in the village or in the forest, which has not been given to him.

He is one who engages in misconduct in sensual pleasures. He has sexual relations with such women as are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both mother and father, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by their fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, those who have a husband, those who are subject to punishment, and even those who are garlanded with a flower-ring in betrothal. In this way, Cunda, there are three kinds of bodily impurity.

And how, Cunda, are there four kinds of verbal impurity? Here, Cunda, someone is one who speaks falsehood. Having gone to a court, or to an assembly, or to the midst of relatives, or to the midst of a guild, or to the midst of the royal family, and being summoned as a witness and questioned: ‘Come, good man, tell what you know,’ if he does not know, he says, ‘I know,’ or...”
474:
If he knows, he says 'I do not know'; if he does not know, he says 'I know'; if he has not seen, he says 'I have seen'; if he has seen, he says 'I have not seen.' Thus, for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some material gain (āmisa), he consciously speaks a lie. He speaks divisive speech; what he has heard here he tells there to divide those people from these, or what he has heard there he tells here to divide these people from those. Thus he is one who divides those who are united, or one who encourages those who are divided. He delights in discord (vagga), rejoices in discord, finds pleasure in discord, and speaks words that create discord. He speaks harsh speech; such words as are rough, hard, bitter to others, offensive to others, bordering on anger, and not conducive to concentration—he speaks such words. He is a frivolous talker; he speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is not true, speaks what is useless, speaks what is not the Dhamma, speaks what is not the Vinaya. He speaks words that are not worth treasuring, at the wrong time, without reason, without limit, and not connected with the goal. Cunda, this is the fourfold impurity of speech.

And how, Cunda, is the threefold impurity of mind? Here, Cunda, someone is covetous. He covets the wealth and property of others, thinking: 'Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!' He has a mind of ill will and intentions of hate, thinking: 'May these beings be killed, or slaughtered, or annihilated, or destroyed, or may they not exist.' He has wrong view and a distorted perspective, thinking: 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously born beings; there are no recluses and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path, who are practicing rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make it known.' Cunda, this is the threefold impurity of mind.
475:
Cunda, these are the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha). Cunda, one who is possessed of these ten unwholesome courses of action, even if he rises early from his bed and touches the earth, he is still impure; even if he does not touch the earth, he is still impure. Even if he touches wet cow dung, he is still impure; even if he does not touch wet cow dung, he is still impure. Even if he touches green grass, he is still impure; even if he does not touch green grass, he is still impure. Even if he tends the fire, he is still impure; even if he does not tend the fire, he is still impure. Even if he worships the sun with joined palms, he is still impure; even if he does not worship the sun with joined palms, he is still impure. Even if he descends into the water for the third time in the evening, he is still impure; even if he does not descend into the water for the third time in the evening, he is still impure. For what reason? Cunda, these ten unwholesome courses of action are themselves impure and cause impurity. Cunda, because of being possessed of these ten unwholesome courses of action, hell (niraya) is manifested, the animal realm (tiracchānayoni) is manifested, the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) is manifested, or any other unhappy destinations (duggati) are manifested.

Cunda, there is a threefold purity of body, a fourfold purity of speech, and a threefold purity of mind. And how, Cunda, is the threefold purity of body? Here, Cunda, someone, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life; with the rod laid down, with the weapon laid down, he is conscientious and compassionate, dwelling with sympathy for the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he does not take by way of theft the property and possessions of others in the village or in the forest. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have intercourse with such women as are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by their mother and father...
476:
...protected by elder or younger brothers, protected by sisters, protected by relatives, protected by clan, protected by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, those who have a husband, those subject to punishment, and even those garlanded with a wreath [as a sign of betrothal]; he is one who does not have sexual relations with such women. Cunda, this is the threefold purity of body.

And how, Cunda, is the fourfold purity of speech? Here, Cunda, a certain person, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech. When summoned to an assembly, a congregation, among relatives, a guild, or a royal court, and questioned as a witness: 'Come, good man, tell what you know,' if he does not know, he says, 'I do not know'; if he knows, he says, 'I know'; if he has not seen, he says, 'I have not seen'; if he has seen, he says, 'I have seen.' Thus, he does not consciously speak a lie for his own sake, for the sake of others, or for the sake of some material gain or bribe.

Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech. He does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide these people from those, nor does he repeat to these people what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide those people from these. Thus, he reconciles those who are divided and encourages those who are united. He delights in concord, rejoices in concord, loves concord, and speaks words that create concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are blameless, pleasing to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, liked by many, and agreeable to many.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks what is Dhamma, speaks what is Vinaya. At the right time, he speaks words worth treasuring, accompanied by reasons, defined, and connected with the goal.
477:
Cunda, this is the fourfold purity of speech.

And how, Cunda, is the threefold purity of mind? Here, Cunda, a certain person is not covetous. He does not covet the wealth and property of others, thinking: 'Oh, may what belongs to others be mine!' He is one without a mind of ill will, with intentions free from hate, thinking: 'May these beings be free from enmity, free from anxiety, free from suffering, and may they maintain themselves in happiness.'

He has right view and a correct perspective: 'There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is [the result of] conduct towards mother, there is [the result of] conduct towards father; there are spontaneously reborn beings; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who proclaim this world and the other world after having realized them for themselves with direct knowledge.' Cunda, this is the threefold purity of mind.

Cunda, these are the ten wholesome courses of action. Cunda, one who is endowed with these ten wholesome courses of action, even if he touches the earth upon rising early from bed, he is pure; even if he does not touch the earth, he is pure. Even if he touches wet cow dung, he is pure; even if he does not touch wet cow dung, he is pure. Even if he touches green grass, he is pure; even if he does not touch green grass, he is pure.

Even if he tends the fire, he is pure; even if he does not tend the fire, he is pure. Even if he worships the sun with joined palms, he is pure; even if he does not worship the sun, he is pure. Even if he descends into the water for the third time in the evening, he is pure; even if he does not descend into the water, he is pure. Why is that? Cunda, these ten wholesome courses of action are themselves pure and are makers of purity.
478:
...they bring about purity. "Cunda, it is because of the fulfillment of these ten wholesome courses of action that the heavenly realms are manifested, the human realm is manifested, or any other happy destinations are manifested."

When this was said, Cunda the smith's son said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Bhante! [The Dhamma is] most pleasing. ... May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Jāṇussoṇi Sutta

177. Then the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One, and after exchanging pleasant and memorable greetings with the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. While seated at one side, the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said to the Blessed One:

"Master Gotama, we Brahmins give gifts and perform rites for the dead, saying: 'May this gift reach our deceased relatives and kinsmen; may our deceased relatives and kinsmen enjoy this gift.' We also prepare rice-offerings dedicated to the deceased. Master Gotama, does that gift reach the deceased relatives? Do those deceased relatives enjoy that gift?"

"Brahmin, it reaches in a possible place, but not in an impossible place."

"Master Gotama, what is a possible place and what is an impossible place?"

"Brahmin, here some person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, engages in frivolous chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill-will, and holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in hell. He subsists there on the food of hell-beings; he remains there on that food. Brahmin, this is an impossible place; for one situated in that hell, that gift does not reach.

Brahmin, here some person kills living beings... [as above] ...and holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the animal realm. He subsists there on the food of beings in the animal realm;"
479:
he remains there on that food. Brahmin, this too is an impossible place; for one situated in the animal realm, that gift does not reach.

Brahmin, here some person refrains from killing living beings, refrains from taking what is not given, refrains from sexual misconduct, refrains from speaking falsehood, refrains from malicious speech, refrains from harsh speech, refrains from frivolous chatter, is not covetous, has a mind without ill-will, and holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of humans. He subsists there on the food of humans; he remains there on that food. Brahmin, this too is an impossible place; for one situated in the human realm, that gift does not reach.

Brahmin, here some person refrains from killing living beings... [as above] ...and holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods. He subsists there on the food of the gods; he remains there on that food. Brahmin, this too is an impossible place; for one situated in the deva realm, that gift does not reach.

Brahmin, here some person kills living beings... [as above] ...and holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the realm of the departed (Pettivisaya). He subsists there on the food of beings in the realm of the departed; he remains there on that food. Or else, he subsists there on the gift offered by friends, companions, relatives, or kinsmen from here; he remains there on that gift. Brahmin, this is a possible place; for one situated in the realm of the departed, that gift reaches."

"Master Gotama, if that deceased relative has not been reborn in that place, who enjoys that gift?"

"Brahmin, other deceased relatives who have been reborn in that place enjoy that gift."

"Master Gotama, if that deceased relative has not been reborn in that place, and other deceased relatives have also not been reborn in that place, who enjoys that gift?"
480: "Brahmin, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that over such a long period of time that place would be devoid of departed kinsmen and relatives. Furthermore, Brahmin, the donor is not without fruit." "Does Master Gotama prescribe the fruit of giving even in a place where it is not possible?" "Brahmin, I do prescribe the fruit of giving even in a place where it is not possible. Here, Brahmin, some person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisive speech, speaks harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view. Yet, that person gives food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of elephants. In that elephant existence, he receives food, drink, garlands, and various ornaments. Brahmin, because he killed living beings, took what was not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisive speech, spoke harsh speech, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had a mind of ill will, and held wrong view in this life, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of elephants. However, because he gave food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins, he receives food, drink, garlands, and various ornaments in that elephant existence. Furthermore, Brahmin, here some person kills living beings... p... holds wrong view. He gives food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of horses... p... reborn in the company of cattle... p... reborn in the company of dogs. In that dog existence, he receives food, drink, garlands, and various ornaments. Brahmin, in this life, killing living beings... p..."
481: "...because of holding wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of dogs. Because he gave food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins, he receives food, drink, garlands, and various ornaments in that dog existence. Brahmin, here some person abstains from killing living beings... p... holds right view. He gives food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of humans. In that human existence, he receives the five human sensual pleasures. Brahmin, because he abstained from killing living beings... p... held right view in this life, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of humans. Because he gave food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins, he receives the five human sensual pleasures in that human existence. Brahmin, here some person abstains from killing living beings... p... holds right view. He gives food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of devas. In that deva existence, he receives the five divine sensual pleasures. Brahmin, because he abstained from killing living beings... p... held right view in this life, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of devas. Because he gave food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or Brahmins, he receives the five divine sensual pleasures in that deva existence. Furthermore, Brahmin, the donor is not without fruit." "It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is amazing, Master Gotama! Master Gotama, it is indeed proper to give gifts, it is proper to have faith, since..."
482:
"It is only right to perform the Kubbhī rice offering." (The Brahmin said). "So it is, Brahmin, so it is. Indeed, Brahmin, the donor is not without fruit." (The Buddha said).

"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts." (The Brahmin said).

Eleventh Sutta.

The second Jāṇussoṇi Vagga is finished.

## (21) 1. Karajakāya Vagga
## 1. Paṭhama Nirayasagga Sutta

211. "Monks, a person endowed with ten qualities is cast into hell as if carried there. What ten? Here, monks, a certain person takes life; he is cruel, bloody-handed, given to striking and killing, and merciless to all living beings.

He takes what is not given; he takes with the intent to steal the wealth and property of others, whether in a village or in a forest.

He engages in sexual misconduct; he has sexual relations with those women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both parents, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by their fellow Dhamma-practitioners, those who have a husband, those who are subject to punishment, and even those who are garlanded with a string of flowers [betrothed]; he commits such misconduct with these women.

He speaks falsehood; when he has gone to an assembly, a congregation, among relatives, among a guild, or into the presence of the royal family, and is summoned as a witness and asked: 'Come, good man, tell what you know,' not knowing, he says, 'I know,' or knowing, he says, 'I do not know'; not seeing, he says, 'I see,' or seeing, he says, 'I do not see.' Thus, for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of some material gain, he consciously speaks falsehood.

He speaks divisive speech; what he has heard here he tells there to divide those people, or what he has heard there he tells here to divide these people. Thus, he is a divider of those who are united, an encourager of those who are divided, one who delights in factions, enjoys factions, rejoices in factions, and speaks words that create factions.

He speaks harsh speech; he speaks such words as are rough, hard, bitter to others, offensive to others, bordering on anger, and not conducive to concentration. He speaks idle chatter;"
491:
He speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is not true, speaks what is useless, speaks what is contrary to the Dhamma, and speaks what is contrary to the Discipline. He speaks words that are not worth treasuring, at the wrong time, without reason, without limit, and unbeneficial. He is covetous. He covets the wealth and property of others, thinking, 'Oh, may what belongs to others be mine!' He has a mind of ill-will and intentions of hate, thinking, 'May these beings be killed, or slaughtered, or annihilated, or destroyed, or may they not exist.'

He has wrong view and a distorted perspective, thinking, 'There is no merit in giving, no merit in sacrifice, no merit in offerings. There is no fruit or result of good or bad deeds. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father [in terms of moral result]. There are no spontaneously reborn beings. There are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path, who practice rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world by their own direct knowledge, make it known.'

Bhikkhus, one possessed of these ten qualities is cast into hell as if carried there. Bhikkhus, one possessed of ten qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there. What ten? Here, bhikkhus, someone, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life. With rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious and kindly, he dwells compassionate toward all living beings. Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. He does not take by way of theft the wealth and property of others, whether in the village or in the forest. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct. He does not have sexual relations with those women protected by their mother... [etc.] ... even those adorned with a garland of flowers. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech. When summoned to a council, an assembly, a gathering of relatives, a guild, or a royal court, and questioned as a witness, 'Come, good man, tell what you know,' if he does not know, he says, 'I do not know'; if he knows, he says, 'I know'; if he has not seen, he says, 'I have not seen'; if he has seen, he says, 'I have seen.' Thus, he does not consciously speak a lie for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some material gain. Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech. What he has heard here, he does not repeat there to divide those people...
492:
...What he has heard there, he does not repeat here to divide these people. Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of unity for those who are united. He loves concord, delights in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks words that create concord. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks words that are blameless, pleasing to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, liked by many, and agreeable to many. Having abandoned frivolous talk, he abstains from frivolous talk. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks what is Dhamma, and speaks what is Discipline. He speaks words worth treasuring, at the right time, with reason, with limits, and connected with the goal. He is not covetous. He does not covet the wealth and property of others, thinking, 'Oh, may what belongs to others be mine!' He has a mind without ill-will and intentions of non-hate, thinking, 'May these beings be free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from suffering, and may they maintain themselves in happiness.'

He has right view and an undistorted perspective, thinking, 'There is merit in giving, merit in sacrifice, merit in offerings. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is this world, there is the other world. There is mother, there is father. There are spontaneously reborn beings. There are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path, who practice rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world by their own direct knowledge, make it known.' Bhikkhus, one possessed of these ten qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there.

The First Sutta.

## 2. Second Sutta on Hell and Heaven

212. Bhikkhus, one possessed of ten qualities is cast into hell as if carried there. What ten? Here, bhikkhus, someone is a destroyer of life; he is cruel, bloody-handed, given to killing and striking, and merciless to all living beings. He takes what is not given. He engages in sexual misconduct. He speaks falsehood. He speaks divisive speech. He speaks harsh speech. He engages in frivolous talk. He is covetous.
493:
He has a mind of ill-will. He has a distorted view: ‘There is no fruit in giving... [pe]... there are no ascetics and brahmins who, having realized for themselves by direct knowledge, proclaim this world and the other world.’ Bhikkhus, possessed of these ten qualities, one is cast into hell as if carried there.

Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, one is laid in heaven as if carried there. What ten? Here, bhikkhus, someone, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life; he has laid aside the rod and the weapon, is conscientious and compassionate, and dwells sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings.

Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech. Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter. He is uncovetous. He has a mind of good-will. He has right view and an undistorted vision: ‘There is what is given... [pe]... there are ascetics and brahmins who, having realized for themselves by direct knowledge, proclaim this world and the other world.’ Bhikkhus, possessed of these ten qualities, one is laid in heaven as if carried there.

The Second Sutta.

## 3-Mātugāmasutta

213. Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, a woman is cast into hell as if carried there. What ten? She destroys life... [pe]... she takes what is not given. She engages in sexual misconduct. She speaks falsely. She uses divisive speech. She uses harsh speech. She engages in idle chatter. She is covetous. She has a mind of ill-will. She has wrong view. Bhikkhus, possessed of these ten qualities, a woman is cast into hell as if carried there.

Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, a woman is laid in heaven as if carried there. What ten? She abstains from the destruction of life... [pe]... she abstains from taking what is not given. She abstains from sexual misconduct. She abstains from false speech.
494:
She abstains from divisive speech. She abstains from harsh speech. She abstains from idle chatter. She is uncovetous. She has a mind of good-will. She has right view. Bhikkhus, possessed of these ten qualities, a woman is laid in heaven as if carried there.

The Third Sutta.

## 4-Upāsikāsutta

214. Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, a female lay follower is cast into hell as if carried there. What ten? She destroys life... [pe]... she has wrong view. Bhikkhus, possessed of these ten qualities, a female lay follower is cast into hell as if carried there.

Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, a female lay follower is laid in heaven as if carried there. What ten? She abstains from the destruction of life... [pe]... she has right view. Bhikkhus, possessed of these ten qualities, a female lay follower is laid in heaven as if carried there.

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5-Visāradasutta

Bhikkhus, possessed of these ten qualities, a female lay follower dwells at home without confidence.

Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, a female lay follower dwells at home with confidence. What ten? She abstains from the destruction of life. She abstains from taking what is not given. She abstains from sexual misconduct. She abstains from false speech. She abstains from divisive speech. She abstains from harsh speech. She abstains from idle chatter. She is uncovetous.
